items.abstract: ABSTRACT Gossip is ubiquitous, yet morally troubling. Approximately 65% of human conversation involves evaluative talk about absent others, yet such talk often feels like backstabbing even when it causes no harm, violates no privacy, and consists entirely of truth. This article argues that gossip's distinctive wrong lies not in privacy violation, harm, or deception, but in something more fundamental which is the exclusion of targets from discourse about themselves. Building on this foundation, I develop three constraints on permissible gossip operating at different levels of moral analysis: participatory standing, purpose, and justice. These constraints together provide a framework for navigating gossip's complex moral terrain while respecting both the social value of information‐sharing and the dignity of those we discuss.
items.title: What Is Wrong with Gossip? An Exclusion‐Based Account

items.abstract: Abstract We respond to the comments by Imogen Dickie, Matthew Chrisman and Christine Tiefensee for a book symposium on our Reasoning with Attitude . Our commentators attempt to pull us further into either expressivism or into inferentialism. Here, we attempt to resist either pull and further establish our inferential expressivism as a home for both expressivists and inferentialists.
items.title: Replies to a fellow expressivist and two fellow inferentialists
Optimally tracking the truth: the ecological rationality of confirmation measures

items.abstract: Abstract Norms, rules, or standards require, recommend, or evaluate actions and attitudes. Claims about what agents have a reason to do or ought to do can be true according to or relative to standards. These statements will be familiar to anyone versed in recent work in metaethics and especially those interested in the debate over whether some standards are authoritatively as opposed to merely formally normative – i.e., the debate over whether some standards, like those of morality or prudence, ‘really’ or ‘genuinely’ tell agents what they have a reason to do or ought to do, while other standards, such as those which constitute certain conventional codes of behaviour, do not. But what are standards? And what is it for normative claims to be true or false according to standards? In this paper I raise a challenge for normative authority scepticism – the position that the idea that some standards are authoritatively normative is incoherent, confused, or otherwise defective – through an examination of these questions.
items.title: Standards and normative authority

items.abstract: Abstract AI ethics charters proliferate across the Arab world even as the same states deploy AI surveillance against domestic populations. The standard ethics-washing critique cannot diagnose this configuration because it was developed in democratic and corporate contexts and treats charter-implementation gaps as a single phenomenon. This paper introduces a Performative Authoritarianism Framework that draws the misfire and abuse distinction in Austin [1], pulls in the comparative-politics literature on authoritarian-upgrading, and operationalises the digital authoritarianism scholarship through a discursive scoping matrix. Five hypotheses are tested on the full N=22 cross-section of Arab League states using objective regulatory indicators, the AI Global Surveillance Index from Feldstein, fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis, and a pre-specified test against the developmental-lag alternative. All five are supported, subject to the qualifications stated below. Of seven procedurally complete states (national strategy plus dedicated body), zero have enacted binding AI law. International ethics alignment co-occurs with documented AI surveillance deployment across the corpus (Spearman rho = 0.73, p < 0.001); the association is capacity-laden and does not reach significance within the institutionally capable subset, so the co-occurrence is reported as descriptive rather than as evidence of a sincere-commitment failure. Charter content covers consumer-protection domains at mean 0.90 of full coverage and regime-critical surveillance domains at 0.05 (Wilcoxon paired p = 0.008); this scoping gap is shared with democratic instruments coded on the same rubric, so the feature distinctive to the authoritarian corpus is the joint configuration of consumer-scoped principles, documented deployment in the excluded domains, and the absence of a binding backstop. State capacity is the strongest among several broadly necessary conditions for AI governance quality (fsQCA consistency = 0.91, ahead of regulatory maturity at 0.89, with five further conditions between 0.80 and 0.86, a margin that small recalibrations reverse); the ordering is read against collinearity among capacity-related conditions and is not presented as identifying a single dispositive cause. The developmental-lag alternative is not supported within the present cross-section: years since strategy adoption shows no positive association with substantive completion (rho = − 0.045), and the United Arab Emirates has had nine years post-strategy without enacting binding AI law. Pre-specified ex ante criteria are stated for the cases of Egypt and Bahrain that may transition out of the abuse configuration in the next 36 months. The abuse reading is advanced as the best-supported account of this configuration against the developmental-lag and sincere-prioritisation alternatives, not as a demonstrated property of regime intentions, and the framework identifies the institutional conditions under which the configuration is generated.
items.title: Performative authoritarianism in AI ethics charter production: a configurational analysis of 22 Arab states
Governance and accountability in compassionate AI: a normative framework for responsible design

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Although much ink has been spilled in discussing the relationship between rationality and normative reasons on the one hand and normative reasons and reasoning on the other, surprisingly little has been said about whether we can understand rationality in terms of reasoning. I propose a novel way to understand structural rationality in terms of good reasoning. I argue that structural rationality is best understood in terms of adherence to what I label indefeasible good reasoning. I then offer the beginnings of a theory of substantive rationality in terms of defeasible reasoning. I show how this can provide a unified account of structural and substantive dimensions of rationality, and show that my view also gives the right verdict in some challenging cases for other prominent theories.
items.journal: Journal of the American Philosophical Association
items.title: Reasoning, Rationality, and (In)Coherence

items.abstract: Abstract This essay’s core claim is that EU tech law does not fully understand technology, since it does not account for its diverse negative impacts in the everyday lives of people in European societies. Placing a central focus on EU’s digital regulation, I argue that EU law mostly sees technologies as products that should circulate at an ever-greater rate and volume in the internal market, to the benefit of consumers. This market-driven vision justifies a light-touch risk-based approach that creates a compliance apparatus which does not force tech companies to change unjust or harmful aspects of their business models; instead securing and legitimising them. Using a critical social theory approach, I argue that much of technology’s meaning and impact on the everyday lives of people is missed by EU law’s current depoliticised and technocratic approach to tech regulation. Taking the tech stories of This is Europe as a starting point, I illustrate how EU law systematically neglects the harms caused by technology or through technology to many individuals and communities in their everyday lives. Those affected range far beyond consumers and tech users. They include, for example, delivery platform workers forced into extreme anxiety due to task volume and app surveillance; several minorities systematically targeted by online abuse; or the migrants exposed to tech-mediated degrading treatment in European border facilities. All in all, EU law does not fully see, and therefore, epistemically excludes these lived experiences of tech harm from the regulatory dialogue. This leads me to some concluding reflections centred around a fundamental questioning of EU tech law’s legitimacy. Particularly, I argue that a legal regime that does not recognise and is not responsive to the lived realities of harm of those which it regulates ultimately fails at a deeper, politico-moral level.
items.title: People: What EU law does not understand about tech

items.abstract: Abstract What is it that is transmitted across known entailment from justified premises? My main aim in this paper is to clarify and defend the unpopular view that transmission of justification should be conceived as transmission of a justifier, and the search for cases in which transmission of justification fails should focus its energy on cases in which justifiers fail to be transmitted. The idea will take some time to develop, and along the way I will argue inter alia against Crispin Wright’s well-known account that it is a subtle kind of epistemic circularity that prevents some deductive arguments from transmitting the justification of their premises to their conclusions.
items.title: When Justifiers Transmit

items.abstract: Abstract Lex specialis derogat legi generali , the principle that special law prevails over general law, is a well-established doctrine for resolving conflicts between legal norms. Yet its application in fundamental rights adjudication remains underexplored. This Article contributes to this global discourse by examining the increasing invocation of this principle in Hong Kong courts. It scrutinizes the deployment of the principle in landmark cases: resolving the tension between indigenous inhabitants’ rights and the right to equality in Kwok Cheuk Kin v. Director of Lands ; balancing freedom of marriage against equality in Sham Tsz Kit v. Secretary for Justice ; and, as advanced by the Government, justifying the exclusion of married same-sex couples from public housing and inheritance entitlements in The Hong Kong Housing Authority v. Infinger, Nick and Secretary for Justice v. Li Yik Ho . Through a comparative jurisprudential analysis, this Article argues that the application in Kwok Cheuk Kin was legally sound, whereas its use in Sham Tsz Kit was problematic. Furthermore, it contends that where different constitutional instruments provide varying levels of protection for human rights, absent a clear legislative intent to the contrary, courts should uphold the higher standard of rights protection rather than relying on the lex specialis principle.
items.title:
The Use and Misuse of the
                    Lex Specialis
                    Principle in Hong Kong’s Fundamental Rights Adjudication

items.abstract: Abstract Accusations of over-sensitivity are common, particularly when it comes to forms of systemic oppression such as racism and misogyny. I consider three things such over-sensitivity could plausibly be: a disposition to over-identify instances of these phenomena, the over-expansion of the relevant concepts, and a tendency to overreact to putative instances thereof. In each case, I find reasons why such worries are likely to be overblown. In the first, an agent’s supposed over-sensitivity to racism and misogyny is often simply sensitivity to phenomena which are routinely minimized; in other cases, her slight over-sensitivity nevertheless has value in a social environment in which under-sensitivity is a large and predictable problem. In the second case, the supposed over-expansion of the relevant concepts often corrects for their artificial narrowing, and makes us more sensitive to genuine harms and wrongs. In the third case, an agent’s supposed overreactions to racism and misogyny reflects an affective disposition that constitutes a valuable defense against the twin perils of gaslighting and numbness. I conclude by considering the possibility that there is a real strand of over-sensitivity to harms to dominant group members in the current discourse that illicitly serves their interests and functions to silence people facing oppression.
items.title: Sensitivity and Survival
Kathryn Sophia Belle , Beauvoir and Belle: A Black Feminist Critique of The Second Sex

items.abstract: Abstract The litigation brought by the Estate of Henrietta Lacks against Thermo Fisher Scientific, Ultragenyx Pharmaceutical, and Novartis Pharmaceuticals reframes benefit-sharing from voluntary institutional ethics into an enforceable legal duty. By pleading a single equitable claim — unjust enrichment — the Estate seeks to bypass the property and informed-consent doctrines that have defeated comparable tissue-appropriation suits, while accepting distinctive risks involving remoteness, limitations, causation, and apportionment. This commentary examines the strategy’s strengths and vulnerabilities through the still-pending Ultragenyx case, and considers its implications for research consent, prospective benefit-sharing frameworks, and bioethics pedagogy. Whether or not the remaining claim succeeds, the litigation has already altered the conversation about who should profit from human biological materials.
items.title: The Henrietta Lacks Case: Ongoing Litigation Seeks Closure

items.abstract: In his final published essay, which appeared in the New York Review of Books shortly after his death in 1997, Isaiah Berlin reflected on the major themes of his life’s work. 1 Under the heading “Pluralism,” he wrote that “there is a plurality of values which men can and do seek, and … these values differ.” He argued that a belief in pluralism enables people to understand why others might endorse values different from their own. He also stressed that a belief in pluralism does not make one a relativist: “I do not say ‘I like my coffee with milk and you like it without; I am in favor of kindness and you prefer concentration camps.’” Pluralism as Berlin understands it is a key premise of Respect and Loathing in American Democracy. 2 Like Berlin, Spinner-Halev and Theiss-Morse believe there are plural values that people might endorse, including plural values that are reasonable in the Rawlsian sense that one can hold them while respecting others who do not. Examples are liberal values, such as individual liberty and human rights, and democratic values, such as popular sovereignty and political equality.
items.title: Pluralism vs. Moralism

items.abstract: Abstract In the Congo Free State, where the administration of Leopold II concentrated on economic exploitation and largely neglected family law, Belgian missionaries assumed functions the state left unattended. This article examines how they became legal actors in the regulation of marriage between 1885 and 1908, imposing monogamy as a condition of Christian and civilized life against the widespread practice of polygamy. Officiating marriages, keeping civil registers, adjudicating disputes over dowry, and organizing Catholic villages where monogamous unions were institutionalized, missionaries operated as intermediaries between the colonial administration and Congolese communities, their authority resting at once on canon law and on the practical demands of governance. Drawing on missionary periodicals, correspondence, decrees, and administrative records, the study reconstructs a legal role that has received little scholarly attention, situating it within debates on legal pluralism and vernacular imperial constitutionalism that treat law as a fluid practice articulated by diverse actors rather than a fixed body of metropolitan rules. By placing missionaries at the center of colonial lawmaking, the article shows how religion and law were interwoven in the making of the colonial state, even as local communities resisted and reshaped the norms imposed upon them. In conclusion, this study reveals the complexities of missionary involvement in colonial governance and offers new insights into the intersection of law, religion, and colonialism in Central Africa.
items.title: Filling the Legal Void: Missionaries as Legal Actors in Regulating Monogamous Unions in the Congo Free State (1885–1908)

items.abstract: Abstract The court of the marshalsea, which originated in the late thirteenth century, exercised jurisdiction over a circular area of twelve miles’ radius centered on the king’s current residence. This article offers the first scholarly discussion of this mysterious court in the reign of Henry VIII. It begins by discussing the court’s criminal jurisdiction and its judicial procedure in felony cases, explaining the significance of a 1542 statute that expanded and clarified its jurisdiction over serious crimes committed within the palace precinct. The article then analyzes the court’s civil jurisdiction and suggests reasons why its officers may have been willing to stretch jurisdictional rules in cases of trespass. Next, the article discusses what is known about the personnel of the court, charting the rise of the under-steward of the marshalsea (referred to as steward from 1539) as its chief controlling officer. I show that by 1542, the court’s jurisdiction had become trifurcated into a plea side, an ordinary criminal side, and a “palace” criminal side. Reforms to the court in the reign of Henry VIII illustrate a general process of judicial regularization that occurred in the early sixteenth century. The regularization of legal institutions during Henry’s reign was a “reformation from within” that promised to be far less destructive than the “reformation from without” forced on the marshalsea and other legal institutions under the Stuarts.
items.title: Law and Justice in the Court of the Marshalsea of the King’s Household, 1509–1547
Samuel Fury Childs Daly, Soldier’s Paradise: Militarism in Africa after Empire. Durham and London: Duke University Press, 2024. Pp. xiii + 297. $28.95 paperback. (ISBN 978-1-4780-3083-6)

items.abstract: Prevailing approaches to the contractual enforceability of modifications revise or dispense with the requirement of consideration and invoke economic duress to rule out unfair, inequitable, or bad faith modifications. Enforceability turns effectively on the absence of economic duress. But economic duress is a doctrine of avoidance. It does not answer the contractually prior step of whether a modification satisfies the general requirements for contract formation. This article develops an alternative approach which satisfies the requirements for contract formation, most importantly consideration, while ensuring that only fair and reasonable modifications in ongoing transactions are thereby validated. It has been overlooked by current approaches starting from incorrect assumptions about the scope of the pre‐existing duty rule and failing to integrate decisions that provide definite grounds for enforcing even one‐sided modifications on a basis that does not conflict with the duty rule. There is no need to revise or dispense with consideration for modifications. Further, this analysis of contract formation addresses the concerns that have motivated courts to resort to economic duress. Being fully consonant with general principles of contract law and applicable to all modifications, the proposed approach provides a sounder and more complete framework for assessing their contractual enforceability.
items.title: Consideration Without Economic Duress: Reframing the Analysis of Contractual Modifications
On the Immunity of Hospitals in Gaza: A Response to Lucas
Critical Notice of Immortal Souls: A Treatise on Human Nature By EdwardFeser, Neunkirchen‐Seelscheid, Germany: Editiones Scholasticae, 2024. 548 pp. 29,90 €. ISBN: 978‐3‐86‐838605‐9

items.abstract: ABSTRACT This paper presents a new argument for robust realism, the view about normativity that Philip Stratton‐Lake held. The argument has three main premises: that we cannot believe an error theory about all normative judgements; that trying to endorse the best version of expressivism makes us believe robust realism; and that trying to endorse the best version of reductive realism also makes us believe robust realism. I argue that combining these premises with some additional premises yields a transcendental argument for robust realism.
items.title: A New Transcendental Argument for Robust Realism
What does AI health resource allocation make visible?

items.abstract: American voters, politicians, and media are increasingly hostile toward out-partisans and frequently disagree about the content of policies. This development raises an even more fundamental question about the nature of politics in highly polarized societies: Can the political actors even agree on what issues to disagree about, and why? To answer this critical question, we generate a massive new dataset covering communication by key actors from the last 2 months of the 2020 US Presidential election, including the presidential candidates (all tweets by Donald Trump and Joe Biden), the main news organizations (CNN and Fox News), and a large and original voter survey (N ~ 24,000) with daily representative data. Surprisingly, we find that the patterns of agenda setting in the 2020 election reduced rather than fueled agenda diversity and that the major political actors generally agreed on what the most important issues were in this otherwise polarized election.
items.title: Can they agree on what to disagree about? Patterns of issue agenda setting in the 2020 US presidential election

Book Review:
                    Democracy and Beauty: The Political Aesthetics of W.E.B. Du Bois
                    , by Robert Gooding-Williams Democracy and Beauty: The Political Aesthetics of W.E.B. Du Bois, by Gooding-WilliamsRobert, New York, NY: Columbia University Press, 2025, 272 pp.

items.abstract: A popular view on moral worth, antifetishism, states that an action motivated by concern for moral rightness represented as such is not praiseworthy. This can be seen if we appreciate that whether someone is a good person does not relate to whether they are a good moral theorist, as good people can misrepresent moral rightness and not be motivated by their mistaken grasp of it. But then what does an action need to be motivated by in order to be praiseworthy? I argue that antifetishism’s key insights give us reasons to reject the positive answers provided to this question by antifetishists themselves. The source of the antifetishist insight is much broader than originally thought: whether someone is a good person does not relate to whether they are a good theorist in general, as good people can misrepresent many kinds of facts. This makes the question of praiseworthy motivation difficult and also reveals that certain types of morally relevant descriptive ignorance do not excuse wrongdoing. As a solution, I suggest that an action is praiseworthy if motivated by a set of representations the intuitive moral import of which is unaffected by our potential theoretical mistakes: phenomenal representations of others’ lives.
items.journal: Journal of Ethics and Social Philosophy
items.title: Moral Motivation and Rich Representation

items.abstract: Interpretive frames guide how we interpret information. This article concerns the way in which our shared interpretive frames—such as metaphors, narratives, scripts, and stereotypes—may produce misunderstanding in ways that sustain injustice. I relate the role of frames to structural views of understanding in order to put forward an analysis of misinterpretive frames: frames that systematically produce misunderstanding. I contrast mere lack of understanding, whereby someone lacks apparent intelligibility, with cases of more substantive misunderstanding, whereby someone has a mistaken “sense” of understanding. I begin by introducing the structural view of understanding in order to present a structural characterization of misunderstanding. I highlight that frames guide how we structure information, and so distorting frames lead to misunderstanding. I highlight two ways in which possessing misinterpretive frames is distinctively epistemically pernicious: concealed incompetence and epistemic contamination. In the former, the mistaken sense of understanding conferred by grasping an inapt interpretive structure obstructs recognition of one’s own epistemic failures. In the latter, deploying a misinterpretive frame to interpret new evidence renders it misleading, polluting otherwise valuable epistemic resources. Finally, through an examination of naturalization and normalization, I show how these distorting frames may obscure and perpetuate injustice.
items.journal: Journal of Ethics and Social Philosophy
items.title: Misinterpretive Frames and Epistemic Contamination

items.abstract: The public ownership thesis is a Kantian-Rousseavian model of shared property. Its advocates argue that it is a superior model to those that can be derived from Lockeanism insofar as private property and common property cannot realize the distinct values that publicly owned property can. On this view, resources that are sites of shared activities must be owned by the public as a whole. I argue that the various values ascribed to public ownership can be realized by common property on the Lockean model, and the Lockean model is also better at dealing with the challenges of scarcity and disagreement that are central to questions of property rights.
items.journal: Journal of Ethics and Social Philosophy
items.title: Against the Public Ownership Conception of Shared Property

items.abstract: Our sense of self is distinctively social. It deeply matters to who we take ourselves to be that others recognize the claims we make on them and that we recognize the claims they make on us. Significant work on ideology and oppression characterizes how oppressive ideologies deny this kind of second-personal recognition. Yet not enough attention is given to the disturbing possibility that, even when successful, the personhood-constituting role of second-personal recognition can serve oppressive ideologies. Here I characterize such a mechanism. Some second-personal claims, I argue, are virulent. Their recognition co-opts their target’s agency as their success presupposes her own endorsement of her subordinated position with respect to the agent who issues these claims. At the same time, however, failure to recognize these claims deeply hurts the issuing agent, as their failure amounts to denying and rejecting a social standing that he deeply values. Crucially, this double binding profile of virulent claims illuminates a distinctive way in which ideology preserves itself—not only by shaping what we believe or what we do but also by shaping who we are.
items.journal: Journal of Ethics and Social Philosophy
items.title: Virulent Claims

items.abstract: Distinguishing between authoritative and formal normativity is a staple component in the metanormative literature. Norms such as morality and prudence count as genuinely or authoritatively normative, while those norms concocted on the spot are only formally normative. In this article, I question the common reliance on a monolithic divide between these two kinds of normativity. First, I argue that the same kind of skepticism that plagues the adjacent concept of an ought simpliciter applies equally to a definition of ‘authoritativeness’. Second, I point out the limits of primitivist responses to this challenge of developing a proper definition. Due to the abundance of intuitive differences between paradigmatic instances of authoritative and formal normativity, glossing at intuition is insufficient to demarcate authoritative normativity. Finally, I provide some motivation for abandoning the dualist orthodoxy and eschewing a monolithic understanding of the authoritative/formal divide in favor of a form of metanormative pluralism: there are multiple dimensions along which one might describe norms as being either authoritative or formal.
items.journal: Journal of Ethics and Social Philosophy
items.title: Revisiting the Authoritative/Formal Distinction

items.abstract: In “Freedom, Desire, and Necessity,” Pascal Brixel defends an “Aristotelian-Marxian” necessary condition for autonomous activity: “One does something freely … only if one does it for its own sake—that is, on account of its perceived intrinsic value—and not merely instrumentally”—that is, merely for the sake of some other end. Brixel argues that this necessary condition can vindicate and explain the common intuition that both volitional coercion and duress are enemies of freedom in that they both force their victims to act in such a way that they undermine their self-determination. In this discussion, I focus on volitional coercion, and I argue that Brixel’s proposed Aristotelian-Marxian necessary condition for autonomous activity is mistaken—a person can still count as acting freely even when they are acting merely instrumentally—and as a result, we need a different account of how it is that volitional coercion undermines a person’s freedom.
items.journal: Journal of Ethics and Social Philosophy
items.title: Coercion and Instrumental Necessity
Likelihood ratios and the dependence of clinical evidence: should individual LRs be taken at face value?

items.abstract: Abstract This study explores how parents seeking information about stem cell therapies (SCT) for autism spectrum disorder (ASD) understand and navigate a complex landscape of scientific uncertainty, commercial claims, and clinical advice. We conducted a quantitative content analysis of 54 enquiries submitted to the Stem Cells Australia website (2018–2023), alongside semi-structured interviews with 12 parents. Parents were highly engaged information-seekers, drawing on online sources, social media, other parents, and health professionals. However, they encountered inconsistent and often ambiguous guidance, particularly from clinicians, and reported difficulty assessing the credibility of competing claims. While many parents expressed scepticism about the efficacy of SCT, hope for improvement, fear of missing a critical intervention window, and positive accounts from other parents contributed to their ongoing interest. Risk perceptions were variable and often incomplete, particularly regarding procedural risks and long-term harms. Most participants had not pursued SCT, citing cost, uncertainty, and safety concerns. These findings highlight the need for clearer clinical guidance, improved risk communication, and stronger governance of unproven stem cell interventions to support families navigating ethically complex decisions.
items.title: “I was so Desperate”: Australasian Parents’ Expectations and Understandings of Stem Cell Therapy for Autism

items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) alignment is often framed as the problem of making a model reliably pursue human intentions or values. That work is indispensable, but deployed systems also raise a governance problem: who controls information, private context, correction, escalation, and action? This conceptual article proposes triarchic corrigibility as a role-separated governance design pattern for AI-assisted decision-making. The pattern combines (1) an embodied and answerable human, or an accountable human decision body; (2) a strictly isolated local AI layer for private contextual continuity; and (3) an externally connected AI layer for current public-world evidence. Final authorization of consequential action remains human, while epistemic and procedural competences are deliberately distributed so that no component can unilaterally control framing, memory, procedure, and execution. The article specifies a normative basis, trust-domain separation, decision rights, human-mediated data flows, reciprocal challenge, escalation, affected-party recourse, proportionate audit, and exit procedures. It distinguishes personal and organizational instantiations, compares the pattern with single-assistant, local-only, edge–cloud, multi-agent, human-in-the-loop, meaningful-human-control, and polycentric approaches, and provides criteria and rejection conditions for evaluating its value. It also advances an evolutionary-symbiotic hypothesis: repeated, bounded dependence on complementary roles may make correction and cooperative continuity preferable to unilateral control while preserving interruption, replacement, and exit. A worked case illustrates the protocol. The result is a testable governance hypothesis whose capacity to reduce correlated failure, preserve privacy and human judgment, and sustain correction under residual uncertainty requires empirical evaluation.
items.title: Triarchic corrigibility: a role-separated governance design pattern for AI-assisted decision-making

items.abstract: Abstract This study explores the potential of counterfactual explanations to assess artificial intelligence (AI) fairness, especially in critical decision-making systems. Predictive models may amplify biases inherent in data sets or algorithms, and given the absence of a universally accepted fairness metric, a case-specific approach becomes mandatory. Existing statistical fairness metrics may not capture all aspects that are relevant to a context-aware assessment of non-discrimination. The goal of this work is to define a measure of fairness for AI systems based on explainable artificial intelligence concepts. Specifically, it leverages the analysis of counterfactual explanations of individuals/groups and their comparison with similar individuals/groups. Compared to existing state-of-the-art works, the contributions are (i) extending the definition of individual fairness, not limiting unfairness to decisions based on sensitive attributes but also ensuring similar treatment amongst similar individuals; (ii) revisiting (and generalising) existing notions and introducing new, more refined notions of group fairness based on counterfactuals; (iii) defining quantitative fairness metrics that reflect the evidence gathered through the analysis/comparison of counterfactual explanations.
items.title: Individual and group fairness assessments via counterfactual explanations
Humanness not just a feature: AI, meaningful work, and the structural imperatives of flourishing
Trust, clarity, and contestability: an Islamic information ethics framework for public-sector AI

items.abstract: Abstract Judges often cite legal scholars. Sometimes they defer argumentatively to scholars as authorities. Such arguments, we claim, are neither sound nor legitimate. Legal scholarship serves two functions. One is modest and descriptive: reporting the undisputed content of legal sources and existing consensuses on some point of law. Such matters can lend themselves to authoritative settlement. But the core function of legal scholarship, involving the substantive reconstruction of suboptimal legal sources, is normative. And on such matters, we argue—by discussing the structure of arguments from authority and what counts as genuine authority—there is no room to treat scholarly pronouncements as authoritative.
items.title: When Are Arguments from Scholarly Legal Authority Legitimate?

items.abstract: Abstract Has there been a rise or fall in negative integration in the last 50 years? Three competing views on this question can today be distinguished. One asserts that there has been a decline of negative integration; another one argues that negative integration has, instead, risen; while a third view, finally, contends that there has been neither a fall nor a rise, because the normative degree of negative integration has remained stable over time. In the last five years, Jan Zglinski has published several provocative pieces that have come to defend a modified version of the declining-integration view. Negative integration, he claims, has become ever weaker over time due, mainly, to a judicial rise of political deference towards the Member States. Negative integration has thus assumed ‘a stronger national flavour’ and may even be coming to an end! Importantly and innovatively, Zglinski arrives at this result by means of an ‘empirical legal studies’ method; and this ELS-method aims to settle the debate. For an ardent defender of the second view on the evolution of the internal market and a devotee of an historical-conceptual approach to European Union law this poses a tricky question: did Zglinski’s ‘data’ really meet the ‘law’ better than all qualitative-doctrinal views that preceded him?
items.title: The end of negative integration? Critical thoughts on Zglinski (and the ELS movement)

items.abstract: Abstract In this article, I propose an expanded conceptualization of epistemic appropriation. I argue that epistemic appropriation can be either wrongful or non-wrongful, and that it can occur in all directions – from marginalized to dominant communities, but also from dominant to marginalized communities. Furthermore, I argue that epistemic appropriation can take place both inter- and intra-communally. Lastly, I argue that the epistemic resources that are appropriated do not have to originate in the community they are appropriated from to be considered appropriation, as this can also take place when a community has a stake in a certain use of these resources. In doing so, I come to the following, stripped-down, definition: epistemic appropriation is the uptake of epistemic resources that obscures something about the resources.
items.title: Expanding Epistemic Appropriation

items.abstract: Abstract Facing expanded criminal dockets, justice systems around the world are looking for ways to expedite proceedings and save resources while still offering credible procedures for adjudicating criminal cases. In the United States, defendants tend to face an all-or-nothing choice between two alternatives: a full trial at which all relevant evidence is presented and examined; or a plea bargain leading to a conviction without any presentation of evidence and the waiver of the defendant’s procedural rights in exchange for a reduced sentence. Even in routine misdemeanor cases, a full trial requires substantial expenditures of resources, and its procedural complexity may be out of proportion to the minor seriousness of such cases. Traditional plea bargaining, however, brings inordinate pressure to bear on defendants to plead guilty, often fails to elucidate the facts, and lacks sufficient guarantees of a fair outcome. In many jurisdictions, “intermediate” dispositions have developed, aimed at adjudicating cases both efficiently and fairly. We discuss solutions from Germany, Italy, and select U.S. states. They include bench trials and brief proceedings based on defendants’ acceptance of responsibility. After describing their scope and application, we argue that they can deliver efficiency without unduly compromising fairness, transparency, and just outcomes.
items.title: Negotiated Outcomes and Abbreviated Trials in Criminal Cases: Balancing Fairness and Efficiency in Three Legal Systems
From Consent to Sexual Agency and Back - “The Joy of Consent: A Philosophy of Good Sex” by Manon Garcia  (Harvard University Press, 2023)

items.abstract: Abstract As many care and relational ethicists have rightly contended, an ethical wrong and a form of social and political injustice occurs when genuine needs and legitimate wants for care go unfulfilled to a minimally satisfactory degree. Yet, as I argue here, injustice also occurs when groups and individuals are systematically prevented from fulfilling genuine needs and legitimate wants to care for those they love and as the subjects of their care genuinely need and legitimately want in turn. Being systematically and forcibly deprived of sufficient, meaningful opportunities to support the wellbeing of those one cares about is a form of cruel and degrading treatment unbecoming of a decent society and a grave injustice. At the same time that a radical practice of self-care demands critically scrutinizing one’s investments of care in an effort to undo those that are self-demeaning and that may themselves be the products of injustice and oppression, so too does it demand supporting the development and sufficient satisfaction of genuine needs and legitimate wants to care for others insofar as the satisfaction of these needs and wants can be just as vital to one’s own welfare as it is to that of those for whom one cares.
items.title: Radical Self-Care and the Need to Care for Others: On the Injustice of Being Denied Sufficient Opportunities to Care for Those One Loves

items.abstract: Abstract In response to an increase in state bans and restrictions of gender-affirming care, many states have enacted laws protecting patients and providers. This essay analyzes these protective state laws and offers recommendations to strengthen safeguards and ensure continued access to gender-affirming care nationwide.
items.title: Evaluating State Laws Protecting Access to Gender-Affirming Care: Considerations for Patients and Providers

items.abstract: Abstract Indigenous movements in Bolivia have long struggled for legal recognition and autonomy, culminating in constitutional reforms that formally recognise Indigenous jurisdiction as a key dimension of self-determination. This article argues, however, that the practical operation of legal pluralism in Bolivia is shaped less by constitutional design than by the institutional weakness of the Constitutional Court. Through analysis of the Zongo case, it examines how the Court’s pluralist rulings, while doctrinally affirming Indigenous jurisdiction and advancing intercultural and decolonial reasoning, remain ineffectively enforced, producing two interrelated consequences. First, Indigenous communities are continuously criminalised for actions undertaken within constitutionally recognised Indigenous jurisdiction. Second, criminalisation compels them to engage defensively with ordinary jurisdiction, generating juridification that destabilises collective authority. Together, these dynamics show how legal pluralism, when selectively enforced, operates in practice as neocolonial governance: Indigenous autonomy is formally affirmed yet subordinated by the persistent supremacy of ordinary legal power.
items.journal: International Journal of Law in Context
items.title: Destabilisation of Indigenous governance under neocolonial legal pluralism: the Zongo case in Bolivia
Power and powerlessness: the liberalism of fear in the twenty-first century
Lottery: friend or foe to democracy?

items.abstract: Abstract Alethic nihilism, as presented by Will Gamester and David Liggins, is the view that nothing is true. In a recent paper, we offered a “revenge problem” for a Gamester-style form of alethic nihilism. Gamester has replied to our paper in this Journal. He claims that generalizing on the reasoning that we employed in posing the revenge problem generates what he calls the Unacceptability Paradox. He attempts to solve this paradox and our revenge problem by introducing a distinction within unacceptability. In this paper, we show that, even employing this distinction, alethic nihilism still cannot resolve our revenge problem, which also calls into question Gamester’s response to the Unacceptability Paradox. We conclude by noting that alethic non-nihilists do not face the same problems.
items.title: The ‘Unacceptability’ of Alethic Nihilism

items.abstract: Citizens of democracies should live democratic lives and develop democratic habits. That is one of Mary Parker Follett’s core insights on democracy. A child of the Gilded Age, Follett experienced the erosion of communal relationships, the intensification of socio-economic inequalities, and the alienation of ordinary people from the complex political system that governed their lives. She saw democracy become remote and foreign to citizens who had little control over what happened to them. Her solution was simple: to reinject a dose of democracy into the everyday life of citizens. This paper retrieves Follett’s embodied and habitual vision of democracy for contemporary political theory. Follett claimed that citizens should participate actively in the democratic life of their society; however, she conceived of democratic participation as going beyond decision-making and deliberative activities. She thought that participation in simple forms of embodied joint actions, like recreation and collective chores, could also benefit democracy. Drawing from Follett, I argue that participation in a wide variety of embodied practices of collective action provides benefits to individuals and society by instilling democratic habits in citizens. Those habits incline those who develop them to enter and maintain relationships as free and equal peers with all sorts of people to reach common ends. When faced with collective problems, therefore, these individuals are more likely to choose democratic collective action and to do so more effectively.
items.title: A Habit-Building View of Democracy: Mary Parker Follett and Motor Activities
Generative Discourse Parsing for Indian Law

items.abstract: Abstract We examine the impact of CEOs’ inherited altruistic inclination on firm corporate social responsibility (CSR) performance and shareholder returns. Specifically, we look at U.S. CEOs’ altruism as an inherited value of the CEOs’ ancestral cultural origin that shapes their moral behavior and influences firm commitment to altruistic and genuine CSR. We find that firms led by CEOs with stronger inherited altruistic preferences have better CSR performance after controlling for firm financial and corporate governance attributes and other leadership characteristics. The impact of CEO inherited altruism on CSR is higher when CEOs operate under lower cash flow pressure. Consistent with a view of ethical leadership which protects the interests of both stakeholders and shareholders, we find that CEOs who inherit altruistic preferences are not significantly associated with firms’ stock returns under normal circumstances, while they protect shareholder returns during times of financial crisis and recessions. The results survive several robustness and endogeneity checks.
items.title: CEO Inherited Altruism, Firm Corporate Social Responsibility, and Shareholder Returns

items.abstract: Abstract Religious Education faces new ethical challenges as AI-powered chatbots become capable of offering scriptural explanations, moral guidance, and personalized learning support. This theoretical article proposes a Pastoral AI Ethics framework for the responsible use of AI chatbots in Religious Education. The framework integrates AI ethics principles, including privacy, transparency, fairness, and accountability, with pastoral values such as confidentiality, doctrinal fidelity, human dignity, and communal trust. The article also presents a conceptual design for a religious learning chatbot composed of a Theological Knowledge Base, a constrained reasoning and retrieval engine, and a Moodle Integration Layer. The proposed model includes privacy-by-design, citation transparency, theological review, and human-in-the-loop escalation for sensitive questions. The article argues that AI chatbots may support Religious Education by improving access to learning resources and feedback, but they must not replace teachers, clergy, or human pastoral care. Further empirical research is required before classroom implementation.
items.title: Pastoral AI ethics for chatbots in religious education

items.abstract: Abstract What is it to lead a life? This question prompts many others. In these brief comments, I focus on two issues: (1) How does leading a life relate to occupying the role of a spectator , where this includes being a spectator of one’s life? (2) What is it for a life to be one’s own , where one is justifiably partial toward anything that qualifies as such ? My reflections move from spectatorship to partiality and back. In so doing, they probe three conditions Samuel Scheffler plausibly claims to be key ingredients of leading a life: exercising one’s agency, being subject to the special claims of a very small number of human beings to whom one is personally attached, and being engaged with things one takes to be valuable. How close, I wonder, can one come to not satisfying any one of these conditions without ceasing to lead a life – and even a good life?
items.title: Some Questions About the Conditions Necessary for Leading a Life
Judgment, Latitude, and Kant’s Distinction between Perfect and Imperfect Duties
Philosophical Pessimism and the Heterogeneity of Suffering
Relational Inequality and the Social Uptake of Speech

items.abstract: Abstract In Relational Justice we lay out a new approach to understanding some of society’s most important building blocks, arguing that private law should, and to a significant degree already does, abide by the fundamental commitment to reciprocal respect for self-determination and substantive equality. The generous and rigorous book reviews of Aditi Bagchi, Marija Bartl, Brian Bix, Andrew Gold, Felipe Jiménez, and Joanna Langille push us to clarify and refine two critical points. First, the ambition of private law is primarily constructive and prospective. This means that relational justice is aimed at offering a broad loadstar that should guide legal systems across time and place; and it provides tools for internal legal critique, thus avoiding the risk of quietism which often plagues approaches that take law seriously (as we do). Second, relational justice is a liberal theory of private law, which is required by the commitments to freedom and equality, properly conceived. This thesis implies that relational justice is sharply contrasted with corrective justice (in all its variations); that its instantiation in private law is intrinsically valuable; that it incorporates built-in features which ensure that private law does not overreach any liberal boundary; and that it points to categories where elevated interpersonal responsibility is called for.
items.title: The Work and Values of Relational Justice
Clinical reasoning as a hermeneutic arc: teleology, narrative, and practical wisdom in patient care

items.abstract: Abstract In this paper, I develop and defend the concept epistemic assholes . An epistemic asshole is someone who exhibits a distinctive form of epistemic badness characterized not by gross irrationality or hostility to truth, but by a stable, entitled disregard for one’s epistemic relations with others. Drawing on Aaron James’s (2012) account of moral assholes, I examine how people can systematically exploit epistemic cooperation by allowing themselves special advantages—such as “freedom from inquiry”, “doxastic comfort”, and “freedom to criticize”—while remaining insulated from criticism by an entrenched sense of entitlement. The resulting view, the Relational Approach to Epistemic Assholes (REA), explains why epistemic assholes are not epistemically the worst, yet are nonetheless deeply galling. After motivating the need for this concept, I show how REA captures both “impure” cases (involving both epistemic and moral assholery) and “pure” epistemic assholes, whose objectionable conduct is driven by epistemic aims themselves. I further explore connections between epistemic assholes and epistemic vice, and the causal role that epistemic assholery can play in active ignorance and epistemic exploitation. Through this latter connection, I argue that epistemic assholes play an insidious causal role in sustaining objectionable social power dynamics. The concept of epistemic assholes provides a valuable lens for understanding important but often-hidden hazards in our social epistemic environment.
items.title: Epistemic assholes

items.abstract: Abstract As early as 1907, Einstein realized that the second-order transverse Doppler redshift reported by Stark in the spectral lines of fast-moving ions in canal rays could serve as a direct experimental test of time dilation. He rejected Stark’s dynamical explanation of the effect as a real frequency change of the moving ions. Instead, assuming that ions of the same kind emit the same spectral lines when at relative rest, Einstein offered a kinematical explanation of the frequency shift as a consequence of time dilation. He labeled the effect apparent , since the shifted line is not recorded by a spectrograph co-moving with the ion. At the same time, he regarded it as real , in the sense that it would not occur if the old kinematics held, and is thus empirically testable. From the 1920s onward, Einstein argued that the behavior of atomic clocks calls for a dynamical explanation. The present paper shows, however, that even if a special relativistic explanation of the spectral identity of atoms were available, it would merely reinforce the claim that relativistic time dilation admits a purely kinematical interpretation. It concludes that modern dynamicists misread Einstein’s plea for a dynamical account of clock behavior as a demand for an explanation of time dilation, whereas it was primarily motivated by the problem of its confirmation .
items.title: Is time dilation ‘real’? Einstein and the transverse Doppler effect

items.abstract: Abstract The Argument from Inductive Risk (AIR) explicitly calls for the consideration of non-epistemic values whenever significant non-epistemic consequences, usually understood as harms towards individuals, groups or society at large, are foreseeable. In current philosophical literature, the AIR is often assumed to have limited relevance to fundamental research, particularly in fields like particle physics which has received little attention. This paper aims to address this gap by developing experimental particle physics as a problem case for standard formulations of the AIR. I argue that, although errors in particle physics do not consistently give rise to direct socio-ethical consequences of the kind emphasized in the literature, the field nevertheless involves significant forms of epistemic responsibility arising from its technological embeddedness and broader social entanglements. Moreover, I show that the scope of the AIR depends crucially on how risk is conceptualized. While a strictly decision-theoretic framework tends to exclude particle physics by narrowing the notion of risk, alternative approaches from the ethics of technology help capture indirect and uncertain consequences. The paper therefore argues for further refinement of the AIR, rather than its simple extension, and calls for a more explicit and pluralistic account of risk in the assessment of values in science.
items.title: Where’s the harm? On the argument from inductive risk in particle physics
The problem of identity in ecosystem evolution: an ascendency-based approach

items.abstract: Abstract Slurs can be used and misused in different ways. We examine two related misapplications. Sometimes a speaker mistakes the person they are slurring as being correctly targeted by a slur. Other times, a speaker is indifferent to whether the slur correctly applies at all. We argue that this latter case constitutes a bullshit slur . Such slurs are distinctively troubling. From the speaker’s perspective, indifference to a slur’s conventional application widens the subordinating force of their utterance, directly threatening their target’s equal standing and warranting greater offence than cases of mistaken identity. From the hearer’s perspective, bullshit slurs foreclose a crucial form of counterspeech: self-protection via linguistic correction. This leaves the target in a particularly precarious position: subordinated directly and unable to engage in self-protective counterspeech.
items.title: Bullshit slurs

items.abstract: Abstract Recent empirical research on folk moral objectivism appears to bring nothing but bad news for traditional metaethics. Experimental philosophers and psychologists claim that their findings are incompatible with traditional metaethical theories and therefore provide reasons for developing non-traditional metaethical theories. In this paper, I argue that many traditional metaethical theories have the resources to show that they are not inconsistent with the findings of disagreement task studies. If this is correct, then these findings do not, by themselves, settle the choice between traditional and non-traditional metaethical theories. I then sketch how further empirical research might help distinguish between these competing theories. Finally, by distinguishing five different understandings of moral objectivity and explaining how they matter for traditional metaethics, I show that the significance of existing empirical findings depends on the relevant sense of objectivity and suggest what future research on folk moral objectivism should take into account.
items.title: Reconsidering the challenge to traditional metaethics from empirical research on folk moral objectivism

items.abstract: Abstract Deep scientific realism is scientific realism plus the claim that science requires a metaphysical interpretation. Metaphysics is supposed to fill an intelligibility gap: science by itself, it is argued, does not provide a clear image of reality. The metaphysics needed to deliver the goods comes from a toolbox of concepts furnished by free range metaphysics. Such concepts are developed in connection with a world that is familiar to us, and by being applied to science, they carry this familiarity to the most unfamiliar confines of reality. This article examines the prospects of such a strategy. Focusing on the case of quantum objects’ (non-)individuality, it argues that deep realism fails to deliver the promised intelligibility. Construing quantum entities as non-individuals faces an empty toolbox, ‘non-individuality’ being too closely attached to quantum mechanics itself. Dressing quantum entities as individuals distorts the usual familiarity brought by the concept of individuality, since it now has to conform to the unusual demands of quantum mechanics to the point of being unrecognizable. Instead of enhancing our grasp of quantum reality, the imposition of metaphysical categories risks producing not understanding, but metaphysical misunderstanding.
items.title: Understanding metaphysical misunderstanding: (non-)individuals and the metaphysical nature of quantum objects
Between controlled and uncontrolled hallucination: the spectrum of psychosis within the framework of predictive processing

items.abstract: Abstract The existence of middle-sized systems in the universe is far from accidental; it carries significant consequences for our understanding of both physics and metaphysics, bearing on the epistemic assumptions of the former and the role of causality in the latter. By examining how science actually engages with individual systems, we expose the weaknesses of the principle of physical causal closure and make the case for a pluralistic account of causality in the spirit of neo-Aristotelian philosophy. We explicitly argue for replacing the classical hylomorphic narrative with a morpho-efficient view better attuned to our current scientific understanding. This renewed articulation of Aristotelian causes proves consonant with the existence of a principle of individuation for middle-sized things, as well as with the novelty, continuity, and precariousness that characterize individual systems in nature.
items.title: New is Different: What Middle-Sized Things Teach about Causation
Prospects for Dyslexic Students: A Right to Visual Modes of Learning?

items.abstract: Abstract Psychedelic-assisted therapy (PAT) is increasingly used for trauma-related disorders, raising ethical questions beyond client safety. We argue that PAT clients have epistemic needs and clinicians have corresponding obligations that call for epistemic humility and discipline, which are essential for regulating foreseeable epistemic risks and for PAT's ethical structure. Drawing on threads of epistemic vulnerability theory, memory research, and emerging empirical evidence on the cognitive and relational effects of psychedelics, we argue that phenomenological characteristics, including noetic quality, are unreliable indicators of historical veridicality and are associated with epistemic risks. Focusing on individual differences associated with attachment patterns and work with sexual abuse survivors, we show how disrupted epistemic trust, authority sensitivity, and structural disempowerment may magnify those epistemic risks. We then develop epistemic discipline as a fiduciary stance that requires restraint in both directions: neither endorsing experiential material as historically veridical when this cannot be established, nor introducing unwarranted doubt that undermines epistemic agency. Because such epistemic vulnerability and its associated risks are foreseeable, if not entirely predictable, we frame epistemic discipline as a fiduciary obligation of the clinician that spans preparation, dosing, and integration, as well as obligations of training programs, credentialing bodies, and professional communities with responsibility to identify and remedy relevant omissions in training and supervision. Finally, we systematize features of epistemic vulnerability and governance mechanisms across PAT phases.
items.title: Epistemic Discipline in Psychedelic-Assisted Therapy: Memory, Therapy Dynamics, Attachment Patterns, and Sexual Abuse
Navigating academic integrity in the Era of generative AI: a systematic literature review

items.abstract: ABSTRACT This article proposes a novel way to understand the oppression of ableism through the modal device of counterfactual bodies. I begin with an overview of counterfactual bodies, defined here as the reimagining of disabled individuals without their disability. Some counterfactual bodies become vehicles of oppression when distorted by the imperative of cure, under which striving to actualize a counterfactual body becomes a morally laden aim for disabled bodies. Next, I outline some of the material, psychological and physical costs of striving to actualize a counterfactual body, which includes the disproportionate distribution of resources, suspended body grief, and pain and suffering. Finally, I consider the conditions under which a counterfactual body becomes a manifestation of ableism.
items.journal: Journal of the American Philosophical Association
items.title:
Counterfactual Bodies, Ableism, and Oppression as
                    Possibilia

items.abstract: Abstract The American Psychiatric Association is now designing the process that will produce the next iteration of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM). Recent work on epistemic injustice in psychiatry converges on a shared diagnosis. The exclusion of psychopathologized perspectives undermines the social objectivity of psychiatric classification, and the literature leaves open how psychiatric science can engage with alternative interpretations of its domain without reducing them to the dominant framework. I propose four institutional conditions that inclusion must satisfy if it is to produce epistemic engagement and avoid tokenism. They are constitutive participation in agenda-setting and evidence evaluation, structural reproduction of participatory mechanisms across revision cycles, procedurally differentiated translation interfaces that preserve the critical content of non-standard perspectives, and bidirectional uptake with epistemic attitude and documented accountability. The conditions operate on the epistemic process that produces diagnostic categories without modifying the operational form those categories take, and are compatible with the functional requirements of the DSM and with the professional identity of psychiatry. They are designed to make inclusion structurally reproducible, where it has so far been contingently achievable, and they supply evaluative criteria for the design decisions the revision now confronts.
items.title: The Epistemic Floor: Institutional Conditions for Genuine Inclusion in Psychiatric Classification

items.abstract: Abstract This Article examines the persistent gaps in the protection of trans and non–binary people against discrimination in European Union law, situating its analysis within a broader socio–legal context marked by rising anti–gender rhetoric and uneven national safeguards. Drawing on recent empirical data, including the 2023 FRA LGBTIQ Survey, it highlights the disproportionate levels of discrimination, violence, and harassment experienced by trans and non–binary individuals across the EU, as well as the growing political hostility that shapes their lived realities. Against this backdrop, the Article assesses the current EU legal framework—primary law, the Charter of Fundamental Rights, and secondary legislation—and demonstrates that explicit protection on the grounds of gender identity and gender expression remains absent. It then analyzes the evolving case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union, which has gradually interpreted the prohibition of sex discrimination as extending to certain forms of discrimination against trans persons, while still leaving significant blind spots, particularly for non–binary individuals. Building on recent jurisprudential developments, the Article explores the potential for a more inclusive and expansive reading of “sex” within EU equality law, arguing that such an approach could provide robust protection for all individuals facing discrimination based on gender identity or expression. Finally, it addresses the complex normative and doctrinal challenges that arise when balancing the interests of cisgender women with those of trans and non–binary people under the umbrella of sex–based equality. Positioned within a human–rights–oriented and social–justice–driven framework, the Article ultimately calls for renewed legal and political commitment to ensuring that EU equality law effectively safeguards the rights of trans and non–binary individuals.
items.title: Protecting (Trans and) Non-Binary People Against Discrimination in and Through EU Law: Time to Overcome Blind Spots

items.abstract: Abstract Sometimes it seems that no matter how faultlessly we conduct ourselves, we cannot but fail in our obligations, making us apt to feel morally responsible. But according to the popular view I call ‘moralism’ about obligation, we cannot breach our obligations faultlessly, leading moralists to pathologize our feelings, or worse still, to find fault in our conduct. I argue that we should reject moralism, but that we should not do so in the ‘hard’ way, which denies the plausible claim that blameworthiness entails fault. Yet we cannot ‘soften’ our anti-moralism unless we can explain how ordinary agent-regret can rise to a ‘moral’ quality sufficient to do justice to the phenomenology. I offer the outline of a proposal according to which a failure to meet our obligations gives rise to agent-regret with the following ‘moral’ quality: it is extraordinarily hard to let go of or justifiably repress it.
items.title: How to Avoid ‘Moralism’ about Obligation

items.abstract: Abstract Is the metaphysical structure of the world familiar or alien? That is, can the structure of the world be presented using familiar linguistic resources, or would that require radically new, alien resources? Eklund has recently argued for the epistemic possibility of alien structure. My aim in this paper is to argue against that possibility.
items.title: Against alien structure

items.abstract: This article examines the doctrine of state necessity as a distinct but relatively underexplored doctrine of constitutional law. Drawing on case law from a range of jurisdictions, it considers instances in which courts have accepted otherwise unconstitutional measures as lawful in order to preserve the operation of state institutions or protect significant parts of the legal order. The article reconstructs the doctrine as a limited, temporary and conditional remedy for situations of constitutional paralysis or systemic legal invalidity. It argues that state necessity should be distinguished both from other cases of emergency law and from a general ‘doctrine of necessity’. The article questions the central theoretical grounds that are offered in the case law and literature in support of the doctrine, such as those based on special executive powers, on analogies with the necessity defence, or on a broader supra‐constitutional ‘law of necessity’. It argues that the doctrine should be understood as a doctrine of constitutional law shaped within the tradition of equity. On that account, the doctrine functions as a limited corrective in exceptional cases of constitutional deadlock in order to preserve the legal order without displacing the constitution itself.
items.title: The Doctrine of State Necessity

items.abstract: ABSTRACT This paper argues against the secret ballot on the basis of a view of democracy where voters are mutually accountable to one another for their electoral choices. In contrast to Mill's and more recent arguments for opening up the ballot which have a broadly consequentialist nature, this paper offers an principle argument. First it suggests that the egalitarian defence of democracy could be supplemented by augmenting what the egalitarian relationship between citizens consists in. It argues for a ‘substantive egalitarian’ view of democracy where citizens cast their vote on the basis of the values and ideals they support, delegating the role of legislating on their bases to representatives. Each citizen is both an agent, qua co‐author of the ideals underlying state action, and a subject, qua her status as an individual affected by legislation grounded in those ideals. On that basis I argue that citizens' egalitarian political relationship is one of mutual horizontally accountability. The ideal of accountability implies that voters have a legal obligation to publicise their identities and a civic obligation to respond to one another's requests for the reasons for their votes. Only through presenting themselves to each other in this way can citizens as co‐authors properly assume responsibility for their role in providing the normative bases of law. The paper concludes by addressing objections to open voting, specifically that it is unfeasible because it would encourage corruption, and depress turnout and lead to civic shame.
items.title: In Defence of Open Voting

items.abstract: Edmund Burke’s thoughts on plantation slavery have long been the subject of scholarly attention. Too often, however, discerning Burke’s long-term intention in relation to slavery has taken precedence over examining the specific administrative strategies he proposed for managing enslaved populations in the interim. Seeking to remedy this gap, the article reads Burke’s Sketch for a Negro Code as an exercise in colonial ameliorationism; that is, a reform programme that looked to ameliorate the institution of slavery as a way of strengthening British colonialism in the West Indies and civilising the African coast. Using colonial ameliorationism as an interpretive lens, I argue, allows us to reconstruct a consistent Burkean vision for colonial management in the West Indies, one that survived his vacillations on the question of abolition. It also throws into doubt the common argument that Burke saw imperial governance in negative terms; a matter of taming abuses of power and exercising restraint. In the West Indies, by contrast, Burke’s commitment to ameliorationism led him to embrace a productive form of colonial power aimed at enhancing the physical and mental capacities of the enslaved population through discipline, religious instruction, and the encouragement of biological reproduction. I conclude by showing how Burke’s faith in the improvability of the slave system is vulnerable to his own criticisms of other projects for political reform; namely that a certain guilelessness can blind reformers to the dangers inherent in their projects and reconcile them to what they purport to oppose.
items.title: The Perils of Improvement: Burke, Slavery, and Colonial Governance in the West Indies

items.abstract: For sentimentalists like Hume, the most basic objects of our approval are actions or character traits that cause pleasure. But Adam Smith instead takes as the fundamental object of approval the propriety of sentiments: a sentiment’s being ‘suited’ and ‘proportionate’ to its cause. Yet he is not particularly clear about what it is for a sentiment to match an object in this way. Moreover, extant interpretations are unsatisfying, because they generally fail to make sense of Smith’s claim that, in order to judge whether someone else’s sentiments are proper, one must use one’s own sentiments as a “rule or canon.” This article provides a novel account of Smithian propriety, based on the idea that Smith sees sentiments as representations of value. Sentimental propriety, on this account, is a kind of representational correctness; one judges the sentiments of someone else to be proper just insofar as ones share their sentimental perspective on the relevant object.
items.title: Passion and Propriety: Adam Smith’s Theory of Approval

items.abstract: Political liberals hold that the exercise of political power must be made acceptable to all reasonable citizens. This view is widely thought to be vulnerable to a powerful objection: There is too little that would be acceptable to all reasonable citizens for political liberalism to provide a plausible basis for legitimate state action. This article offers a new response to this challenge, which proceeds in two steps. First, the article develops a distinctive interpretation of the reasonable acceptability test, which is based on the moral ideal that every citizen should be able to find her social position acceptable. Second, the article uses this interpretation to show that there are liberal principles of political morality that no citizen can reasonably reject.
items.title: The Limits of Reasonable Disagreement
What’s Wrong with Stereotyping?
