items.abstract: Abstract The exponential rise of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has seamlessly woven intelligent systems into nearly every sphere of human life from smart homes and healthcare to transportation and entertainment. Yet, beneath this technological revolution lies a deeper psychological question: are humans truly benefiting from AI, or gradually examining the implications of increasing reliance on intelligent systems. Preliminary data suggests that over 78% of individuals in developed societies engage with AI-driven devices at least 12 times a day, while 62% admit to relying on automated systems for decisions once made intuitively. This study employs quantitative performance metrics and psychological dependency assessments across a diverse sample of 80 + participants to analyze the cognitive, emotional, and social implications of daily AI exposure. Comparative experiments between AI-assisted and manual task environments will measure productivity, satisfaction, and creative independence to determine whether constant AI support enhances or inhibits human potential. While the findings are expected to reveal fascinating insights into how humans psychologically adapt to machine intelligence, one crucial question remains unresolved does AI genuinely enrich human life, or subtly condition it for convenience at the cost of individuality. The answer, as the forthcoming analysis will uncover, may challenge the very foundation of our belief in progress.
items.title: The psychology of machine intelligence: evaluating the necessity of artificial intelligence in everyday smart devices and automated systems

items.abstract: Abstract The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has historically exercised substantial regulatory flexibility to adjust the type, amount, and quality of evidence necessary to support drug approval for areas of unmet need. Our objective was to characterize how FDA officials described and justified regulatory flexibility in recent public statements. We conducted a thematic analysis of quotations related to regulatory flexibility from 31 FDA officials published in Pink Sheet and STAT, two leading news sources covering FDA, from January 2021 to June 2024. In these statements, FDA officials typically justified prioritizing patient access to promising treatments over certainty regarding efficacy at the time of approval, even outside the accelerated approval pathway. Regulators also highlighted confirmatory studies conducted after accelerated approval as important for establishing drug efficacy. However, they recognized challenges to their completion, including insufficient industry incentives and FDA enforcement, and were reticent to interpret failed studies as evidence of failed drugs. Overall, in public statements from 2021–2024, FDA officials acknowledged challenges posed by regulatory flexibility but publicly justified its broad use to improve patient access for serious diseases despite even extended uncertainty. Under the Trump Administration, many officials have changed but efforts to advance regulatory flexibility continue.
items.title: US Food and Drug Administration Officials’ Public Statements on Regulatory Flexibility in New Drug Approval, 2021–2024

items.abstract: Abstract Patents listed in the US Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA) Orange Book can delay generic competition, yet little is known about how often patents are removed before expiration or why these delistings occur. We reviewed Orange Book records from 1998 through 2024 to identify patents removed before their expiration dates, classified patents according to the subject matter of their claims and assessed potential reasons for delisting using patent litigation and prosecution databases, FDA records, and Federal Trade Commission (FTC) actions. Among 9,980 patents listed during the study period, 535 (5%) were delisted before expiration. Only 71 (13%) claimed active ingredients; most delisted patents instead covered methods of use (177, 38%), formulations (167, 36%), or delivery devices (75, 16%). Potential reasons for delisting included potential invalidation in litigation (226, 42%), product discontinuation (207, 39%), and patent reexamination or reissue (60,11%). Orange Book patent delistings predominantly involved secondary patents rather than active-ingredient patents. Greater clarity and oversight regarding Orange Book listing requirements could reduce questionable listings and unnecessary barriers to generic competition.
items.title: Delisted Patents on Pharmaceuticals, 1998–2024

items.abstract: Abstract Rachael Wiseman (2019) has challenged the standard understanding of Wittgenstein’s Blue Book discussion of ‘two different cases in the use of the word “I”’. Wittgenstein is standardly read as identifying an important distinction between the use of ‘I’ as object, which involves the recognition of a person and is vulnerable to errors of misidentification, and the use of ‘I’ as subject, which involves no recognition of a person and is immune to error through misidentification. Wiseman argues that Wittgenstein does not in fact endorse such a distinction but warns against it. She contends that the standard interpretation ignores the context of the passage in the Blue Book discussion of solipsism and that it misunderstands the nature of self-consciousness. This paper defends the standard reading of Wittgenstein against Wiseman’s revisionary interpretation. It shows how it fits with his discussion of solipsism. And it defends the conception of self-consciousness it involves.
items.title: Wittgenstein and Immunity to Error Through Misidentification

items.abstract: Abstract In prominent legal historical works, Michael Clanchy and Stephen D. White constructed an important paradigm for medieval dispute settlement by adapting the phrase “law and love” from the Anglo-Norman Leges Henrici Primi . Yet, rarely has this aphorism’s background been explored. This article argues that “love or law” has roots in Viking-Age Scandinavia, where this Old Norse terminology represented a unique dynamic of dispute resolution revolving around harsh “law” pressuring parties to make “love” settlements outside of court. Contrasting sharply with Anglo-Saxon disputing norms centered on formal compensation tariffs, “love or law” found its way to England’s tenth-century Danelaw, first recorded in the Wantage Code. This alliterative pair continues in English writings, while “love-days” become a major cultural feature, and more broadly, the dynamic of threateningly punitive “law” inducing “love” agreements appears in action within early common law case records. In ways that recollect Icelandic and Danelaw practices, negotiated compensation occurring “under the shadow of law” may have been a major feature of medieval English dispute as hinted by our surviving sources. Scandinavian dispute concepts, occasionally coined by unique “love or law” vocabulary, may have had a subtle yet profound influence on some of the grounding assumptions of English common law.
items.title: Love or Law: Viking Foundations of Medieval English Dispute Settlement

items.abstract: ABSTRACT The syntactic interpretation of mathematics (SIM) refers to the view that interprets mathematical propositions as true expressions solely by virtue of the syntactical conventions governing the use of those expressions and not by corresponding to objective mathematical facts. This view, exemplified by the Vienna Circle and particularly Rudolf Carnap, is the target of Gödel's sustained critique and his defence of mathematical realism and intuition. I analyse Gödel's central arguments against SIM: the arbitrariness and asymmetry arguments, which challenge the notion that mathematics is contentless, and the circularity argument, which concerns the role of consistency proofs. I also examine two contemporary defences of Carnap: one appealing to dependable rather than provable consistency, and another recasting Carnap's project as transforming justificatory questions into pragmatic choices of linguistic frameworks. I contend that both defences fail to fulfil the original philosophical ambitions of the syntactic view, and that this failure indirectly bolsters the case for mathematical realism.
items.title: Syntax and Intuition: On Gödel's Critique of Carnap
Debate:  Why Exchange Reasons? Rejecting the Epistemic Inference
Self-Determination and the Right to Do Wrong
Moral Mirage Cascades: Ethical Vulnerabilities in ESG Reporting

items.abstract: Abstract The negative sustainability impacts of business keep escalating despite the profusion of research-based evidence regarding problems and solution pathways. Sustainability knowledge is complex and value-laden, thus often difficult to act upon. Co-creation between researchers and practitioners stands as a fruitful means of making sustainability knowledge more actionable, yet we lack insight into what motivates and facilitates sustainability knowledge co-creation. Boundary objects, which assist collaboration among diverse groups, can facilitate knowledge co-creation between researchers and practitioners, but little is known of their workings in the context of tackling value-laden sustainability issues. Based on rich qualitative data from two empirical cases, we examine how boundary objects motivate and facilitate knowledge co-creation between practitioners and researchers, helping to make sustainability knowledge more actionable. Our analysis illuminates three main dynamics whereby boundary objects do so: boundary objects initiate dialogue on complex issues through conveying clarity, provide a physical realm for co-creation in a value-laden domain, and motivate participation despite ethical vulnerability. These insights elaborate and challenge previous research regarding the boundary object ambiguity-clarity tension in the context of sustainability knowledge co-creation among diverse actor groups. Specifically, our findings foreground boundary object clarity, rather than ambiguity, in helping to initiate dialogue on complex sustainability issues. Furthermore, our analysis extends understanding of participant motivations to engage in sustainability knowledge co-creation, indicating that objects provide instrumental value and more intrinsic learning value, as well as help parties be with ethical vulnerability induced by knowledge co-creation around value-laden issues.
items.title: Objects as Means of Sustainability Knowledge Co-Creation: Working on Value-Laden Issues Across the Research-Practice Boundary

items.abstract: Abstract When do workers have good reasons to endorse a specific resistance strategy against managerial injustice? The answer partly requires clarifying whether that form of resistance is effective. But how should we understand efficacy? Political theorists cannot simply refer this question to empirical researchers. There is conceptual unclarity on what counts as efficacy. This paper shows that efficacy is a complex concept with multiple politically relevant dimensions. We illustrate this complexity by developing an epistemic notion of efficacy through a method of ideology critique, articulating a distinct dimension of effective resistance. A practice of resistance is epistemically efficacious if it reliably disrupts the mechanisms of ideological legitimation in the workplace by creating opportunities for egalitarian and collective contestation. Epistemic efficacy is a distinct evaluative lens that can assess the effectiveness of a resistance practice. After presenting the main argument, we apply our framework to the case of gossip as workplace resistance.
items.title: Effective Worker Resistance and Realist Ideology Critique
Rethinking Happiness Through Kant’s Philosophy of History
The Unanswerable Arguer: Large Language Models, Argumentative Injustice, and the Structural Displacement of Epistemic Standing

items.abstract: ABSTRACT This article's central object of critical reflection is the ableist anthropological and ethical assumptions underpinning the transhumanist project's implicit normative stance towards people with disabilities, who are framed as defective and futureless beings. It argues that the transhumanist conviction that improving the human condition requires eradicating disability is unjustified. Drawing on the human rights model of disability, as embodied in the principles of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, and on concepts of disability developed in disability studies, it defends the view that disability can represent a generative human gain that expands the existential boundaries of humanity. This article further proposes that the human rights model of disability could provide a conceptual framework for improving the transhumanist project by broadening its vision of human potential and reorienting it from the pursuit of human perfection towards an embrace of human diversity. Ultimately, this article argues that human potential and its humanity‐enhancing effects can unfold in different ways, including through the experience of disability.
items.title: Disability as Human Potential: Reorienting Transhumanism Through the Human Rights Model of Disability

items.abstract: Abstract The audit expectation gap exists and persists due to changing “…social, economic, and political developments of the time.” (Sikka, et al., 1998) Like stakeholders’ demands for and the profession’s response to fraud detection in the 2000s, investors are increasingly interested in C-suite employees’ and entity’s illegal acts, finding them both relevant and material (Cline, Walkling & Yore, 2018). This study identifies a gap between auditors’ and investors’ relevance and materiality judgments of a CEO’s illegal act. Varying role (auditor vs. investor) and using experience as a control (audit vs no audit), results show that non-auditor investors rate a CEO’s illegal act as significantly more relevant and material than do auditors placed in either role, while auditors in an investor role find a CEO’s illegal act significantly more material than auditors in an auditor role. Qualitative comments indicate that investors see managers’ personal misconduct as indicative of their lack of personal integrity and lose trust in them across personal to work situations. Auditors do not make the same connection. Our findings highlight challenges for the audit profession in meeting investors’ expectations in the context of managers’ illegal acts.
items.title: The Relevance and Materiality of Illegal Acts: Examining Auditor and Investor Judgments
Ethical Foundations of Social Entrepreneurship Competencies: A Systematic Review and Integrative Framework
A new double prevention model of dualist interaction

items.abstract: Abstract This article argues that the European Union’s (EU) sanctions packages against Russia are developing into a long-term governance structure that goes beyond the classical instruments of foreign policy. Without being legally permanent, Russia sanctions occupy a novel legal-political space: Repeated and expansive packages and their links to EU economic policy and criminal-law measures have created a durable framework for making, applying, and enforcing sanctions. Arguing that this emerging governance structure is extending beyond the Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP) into other areas of EU regulation, this article focuses on this institutional development.
items.title: Unpacking the Package: EU Sanctions Against Russia as a Governance Structure
“Us” and “them” and the “moral tribes” of AI: new theorizing of the human–machine relationship through a dual-process theory of moral cognition
AI auditing through professional tools: an exploratory qualitative case study of a digital ethics training program
The ethical half-life of AI: moral decay outpaces technical obsolescence
Beyond one-size-fits-all: how adaptability and autonomy shape responsible AI governance
Objective blindness in agentic systems: a taxonomy of behavioral signatures

items.abstract: Abstract Research on the position of intersex persons within the international refugee law system is extremely limited. Intersex persons are commonly grouped with LGBT+ issues within policy guidance, but little attention has been given to the specificity of intersex children’s needs. This Article aims to develop an approach to intersex refugee law from the perspective of children’s rights and health law. To do so, it will largely focus on the ways in which the current refugee law framework should be used to provide effective protection to intersex children, particularly when accompanied by their parents or legal guardians to flee harmful practices. Such research will rely on the work of the Committee on the Rights of the Child and other UN bodies which have slowly centered intersex issues in their works. Altogether, this Article aims to provide an overview of the current situation of intersex children seeking asylum, as well as avenues for developing better practices.
items.title: Protecting the Rights and Health of Intersex Children Seeking Asylum: A Child Rights Approach to Qualification as a Refugee for Intersex Children

items.abstract: Abstract The 2024–2026 reform of the EU return procedure constitutes the most far–reaching transformation of the European return acquis since the adoption of the key instrument governing returns—Directive 2008/115/EC. This Article critically assesses the impact of the reform on the EU return acquis and more generally on the migration regulatory framework. First, it introduces the concept of “exceptionalized pluralism” to describe the defining structural feature of the reform: the multiplication of derogatory return tracks—at external and internal EU borders and extraterritorially—that systematically displace the procedural safeguards constitutionalized by the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU), progressively relegating the common return procedure from norm to residual exception. Second, it argues that this architecture raises constitutional concerns on four interconnected fronts: the codification of numerous accelerated border transfer procedures institutionalizing harmonization as the coordination of coercion rather than the harmonization of rights; the European Return Order reproducing the structural accountability gaps of the Dublin system; the systematic expansion of pre-removal detention recalibrating the constitutional relationship between the right to liberty and executive power beyond what Article 6 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU (CFR) and the CJEU permit; and the formalization of return externalization through “return hubs” raising rule of law and accountability issues. In conclusion, the Article argues that the legitimacy of the emerging European return system will depend not on its operational speed or uniformity, but on whether enforcement harmonization is matched by concrete implementation of Charter-based safeguards. Moreover, it warns that, absent such implementation, “exceptionalized pluralism” will continue to operate as a self-reinforcing regulatory logic, expanding its derogatory tracks and leaving courts to fulfill, under conditions of mounting institutional pressure, a constitutional function that the legislative design has failed to assume.
items.title: Reforming the EU Return Acquis through “Exceptionalized Pluralism”: From Internal Borders to Offshore Enforcement

items.journal: International Journal of Law in Context
