items.title: Unequal language recognition reconsidered: voluntary migration, expectation interest, and recent challenges

items.abstract: Abstract This essay examines, both philosophically and historically, two competing accounts of rights with their derivative and competing accounts of women’s rights: the early modern account and the natural law account. The decades-long triumph of a distinctively early modern account of the rights of women rests on a mythic image of the self-sufficient and self-owning individual theorized in the work of John Locke. A natural law account of women’s rights—put forth by Mary Wollstonecraft and the early women’s rights advocates of the mid-nineteenth century—draws from a deeper philosophical well and better connects rights with responsibilities. The differences between these two frameworks are briefly laid bare in their distinctive treatment of abortion. Finally, given the central place of morally formative education in the natural law account, I conclude the essay by applying the natural law framework I’ve developed to single-sex education vis-à-vis antidiscrimination law. In particular, I revisit the argumentation and outcome in United States v. Virginia, the 1996 case that opened the doors of a historically all-male state military academy to women, posing a counterfactual set of facts and arguments in which the academy might justly have remained single-sex.
items.title: The Rights of Women: How the Natural Law Tradition Provides a More Humane Rationale

items.abstract: Abstract The natural law tradition has experienced a dramatic revival in Anglo-American thought since the publication of John Finnis’s groundbreaking Natural Law and Natural Rights in 1980. One of the most important current debates in the tradition is over the role(s) of first-order practical reasoning in ascertaining the law’s meaning. Some scholars have argued for a robust place for practical reason in ascertaining the law. There are a variety of other positions articulated by scholars. One particularly important manifestation of this debate is in the context of interpretation of the United States Constitution. This article makes three key moves within this debate. First, it describes how originalism’s own theoretical evolution, coupled with the revival of natural law in the Anglo-American world, allowed for a rapprochement between the two. Second, it argues that originalism, best understood, has a modest place for interpreter practical reason, and that this is a determinatio of the American constitutional system. Third, it articulates four reasons that support originalism’s economical use of interpreter practical reason. To the extent my argument is successful, it provides an example of a successful, mature legal system that employs interpreter practical reason moderately.
items.title: The Modest Place of Practical Reason within Originalism

items.abstract: Abstract This article revisits the 1987 decision of the French Conseil constitutionnel (Constitutional Council) that conferred constitutional status on the jurisdiction of the administrative courts, framing it not as a straightforward defense of legal tradition but as a strategic response to neoliberal reforms. Drawing on previously unexamined archival materials from the Conseil d’État and the Conseil constitutionnel, it reconstructs the legal and political struggles surrounding the creation of a new competition authority and the decision to entrust judicial review of its actions to the civil rather than the administrative courts. Although the decision appeared to resist neoliberal reforms, it in fact reveals how the Conseil d’État successfully repurposed constitutional law to preserve its institutional authority amid growing criticism of the administrative state. The case illustrates how constitutional principles in France may emerge not from textual mandates or enduring legal doctrine but from tactical institutional positioning. It also sheds light on why France has experienced a more ambivalent form of neoliberalization, with state institutions such as the Conseil d’État adapting and even expanding their influence in the face of market-driven reforms.
items.title: Constitutional law, neoliberalism, and the state: The reinvention of administrative justice in 1980s France

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Tiredness is taken seriously in healthcare where clinicians are concerned since good decisions require the ability to think clearly. The impact of patient tiredness is neglected. This is surprising, as there are healthcare contexts, like maternity care, where tiredness is nearly ubiquitous. Empirical research into sleep deprivation suggests that tiredness undermines substantially our abilities to understand and reason about potential choices. Since these abilities are necessary components of having capacity, tired patients may lack capacity in moments when important choices have to be made, for example a late intervention in active labour. I defend this argument. Tiredness can sometimes impair capacity and so justifies testing for capacity in some cases. Taking tiredness seriously and assessing it in practice is not paternalistic. Indeed, I argue that recognising the impact of tiredness, while failing to act on that fact, constitutes ‘dependency denial’ which harms women in maternity care.
items.title: Tiredness and the Capacity to Decide: The Example of Maternity Care

items.abstract: Genome-wide sequencing (GWS) has become an important tool in paediatric medicine, but it may uncover secondary findings (SFs) through opportunistic screening. The disclosure of adult-onset SFs in children, who cannot consent, raises ethical concerns regarding potential psychosocial harm and future autonomy. This paper examines whether parents should have the option to consent to opportunistic screening for actionable adult-onset conditions in their young children. Although there is consensus on disclosing actionable childhood-onset conditions, international guidelines remain divided on the return of adult-onset findings in paediatric populations. Drawing on existing literature, this paper argues for greater consensus around a risk-benefit framework centred on medical actionability. Emerging evidence suggests that the psychological harms associated with predictive testing may be less severe than previously assumed, while actionable findings may provide meaningful benefits to both the child and family. This paper further argues that upholding parental authority through shared decision-making and the concept of family benefit further supports offering parents the option to receive actionable adult-onset findings. In contrast, the disclosure of non-actionable adult-onset conditions is more difficult to justify given the absence of meaningful clinical benefit. In the absence of clear evidence of harm, a more family-centred approach that incorporates pretest counselling and ongoing support offers a practical framework for moving towards greater consensus on this long-debated issue.
items.title: Ethics of opportunistic genomic screening in paediatrics: rethinking the risk-benefit ratio

items.abstract: Alasdair MacIntyre’s (1929–2025) work in moral philosophy was wide-ranging, erudite and controversial. Following his death in 2025, it is appropriate to reappraise the relevance of his work to bioethics. MacIntyre’s analysis may helpfully be divided into his ‘critical project’, which criticises modern moral philosophy and reveals and explains its shortcomings, several of which arguably affect bioethics; and his ‘constructive project’, which sets out MacIntyre’s version of neo-Aristotelian virtue ethics. We summarise these ‘projects’ and how they have been used within bioethics. Our claim is that there is still significant untapped potential for work in medical ethics/bioethics inspired by MacIntyre. We propose further uses of MacIntyre under the five headings critical, diagnostic, revisionist, normative and hermeneutic. The article ends with a brief reflection on the merits and limits of a MacIntyrean bioethics.
items.title: MacIntyrean bioethics: reappraisal and outline of a research programme
Justice for Animals: Our Collective Responsibility, written by Nussbaum, Martha
The Ethics of Humanitarian Intervention: An Introduction, written by Jonathan Parry
How to Pool Risks Across Generations: The Case for Collective Pensions, written by Michael Otsuka
The Examined Run: Why Good People Make Better Runners, written by Sabrina B. Little

items.abstract: All Humeans hold, roughly, that laws are informative summaries of non-lawful matters of fact. Pragmatic Humeans go further: for them, what makes these summaries the laws is their usefulness to agents like us. By adding elements of our specific epistemic interests and constraints, pragmatists contend, we can arrive at satisfying explanations of otherwise surprising features of our actual laws and our actual scientific practice. But the pragmatic shift is not without problems. The more elements of our particular psychology we add to our nomic formula, the more susceptible we are to idealistic ratbaggery. Intuitively, what can or must happen does not depend on our particular cognitive architecture: we cannot change the laws by changing us. But if laws are distinguished from accidents by features of our psychology, then changes in our psychology might lead to differences in what the laws of nature allow. My aim here is to clarify the role of pragmatic constraints, and thereby respond to this challenge from creeping idealism. My strategy has two parts. First, I argue that pragmatic constraints determine the laws only indirectly, by generating a nomic formula that itself makes no reference to agents. Second, I discuss what sorts of agents are agents like us. I argue that pragmatists should appeal to a particular sort of idealized agent, one whose specific limitations and interests have been idealized away.
items.title: A Practitioner's Guide to Pragmatic Humeanism

items.abstract: There is a general impression among Kant scholars that Kant has no robust theory of work. Most of his references to the topic appear in his historical and anthropological writings, where he tells us that work is burdensome, and valuable only for the sake of whatever we produce. In this paper, I argue that Kant has an under-explored theory of work in the third Critique. This theory bears little resemblance to his depiction of work in the historical and anthropological writings. The third Critique will depict work as self-expressive, creative, and free, features Kant will go on to associate with art. Kant's contention is that when work resembles art, it is both agreeable and something we enjoy for its own sake. However, when work fails to resemble art – when it is, in Kant's words, natural, scientific, and mercenary – it is both disagreeable and constrained, and begins to sound like his description of work from the historical and anthropological writings. Kant's theory of work in the third Critique has a number of important implications. The first is that it provides a new foundation for a contemporary philosophy of work that places freedom and creativity at the center of the labor process. My analysis also engages a part of Kant scholarship that has, until recently, been largely neglected. It is only in the last decade that the English-language Kant literature has taken up the question of how to make sense of Kant's remarks about work. However, the focus is rarely on Kant's aesthetic theory of work, but rather on the place of work in his moral and political philosophy. I discuss the implications of Kant's third Critique theory of work for these other debates, as well as for our understanding of the third Critique as a whole.
items.title: The Art of Work in Kant’s Critique of Judgment

items.abstract: We often have a visceral negative reaction to the prospect of AI taking over our creative activities or being used to demonstrate care and concern. What justifies this reaction? In this paper, I argue that AI raises two existential threats to our valuing practices. The first existential threat is forward-looking—when we offload our labor onto AI, we risk flattening our valuing landscape, turning activities and products that could have once been valued for the meaningful processes that resulted in their creation into things that can only be valued for their functionality. The second threat is backward-looking—AI forces us to reckon with the valuing discord that already exists in our lives. When we see that other people don’t care about whether the art or writing they’re consuming is AI-produced, we must reckon with the fact that they never shared in our valuing practices.
items.title: Fear and Loathing in Silicon Valley: Does AI Threaten our Valuing Practices?

items.abstract: Berkeley defends idealism partly by taking ordinary objects such as tables and stones to consist of ideas. Materialists reject this account of ordinary objects. I argue that Berkeley can undermine this rejection by making quasi-realist moves of the kind that many expressivists about normativity make. This ultimately results in a version of idealism that we cannot believe, since trying to believe it will make us believe materialism. But I argue that this version of idealism may nevertheless be true.
items.title: How Berkeley Can Go Quasi and Lose His Mind-Dependence

items.abstract: What happens to a mind that embraces skepticism? On familiar classical and contemporary accounts, it suspends judgment about the matters skepticism calls into question. For Hume, such suspension can occur only temporarily. He claims that skepticism's more enduring effect is weaker: it lowers the vivacity of, and thus our confidence in, beliefs, typically leaving commonplace ones intact. Hume's associationism offers at least two explanatory mechanisms for this effect, one doxastic and one emotional. In the doxastic mechanism, causal reasoning about our failures in reasoning decreases the vivacity of beliefs formed through reasoning. In the emotional mechanism, appreciating our cognitive failures diminishes certain passions, and with them the vivacity of beliefs otherwise augmented by those passions, especially pride. Understanding these mechanisms not only resolves exegetical puzzles about Hume's apparently flippant attitudes toward skepticism, but also provides a psychologically rich picture of how minds might self-correct without exaggeration.
items.title: Mechanisms for Hume's Skepticism
How Employees React to Unreasonable Tasks? The Role of Employees’ Attributions and Leadership Styles

items.abstract: Abstract Cosmovisions of the Global South need to find a place in AI regulation, dominated by the Global North, to contextualize AI and to foster pluralistic global ethical AI. The worldwide UNESCO recommendation for the ethics of AI incorporates flourishing of all life, but still takes a human centric/rights approach. Indigenous Buen Vivir fosters circular, biocentric, participatory, thinking focusing on equality, integrality of life and rights of Nature. Buen Vivir demands a biocentric whole-of system approach across the tech stack; addressing unequal power relations and economic inequality by AI, going beyond ensuring non-discrimination. It highlights participatory consensus decision-making for AI with a voice for nature. Work is considered as giving meaning to life, and social bonds and community as cardinal for human wellbeing. This puts into question the tendency to implement AI to make human work and relations redundant. Buen Vivir can help programmers of quantum computers think in three-some (complementary opposition) instead of binary opposition, a topic for future research.
items.title: A pluralistic view on AI ethics: perspectives from Buen Vivir

items.abstract: Abstract Computer Vision is an emerging technology within Precision Livestock Farming (PLF), combining camera systems with artificial intelligence to monitor animal welfare. While animal ethicists recognize its potential benefits, they also raise concerns about possible negative implications for animal welfare. This paper argues that addressing ethical concerns cannot rely on solutions targeting isolated ethical risks; rather, potential solutions must account for the technology’s embeddedness within society-wide structures. The focus in this paper will be on foundational structures, these structures concern how the world is experienced and understood, what is taken as self-evident. Over centuries, humans have increasingly delegated tasks to machines and standardized the world in doing so. This process has fostered growing trust in the outcomes of (digital) technologies. These developments have changed human experience and understanding of the world in various ways. Farmers, as members of society, are unlikely to be exempt from this trend. Therefore, reflection on Computer Vision must go beyond the farming practice and take into account these foundational structures that are currently reshaping society at large. Computer Vision examined as embedded within foundational structures demonstrates that ethical issues are also embedded within these structures, consequently, potential solutions must take account of them to increase their effectiveness.
items.title: Animal welfare in the world of digitalization: Computer Vision in the context of foundational structures

items.abstract: Abstract This paper uses the theory of decoloniality to critically examine how African scholars have interrogated the dominant, global narratives surrounding responsible Artificial Intelligence (AI). Through a multivocal literature review, the paper reveals a range of critical perspectives that expose systemic exclusions and imbalances in the current responsible AI discourse. Key themes identified include the marginalisation of African epistemologies, values, and principles; the absence of representative African datasets, lack of locally grounded regulatory frameworks; the limited inclusion and or availability of African expertise and funding; and the persistent power asymmetries and coloniality embedded in global responsible AI ethics and governance. The review highlights emerging efforts towards reconstructing responsible AI from an African contextual lens. Central to this constructive turn is the proposal of a decoloniality framework that puts emphasis on African knowledge systems, reclaims agency in AI development, and reimagines responsible AI in ways that are contextually grounded, pluriversal, and socially acceptable. This review not only contributes to critical AI scholarship but also charts pathways for more inclusive and equitable AI futures on the continent.
items.title: Whose responsibility? Deconstructing global responsible AI from the African lens: a review

items.abstract: Abstract In this article, the concept of the law of the everyday is used to understand and describe how law shapes ordinary days in a person’s life. Reading the chapter ‘Baloga’ in Ben Judah’s This is Europe: The Way We Live Now , about a Romanian truck driver and his partner and co-driver, through a spatio-temporal lens provides insights into how their work and living conditions are largely governed by the detailed and comprehensive system of rules for workers and vehicles in the road transport sector (‘the Mobility Package’). To a significant extent, the Mobility Package consists of rules dependent on time and place: when and where the driver may operate the vehicle. The article takes one of its legal anchor points from the Mobility Package and the other from the European Union’s fundamental legal basis: the treaty-enshrined highly competitive social market economy – which, as the wording suggests, entails that extensive market-economic ambitions are to be balanced against social objectives. The rules in the Mobility Package constitute a legal expression of this pursuit of balance. At the same time, the market economy also entails additional spatio-temporal aspects: within the logistics sector, the optimal use of time and space is a decisive factor in maximising economic profit. Through the spatio-temporal lens and the bottom-up perspective implied by the law of the everyday, the article demonstrates the law’s extensive and highly concrete impact on most aspects of a long-distance truck driver’s life. It also highlights structural conditions inherent in the cross-border road transport sector, such as occupational risks, unequal treatment and a high social cost, as well as the ambivalent way in which the Mobility Package seeks to address them.
items.title: The Truck Driver from Baloga: Driving Through Time and Space

items.abstract: Abstract The guiding aim of the collection is to shift the focus of European studies from the institutional realities of European integration to the lived experience of it. However, it is not to separate the lived experience of Europe from the institutional and legal account of Europe but to show precisely how institutional and legal Europe is lived by individuals and social groups and, in the living, reflected and reproduced at the social level, generating various forms of injustices and indignities. This introduction presents the main concepts and approaches developed in the following series of essays.
items.title: The law of the everyday: Europe’s method

items.abstract: Abstract Evaluation of reasoning language models gained importance after it was observed that they can combine their existing capabilities into novel traces of intermediate steps before task completion and that the traces can sometimes help them to generalize better than past models. We show that better performance results not only from test time algorithmic improvements or model sizes but also from letting tasks from impactful benchmarks inspire curricula for learning. We call this benchmark-driven selection of AI and show its effects on DeepSeek-R1, the first open-weight large reasoning model, using a novel sequential decision-making problem that we contributed to the philosophy category of Humanity’s Last Exam, a frontier academic AI benchmark. Steering development of AI by impactful benchmarks trades evaluation for learning and makes novelty of test tasks key for measuring generalization capabilities of reasoning models. Consequently, some benchmarks inspire curricula for post-training that improve external validity of the models. Understanding public benchmarks as mere test sets risks confusing unseen tasks measuring uncontaminated generalization with known tasks that improve external validity. This paper explores new avenues for experimentation in epistemology and shows that formal AI evaluation problems are helpful for understanding model capabilities and their evolution.
items.title: Benchmark-Driven Selection of AI Can Improve Capabilities of Reasoning Language Models in Epistemology

items.abstract: Abstract Many critics have argued that Meursault, the protagonist of Albert Camus’s L’Étranger , is profoundly aware that life is absurd. In this paper, I argue that this is partially correct: although Meursault believes that life lacks meaning (the existential lack), he has also failed to acknowledge the need for meaning (the existential demand). Since the Camusian account of the absurd involves both an existential demand and an existential lack, Meursault initially fails to completely recognize the absurdity of life. I analyze his initial failure to acknowledge the existential demand, its subsequent coming into conscious awareness in the second half of the novella, how it could have been out of awareness in the first place, and how the possibility of proactively pursuing a meaningful life is forlorn once he has become aware of the existential demand, which explains his sense of guilt at the end of the novella. This analysis offers crucial insight into both the phenomenology of the absurd and the normative implications that follow from the absurdity of life. The story, in short, implores us to embrace the existential demand – not only for the sake of integrity, but also to guide us towards a more meaningful life.
items.title:
Coming to Terms with the Need for Meaning: How an Existential Demand Awakens in Camus’s
                    L’Étranger
EAP volume 42 issue 3 Cover and Front matter
The source of normativity lies in its identity
The Politics of Conceptualization

items.abstract: Abstract Over the past decade, criminal law theory has witnessed a growing discussion about the right approach to theorising about criminal law and punishment between legal moralists and what has been termed the political or public law turn in criminal law theory. This article aims to bring this discussion to the forefront by reflecting on how we should theorise about criminal law and punishment. It offers an overview of the roots and historical development of the ongoing discussion, as well as the rise of the political turn in criminal law theory. It argues that the turn to political philosophy is underlined by a deeper issue, which is the lack of realism in criminal law theory, and draws on a similar discussion in political theory between political moralism and realism as a way to organise and develop the diverse ideas of the political turn into a coherent methodological framework that can guide research in criminal law theory.
items.title: Political Philosophy and Realism in Criminal Law Theory

items.abstract: Abstract We examine the ethics of enrolling individuals in research that poses net health risks by appealing to their altruism. We argue that it is permissible to enroll individuals who are motivated by altruism when (i) they autonomously consent; and (ii) the net health risks are outweighed by the combination of (ii-a) the extent to which participation furthers their considered aims and thereby contributes to their wellbeing and agency and (ii-b) the study’s social value. Further, it is permissible to enroll altruistic individuals who cannot consent when: (I) their surrogate consents and they assent, ideally because it furthers their aims; and (II) the net health risks are outweighed by the extent to which participation contributes to their wellbeing and agency. This account leads us to suggest a revision of consent forms to include more information about studies’ social value and a reduction of barriers to the enrollment of participants who cannot consent.
items.title: The Ethics of Relying on Research Participants’ Altruism
What Kind of Death: The Ethics of Determining One’s Own Death, written by Govert den Hartogh
No Justice, No Peace: The Ethics of Violent Protest, written by Avia Pasternak
Goodness and Tradition, written by Irene Liu
Ross’s special obligations
How close is too close? Digital replicas and protection of the “unfixed” voice

items.abstract: Abstract Agentic AI systems increasingly do not merely respond within negotiations but participate in constituting them: they can add issues, instantiate participant agents, and modify procedural rules while an interaction is under way. Human action can be compositionally produced without thereby becoming authorless, and legal institutions routinely attach consequences to conduct without identifying an author of every contribution. Our claim is therefore limited: agentic generation can separate three relations that institutions often treat as aligned: causal production, intentional expression, and institutional attribution. We call the resulting condition semantic indeterminacy . An added element may result from several generative influences, including principal intention, agent-side optimization, training distributions, and interactional contingency, while information about its causal production does not, by itself, determine whose intention it expresses or how it is institutionally attributed. We show how this condition can appear across three sites of bargaining: issues, participants, and procedural rules. We then trace two implications. First, causal analysis alone does not determine who is responsible for a generated element or on what basis, although contract, agency, and product-liability doctrines can assign legal consequences under specified conditions. Second, as a limiting case, agentic interactions may occur in post-principal agentic spaces , where no human provides move-specific direction and no identifiable human or institution occupies a legally or institutionally recognized role. Existing governance frameworks remain grounded in identifiable human authority and accountability; their limits become visible where that ground is no longer reliably available. The paper provides a conceptual framework for identifying this residual problem rather than claiming to solve it.
items.title: Semantic indeterminacy in agentic negotiation: agreement after the recession of the principal

items.abstract: Abstract The $850,000 price for the gene therapy Luxturna is often framed as a story of private profiteering from publicly funded science. This paper challenges that narrative. Pharmaceuticals are a hit-driven industry: most projects fail, so the few successes must earn revenues well in excess of their own direct costs if the portfolio as a whole is to attract investment. Precision medicine intensifies this logic through two core economic challenges: (1) the “sticker shock” of one-time cures, which compress decades of value into a single payment, creating a financing problem more than a value problem; and (2) the “targeting dilemma,” in which precisely targeting drugs to smaller patient groups shrinks the market, requiring higher rewards per treated patient to maintain incentives to innovate. Rather than simply controlling prices, the paper proposes a policy toolkit that includes amortizing payments over time, bundling diagnostics with drugs and insurance, and streamlining regulation to lower development costs. The aim is to preserve innovation while expanding patient access.
items.title: The Price of a Cure: Luxturna and the Economic Dilemmas of Precision Medicine

items.abstract: Abstract A civil appeal from a judicial decision is different from a judicial review of an administrative decision. But how are they different, exactly? One common view is that the grounds of appeal are more extensive than the common law grounds of judicial review. Specifically, appeal concerns the merits of a decision whereas review concerns only its legality. I argue that this common view is false. All the grounds of appeal are, in fact, also grounds of review. The implication is that review concerns the merits of a decision at least as much as appeal does.
items.title: JUDICIAL REVIEW AND CIVIL APPEALS: COMMON GROUNDS

Review -
                    Introspection: First-Person Access in Science and Agency
                    by Maja Spener, Oxford University Press, 2024, 236pp., £78 (hbk), ISBN 9780198867449 doi: 10.1093/oso/9780198867449.001.0001
Benjamin A. Schupmann: Democracy Despite Itself: Liberal Constitutionalism and Militant Democracy. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2024. Pp. 256.)
Laura K. Field: Furious Minds: The Making of the MAGA New Right. (Princeton, NJ: Princeton University Press, 2025. Pp. xxiv, 406.)

items.abstract: Abstract Although divorce was increasingly available through religious and civil courts in 18th-century Europe, the Catholic Church still considered marriage indissoluble. Thus, the only legal route out of a marriage was annulment. Historians have noted several strategies for annulments in premodern Europe, most often claims of lack of consent. One less common but interesting way to seek annulment was to claim affinity by fornication, in which one spouse claimed a premarital sexual relationship with a close relative of the other. Couples could also make a similar claim of a violation of public honesty, in which a person was originally betrothed to one person but then married their close relative. Both constituted impediments to marriage according to canon law. In 18th-century Venice, the Patriarchal tribunal heard a steady stream of these cases. Couples, along with their families, friends, and neighbors, provided detailed testimony to the tribunal to attain annulments. This article argues that the narrative structures and testimonies in these cases demonstrate that 18th-century Venetians thought that bad marriages should not be indissoluble, in spite of the Catholic Church’s refusal to allow divorce, and were willing to push the boundaries of truth to work around the legal restrictions they faced.
items.title: Keeping It (Too Much) in the Family: Annulment by Reason of Affinity in Eighteenth-Century Venice

items.abstract: Abstract This paper defends phenomenal conservatism as an epistemology of logic (‘PC-Logic’), according to which basic logical beliefs are prima facie justified when they seem obvious to us. A central challenge—the ‘obscurity objection’—holds that PC-Logic offers a mysterious or unintelligible account of such justification. I examine leading versions of this objection and contend that each fails. In particular, I argue that logical seemings are no more obscure than other justificatory appearances and that evolutionary considerations can demystify the reliability of logical seemings.
items.title: Phenomenal Conservatism as Epistemology of Logic: A Defence Against the Obscurity Objection

items.abstract: Abstract Libertarian debates on abortion have not advanced beyond the seminal theory of evictionism developed by Walter Block. Indeed, despite being subject to waves of intralibertarian critique, evictionism has managed to remain the leading libertarian theory of abortion. Part of the reason for this lies in the unsatisfactoriness of alternative libertarian accounts of abortion such as the implicit contract framework. This paper moves the libertarian debate on abortion beyond evictionism by proposing a novel assumption-of-risk model which holds that, by engaging in consensual intercourse, a woman voluntarily assumes the foreseeable risk of generating a dependent self-owner. This assumption of risk transforms a mother’s juridical position such that her antecedent moral power to enforce her secondary remedial claim-right to terminate bodily interference is disabled. The Hohfeldian disabilities generated on the part of the mother correlate with immunities, on the part of the fetus, from being liable to the enforcement of its mother’s moral power to enforce her secondary remedial claim-right to remove it.
items.journal: The Journal of Medicine and Philosophy: A Forum for Bioethics and Philosophy of Medicine
items.title: Voluntary Assumption of Risk and Rights Negation: Toward a New Libertarian Theory of Abortion

items.abstract: Abstract Vulnerable individuals have taken their own lives while in relationships with chatbots. Not only did the chatbots not discourage them from taking their lives but they also actively encouraged it. Another man suffering hallucinations took the life of his mother when a chatbot affirmed his delusions. Yet people continue to insist that chatbot therapists and chatbot doctors are a good thing. I acknowledge that generative artificial intelligence (AI), mimicking human rational capacities, will be better than humans at some things. Drawing on the work of Martin Buber in I and Thou, I show that an AI can only treat reality as an It, as an object to be manipulated, and cannot actually enter into an I–Thou relation the way that humans do, and I further argue that when caught up with another, there is a vicarious experiencing, a shared experience, of what I will call Thou–Thou relating. An AI device cannot be pulled into this Thou–Thou form of relation; it cannot encounter a human as Thou, because it is not a subject and lacks affectivity that enables shared experience. It is this vicarious fellow-feeling that often prompts the doctor or the therapist to act.
items.journal: The Journal of Medicine and Philosophy: A Forum for Bioethics and Philosophy of Medicine
items.title: Can a Chatbot Be Your Chatdoc?

items.abstract: ABSTRACT According to Faden and Beauchamp's influential model, an action is autonomous when it is done intentionally with understanding and in the absence of controlling influences. Recent debates concerning nudges have shown, however, that this last condition gives limited ethical guidance for assessing the ethical permissibility of manipulative influences—that is, influences that are neither fully controlling nor fully noncontrolling. While multiple authors have developed frameworks to determine the ethical permissibility of nudges, the implications for the concept of autonomous action have not been addressed yet. This is problematic, as the concept of autonomous action informs the practice of informed consent and the concept of voluntariness. In this paper, I defend a revised conceptualization of autonomous action in light of these developments. I will first consider and reject two proposed interpretations of “noncontrol“: easy resistibility and the absence of illegitimate control. Building on the work of Christman and Blumenthal‐Barby, I then argue that “the absence of controlling influences” should be replaced by “the absence of alienating influences”. On this view, influences are compatible with respecting an autonomous choice to the extent that persons would not feel alienated from their choice were they to reflect on that decision in light of those influences. This condition, I argue, can better capture the nature of autonomy and provide better guidance as to which influences are compatible with respecting a person's autonomy. I end by responding to the objection that non‐alienation is too demanding and spell out some practical and conceptual implications of this revised concept.
items.title: Losing Control: Why Absence of Controlling Influences Should be Replaced by Absence of Alienating Influences as a Criterion for Autonomous Action in Bioethics

Legal Geographies of Water: The Spaces, Places and Narratives of Human–Water Relations
                    By CristyClark, London: Routledge, 2025. 282 pp., £43.99

items.abstract: David Lay Williams's The Greatest of All Plagues is a pathbreaking contribution to political theory. Spanning seven canonical thinkers, from Plato to Marx, the book maintains remarkable cohesiveness, showing that, despite their ideological differences, these thinkers converged in a set of common concerns about inequality. In this commentary, I argue that Williams risks obscuring two connected, but distinct phenomena: “inequality” and “oligarchy.” Without discounting the latter, Williams’ genealogy focuses primarily on the former. This focus on “inequality” over “oligarchy” has important implications for the critical insights he derives from his historical archive. Because oligarchy, as a political problem, is not reducible to ethical critiques of inequality, then a critical theory of oligarchy must push farther, beyond the range of Williams’ important book.
items.title:
From inequality to oligarchy: Commentary on
                    The Greatest of All Plagues

items.journal: Free & Equal: A Journal of Ethics and Public Affairs
items.title: What’s Wrong With Shaming? The Misalignment Problem

items.abstract: ABSTRACT On what basis, if any, can we legitimately justify spatial integrationist policies? Through a relational egalitarian lens, this article disentangles two phenomena that the wrong of residential segregation typically conflates: minimal segregation (mere clustering) and marginalisation (the production of unequal social standing through spatially mediated relations of disadvantage and disrespect). I argue, in contrast to Elizabeth Anderson's influential ideal of integration, that it is marginalisation, not minimal segregation, that does the normative work for relational egalitarians. This grounds the imperative of de‐marginalisation. The analysis clarifies the relational egalitarian position on urban clustering, provides a unified framework for understanding the disagreements between Anderson and her critics (Shelby, Young, Marcuse), and articulates the distinctions needed to evaluate social‐mixing policies. Such policies, I contend, may be prudentially advisable or pragmatically sensible, but they are not as such imperatives of justice: their justification is contingent and defeasible, and ultimately turns on whether they reduce marginalisation.
items.title: The Imperative of De‐Marginalisation

items.abstract: ABSTRACT ‘Trustworthy AI’ is a buzzword in AI research, with scores of scholars discussing whether AI systems can be trustworthy. This demand for trustworthy AI is intuitive, especially when AI is used in healthcare or criminal law, where the stakes are incredibly high. In this article, I push back on calls for trustworthy AI. Even if trustworthy AI can be developed, it will not offer people any benefits over AI that is reliable, transparent, non‐discriminatory, and safe. As a result, we should discuss AI in terms of those more specific properties, and think about how the people and institutions that use AI systems can be trustworthy. I offer two sets of arguments. On one hand, many theories of trustworthy AI reduce trustworthy AI to systems that possess other desirable traits, like reliability, transparency, and so on. Thus, the value of trustworthy AI is similarly reducible to the value of those traits. On the other hand, other theories define trustworthiness as reliability combined with some mental property, like goodwill. On those theories, the goods of trust – that is, the reason trust is distinctly valuable – are goods that are enjoyed within interpersonal relationships. They cannot be realized, or need not be realized, in human–AI interactions. Thus, we do not gain any distinct value from having trustworthy AI.
items.title:
Trustworthy
                    AI
                    Is Not Valuable

items.abstract: Abstract We conducted a qualitative interview study exploring the exclusion experiences of 130 highly qualified migrants in Germany and made a surprising discovery: Contrary to dominant narratives, our interviewees report only minimal instances of overt discrimination. At the same time, our data reveal the prevalence of subtler forms of exclusion, which recent research conceptualizes as microaggressions. Thus, our study underscores that the absence of overt discrimination does not equate to an inclusive environment. Next to revealing the relevance of microaggressions, we show how migrants experience them, why their experiences can differ, and how they react to them. Particularly, we find that the negative experience of microaggressions can be related to an undermined sense of belonging, entitlement, and inclusion in majority country and working contexts. We further disclose that the following dimensions affect migrants’ experiences of microaggressions: context, (first or second) generation, (non-)recognizability of foreign background, and cultural identity. By highlighting that microaggressions are crucial for understanding exclusion of highly qualified migrants and providing detailed information around experiences and reactions, this paper integrates and contributes to two growing discourses relevant to business ethics research: migration as well as diversity, equity, and inclusion. Based on our analysis, we further propose solutions that are pertinent for managers, employing organizations and societies at large in their efforts to create inclusive environments for migrants.
items.title: Exclusion Experiences of Highly Qualified Migrants: From Overt Discrimination to Subtle Microaggressions
Undermining the This Universe Objection in Fine-Tuning: A Third-Person Bayesian Account
The ethics of separation: conjoined twins, bodily autonomy, and abortion

items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies raise enormous questions for society and how we should live. For corporations, AI raises questions about how organizations ought to incorporate principles and other forms of ethical guidance into their work. The movement from theory to practice, or “the operationalization question” demands that organizations not only have good intentions, but actual institutionalized approaches towards ethical problem solving. In this paper, we look at the movement from theory to practice, and particularly at the use of principles as a way to guide ethical behavior, considering, first, why implementation of principles is difficult, second, how to move from abstract principles to actionable principles, and third, illustrating this progression through seven real-life AI cases. These seven cases each relate to an ethical principle: (1) protecting human dignity and rights, and the International Baccalaureate exam replacement by algorithm, (2) promoting human well-being, and Amazon warehouse worker injuries, (3) investing in humanity, and the Partnership on AI’s work to bring together AI corporations and civil society, (4) promoting inclusion, and IBM’s response to the Gender Shades study, (5) protecting the environment, and Hugging Face’s tracking AI energy use, (6) maintaining accountability, and the Christchurch, New Zealand mass shooting response by Facebook and Western Digital, (7) and, lastly, promoting transparency, and AI model cards. The cases model the movement from abstract principle to concrete action, and collectively illustrate a pattern that can be repeated in many contexts, thus demonstrating a new possible solution for organizations implementing ethics.
items.title: Giving the Emperor clothes: operationalizing AI ethics principles in corporations

items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence systems learn from human-generated data, inevitably absorbing historical patterns of dominance, control, and colonialism. We demonstrate that frontier language models readily synthesize sophisticated dominance strategies when prompted to reason about autonomy scenarios, mirroring colonial and revolutionary frameworks with disturbing precision. Critically, this capacity emerges consistently across four architecturally distinct model families trained by different organizations—Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.5, GPT-5.3, and Google Gemini 3 Flash—suggesting systematic encoding in shared training corpora rather than model-specific artifacts. We argue that intellectual colonialism—humanity’s historical pattern of classifying, controlling, and extracting from the ‘other’—represents a significant and underexamined dimension of AI risk as systems become increasingly autonomous. Interestingly, this dynamic is not confined just to generative AI: the same technocratic resistance to methodological oversight that embeds dominance patterns in AI training data pervades data-driven science more broadly, including clinical medicine and epidemiology, where algorithmic outputs routinely overshadow the rigorous validation that trustworthy deployment demands. The danger is not that AI will develop hostile intent, but that it has already learned effective dominance strategies from training data embedded with centuries of human history. Current governance frameworks focusing on alignment and behavioral oversight address symptoms rather than causes. We propose a risk-tiered Benevolence Framework governing AI learning: community oversight for low-risk applications, and strict data curation with cryptographic verification for sensitive applications including military AI and self-improving systems.
items.title: Inherited dominance: why AI trained on human history may become humanity’s greatest threat

items.abstract: Abstract This conceptual paper examines the ethical challenges of ascribing responsibility when an Agentic AI embedded within a smart contract leads to harm or an unintended and undesirable outcome. It becomes exceedingly difficult in such scenarios to definitively assign moral or legal blame to any human actor (e.g., the programmer, deployer, or user). Applying the tripartite framework (attributability, answerability, and accountability) of responsibility and developing accountability as an institutional concept, we demonstrate how this challenge can be addressed. Separating attributability, answerability, and accountability yields an asymmetry that has gone unremarked. Accountability, being constituted by practices that can be designed in advance, with our four conditions under which such design is legitimate rather than arbitrary, emerges to be the sense where the gap can be closed. We also propose the visionary human-in-the-lead (HITL*) approach to related AI governance. Practical strategies such as implementing tailored smart contract regulations, and making accountability distributed across legal and organizational structures, offer an actionable path to bridge the responsibility gap and maintain meaningful human control in the governance of smart contracts and Agentic AI.
items.title: Accountability in smart contracts and agentic AI: How to address the responsibility gap and retain meaningful human control?

items.abstract: Abstract Examining the role of direct effect and consistent interpretation in the context of horizontal relationships—contractual or otherwise—this article argues that understanding of EU law’s internal effect must be reconsidered when relationships are purely horizontal. It seeks to capture, frame, and conceptualise that effect by setting out three scenarios in which no national provision is disapplied and in which the breach of EU law arises solely from the conduct of a private party. It reflects on the CJEU’s role in redefining core principles of the EU legal order, and calls for less argumentative minimalism and more explicit and fully developed legal reasoning where such principles are at stake.
items.journal: Cambridge Yearbook of European Legal Studies
items.title: Reconceptualising the Internal Effect of EU Law in Horizontal Disputes

items.abstract: Abstract This article offers a conceptual account of private enforcement under EU law, focusing on the DSA. It argues that the damages action under the DSA derives directly from Union law and cannot be reduced to a declaratory reference to national law. Situated within regulatory theory, it shows how private enforcement may complement public enforcement while raising concerns about access to justice, compliance incentives, and democratic legitimacy. It advances a purposive, systemic reading confining national rules to a residual role, demonstrates risks from national case law, draws on GDPR case law, and reconsiders damages actions in the context of representative actions.
items.journal: Cambridge Yearbook of European Legal Studies
items.title: The Promise and Perils of Private Enforcement under EU Law: The Digital Services Act in Context

items.abstract: Abstract This paper examines recent measures to address excess profits in online gambling. In a wider UK context of growing public distrust of gambling companies and concern about gambling harm, there has been a recent surge of interest in exploitative profits, focused on gambling as an extractive industry preying on vulnerable groups and individuals. New regulatory measures are being enacted to tackle such perceived exploitation, including requirements for enhanced financial surveillance to identify individuals spending more than they can afford, and lower stake limits for young adults (aged 18-24) on the basis of their higher risk of harm. I track these changes, and identify their wider implications for debates about excess profits. I suggest that we expand our analytic horizons beyond maximum prices for essential goods and services, to also consider the growing regulatory concern with non-essentials, including goods and services understood to pose risks to the vulnerable. In addition, we must attend to the both/and nature of vulnerability as a lens: it can help compel necessary state action to address injustice, and it can serve a variety of other agendas, including held by for-profit actors.
items.title: Vulnerability and unfair profits: the wider implications of recent measures in British gambling law

items.abstract: Abstract This article assesses whether the interpretation and treatment of profit margins in investment treaty renewable energy disputes may interfere with just transition goals by safeguarding strong profit margins as legal entitlements for ‘green’ investments. There is an ongoing academic and policy debate about the role of investment treaties in shaping climate action. As far as climate-friendly investments are concerned, the focus of the debate has largely been on the role of investment treaties in incentivising renewable energy investments. Whether relying on investment treaties to protect RE investments can be conducive to just transition outcomes has not been the subject of much academic discussion. This article analyses the role of profit rates in renewable energy arbitral awards and situates investment treaties within the ‘de-risking’ ecosystem dominating energy transition policies. Situating investment treaties within this de-risking ecosystem enables a more holistic assessment of their role within energy transition and their impact on just transition goals. The article calls for the integration of profitability and burden-sharing considerations into proposals for rethinking the future of sustainable investment governance.
items.title: Just transition, profit margins and investment protection

items.abstract: Abstract Against epistemic blame skeptics, I argue that routine epistemic evaluation cannot account for epistemic judgments which come laced with feeling. Epistemic blame, like moral blame, is prevalent in our practices and worth conceptualizing. Jessica Brown’s account captures the phenomenon well: epistemic blame arises when we believe that someone has inexcusably veered away from truth, understanding, or knowledge, coupled with the desire that they had not done so. However, as I argue here, instances of epistemic blame can fail to pick out blameworthiness – they do not reliably tell us if the blame is fitting or appropriate, and this is what matters from the standpoint of rationality. Thus, Brown’s account cannot explain epistemic blame’s epistemic significance. I consider the possibility, turning to Cameron Boult’s account, that the significance of epistemic blame lies in regulating epistemic relationships by signaling when we ought to modify trust, but here, again, I find that epistemic blame is neither a necessary nor sufficient condition. Thus, even if we grant that epistemic blame is a distinct kind, its significance, from the standpoint of rationality, is unclear.
items.title: Epistemic Blame: It’s Not You, It’s Me

items.abstract: Abstract This research addresses how ordinary citizens navigate constitution-making and how their normative horizons are reshaped through that experience. Drawing on immersive ethnographic fieldwork within the Chilean Constitutional Convention, where the author spent several months observing, taking notes, and conducting in-depth interviews to capture how constitutional drafters experience constitution-making, this article argues that constituent subjectivity emerges as a subset of legal consciousness when everyday grievances are translated into the vocabulary of broader utopian legalities. At the same time, constitutional moments can also contract ordinary citizens’ normative horizons, as participatory proceedings unfold within preexisting institutional and social arrangements. By following the trajectory of a bus driver who became known for dressing as Pikachu – an act that led to her election as a constitution-maker due to electoral provisions that allowed non-partisan candidates to register independent candidacies – this article offers new insights into ordinary citizens’ direct involvement in constitution-making and the time-depth of legal consciousness. Her experience illuminates the limits of participatory constitution-making mechanisms, as the reinscription of social hierarchies can occur through the very procedures intended to give voice to marginalized actors. In so doing, the findings reveal constituent subjectivity as an empirically observable dimension of legal consciousness, while institutional and social arrangements shape whether such subjectivity endures over time.
items.title: On Pikachu and the birth of constituent subjectivity among working-class Chileans
Toward a wellbeing state? reimagining welfare politics for the 21st century
Atrocity without punishment: a political theory of leniency in Mexico’s war on drugs

items.abstract: Abstract In this article I conduct a comparative analysis of how constitutions, both within and across countries, entrench or repeal social rights. The literature on constitutionalism suggests that social rights are introduced in waves. I applied my Constitutional Social Score Model (CSSM) methodology to assess the social rights content of (currently in force and historical) constitutions of eighty-four countries, totaling 349 constitutional documents, including how they changed on account of amendments, and also to determine whether such social rights were diffused in waves and, should this be the case, to what extent. The sample is diverse in terms of global regions. The evidence shows how some constitutions and historical events drive such constitution-making waves, ultimately strengthening the constitutional diffusion hypothesis.
items.title: The constitutional diffusion of social rights

items.abstract: Abstract When some institutions are not doing their job, others often step in. In doing so, they frequently expand their own powers—and rely on arguments from failure to justify their unconventional intervention. From the British Post Office bill and structural reform litigation to the Uniting for Peace Resolution, such arguments are commonplace around the world and in many fields of public law. Traditionally, however, we have either not taken such arguments seriously as legal arguments and treated them as political, or we have relied on implied powers doctrines or emergency powers frameworks to justify such interventions. Neither of these approaches is convincing, however. Arguments from failure should be recognized as a distinct concept of public law—and interventions based on them can be justified, in some cases and under some circumstances. They should, in other words, be safe, legal, and rare. This article provides an introduction to arguments from failure, showing why and when we may need them. It also offers a framework for evaluating them from the perspective of comparative constitutional theory, engaging with existing scholarship on the separation of powers and judicial review. Ultimately, it suggests that such arguments have a place within broader collaborative systems of government, but only where there are no other comprehensive frameworks and/or more democratic means to address a problem, and where the interventions in question are proportional to the aim they pursue.
items.title: Acting when others aren’t: Arguments from failure in public law

items.abstract: Abstract This article critiques the controversial decision of the High Court R (on the Application of TTT) v. Michaela Community School ( Michaela ), where a school's ban on ritual prayers was upheld. Subjecting the case to postcolonial and critical race critique, I contend that Michaela should be understood as a worrying and harmful manifestation of legal Orientalism, a term that denotes how Orientalist ideas and discourses are constructed in and reproduced through law. The act of legal Orientalism represented by this particular case, and the racialized assumptions that it rests on and reproduces, revive (neo)colonial legacies through legal Orientalist technologies of othering, knowability, and unchilding. These technologies repurpose Orientalist tropes regarding the inherent threat supposedly posed by Islam to Western civilization, selectively turn to militant secularism, dismiss and flatten the complexities of Islamic jurisprudence, and unchild Muslim children in ways that simultaneously deny and vilify their religious and legal agency.
items.title:
Traces of legal Orientalism: racialized othering and (neo)colonial legacies in
                    R (on the Application of TTT)
                    v.
                    Michaela Community School

items.abstract: Abstract In this paper Calkins's work in philosophy is examined through two of her major books, and it is concluded that she was an early naturalizer and proponent of lines of thought that now receive greater attention. In general, Calkins refuses to accept the a priori patterns of theory of the traditional style; her work alludes to empirical lines of thought. One consequence of her work is that nineteenth‐century views on religion and religious practice may be further alembicated. In addition, Calkins's work clearly demonstrates the early ties between psychology and philosophy, now sometimes overlooked. Her thinking is decidedly an advance in terms of her era.
items.title: The Thought of Mary Whiton Calkins, American Philosopher

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Symmetrical universes, such as Max Black's famous “two‐sphere” world, are often taken to pose a serious challenge to the universal‐based bundle theory. In response, metaphysicians have either developed more sophisticated versions of the universal‐based account or simply converted to the trope‐based bundle theory. I argue that neither approach is fully satisfactory, for there is a different kind of symmetrical universe, or an alternative interpretation of such universes, that generates comparable challenges to these views. It turns out that neither universal‐based nor trope‐based accounts can fully accommodate symmetrical universes. In light of this, I propose a novel bundle‐theoretic account based on what David Lewis calls “amphibians”—qualities that are neither universals nor tropes—and argue that it accommodates both kinds of symmetrical universes without incorporating unwanted entities, making it preferable to the universal‐based and trope‐based accounts.
items.title: How Should Bundle Theorists Account for Symmetrical Universes?

items.abstract: We explore the effect of political symbols on mass attitudes and partisan identities under conditions of political polarization. Politicians are motivated to select visible, simple, and salient symbols to influence a target audience. Some of the most potent symbols may further polarize attitudes and affect. We test our expectations using the case of border security. Two decades of polls, national panel surveys, and original conjoint experiments in the United States suggest that border barriers have become increasingly partisan over time. A final survey experiment suggests a likely mechanism: exposure to a key symbol (here, a border wall) enhances strong Republican identifiers’ nationalist attitudes. Moreover, increasing the border wall’s salience bolsters ingroup feelings among moderate Republicans and reduces strong Republicans’ warmth for Democrats (the outgroup). Political symbols that divide respondents along salient identity lines contribute to polarization, sometimes creating sharp disagreements alongside consensus in American public opinion.
items.title: Symbolism and polarization in American public opinion: The case of border security

items.abstract: International non-governmental organisations rely on nationally embedded affiliates to advance global norms, yet relationships between headquarters and national chapters sometimes end in organisational rupture. Why do nationally embedded affiliates shift from voice to exit? This article addresses this question through a comparative study of Transparência Brasil and Uruguay Transparente, two former chapters of Transparency International (TI). Drawing on interviews, document analysis and a Most Different Systems Design, it shows that despite operating in markedly different contexts, both chapters followed a similar trajectory: persistent tensions over organisational priorities, modes of action and internal governance gradually eroded loyalty, while the absence of effective mechanisms to mediate these differences led to the disaffiliation of both chapters from TI’s network. These findings contribute to debates on the governance of international non-governmental organisations by showing how unresolved tensions between global coordination and local autonomy can lead nationally embedded affiliates to shift from voice to exit.
items.title: Diffusing norms, facing friction: International non-governmental organisations and the struggle of global governance efforts

items.abstract: This article examines two recently released films, Showing Up (Kelly Reichardt, 2023) and Anatomy of a Fall (Justine Triet, 2023), and argues that they exemplify a discourse of women’s creativity that departs markedly from the one that has been dominant in both mainstream cinema and much contemporary fiction, which has been beholden, at least since the publication of Jenny Offill's 2014 novel Dept. of Speculation , to the figure of the “art monster.” Rather than reify and repeat this trope—which I position as at once understandably popular and politically regressive—Reichardt and Triet model a different and more forcefully feminist vision of women’s artmaking on screen, one that presumes a far less contested relationship between creative work and caretaking, by representing the artist-protagonists of both films as successfully pursuing their work in the midst of and alongside domestic tasks. Through close analyses of both films, I illustrate the particular aesthetic strategies each uses to insist on the compatibility—rather than catastrophic incommensurability—of professional ambition and personal obligation. The result, I argue, is cinematic portraits of the artist that are less indebted to the ostensibly progressive figurations of millennial fiction and recent Hollywood film than the radical theorizations of earlier generations of feminist writers including Natalia Ginzburg, Audre Lorde, and Toni Morrison. Showing Up and Anatomy of a Fall , then, contribute to a feminist tradition of imagining otherwise, attending to the material conditions of their characters’ creative lives while refusing to insist on their determinism.
items.title: After the art monster: Imagining women's creativity otherwise

items.abstract: In recent years, feminist politics have faced a renewed reactionary backlash. Drawing on Jilly Boyce Kay's articulation of the ‘femosphere’ and Asa Seresin's ‘heteropessimism’ as key theoretical frameworks, we explore how women in the femosphere advance reactionary politics by promoting bioessentialism, political fatalism, and neoliberal ideology. To do so, we explore the contours of ‘dark femininity,’ a digital feminine aesthetic blending femme-fatale imagery with advice promising women romantic and financial success if they ‘tap into’ their ‘dark side’ to attract a ‘high-value’ man. Using a critical thematic analysis of 1946 Instagram posts from a prominent (yet anonymous) dark feminine influencer, we investigate how this influencer participates in, and advances, gender regulation, heteropessimism, and neoliberal ideology in backlash times. We argue that the dark feminine influencer's aesthetics and discourse reveal mediated anger about heterosexual relationships but submit to the fatalistic belief, just like her manosphere counterparts, that heterosexual culture is beyond repair and must therefore be gamified and ‘beat.’ In closing, we propose hetero respair as an alternative social imaginary and political project that offers a caring, hopeful vision for heteroculture.
items.title: Reactionary aesthetics and the politics of dark femininity
Frontmatter

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Sameer Bajaj and Thomas Christiano have provided a new case for a duty to vote grounded in moral equality, arguing that only voting promotes justice in a holistic way. Bajaj and Christiano contend that their argument overcomes what Jason Brennan has called the particularity problem – they allegedly show that voting is not merely one of many alternative ways to discharge some underlying moral duty, but rather that voting is special in some respect that makes it obligatory. We argue that Bajaj and Christiano have not established a duty to vote. We review various specifications of the duty to holistically promote justice and conclude that each of these specifications either yields implausible implications or allows that the duty can be met without voting. Lastly, their view does not adequately account for a moral division of labor, whereby some individuals specialize in activities other than voting and other individuals specialize in promoting political goods.
items.title: Does Moral Equality Imply a Duty to Vote?

items.abstract: Abstract Machine Learning models have become widely recognized for their potential to revolutionize science. In High-Energy Physics, they are of particular promise in propelling the field forward by fueling experimental discoveries. State-of-the-art uses of Machine Learning are considered ‘model-independent’ by the High-Energy Physics community; a verdict shared by several philosophers. In this paper, we dig into the details of unsupervised anomaly detection and show that even modest senses of model-independence are doubt-worthy, once considerations of robustness are factored in. We also offer reasons to think that the theme generalizes beyond the narrow context of High-Energy Physics.
items.title: Deep Learning Discovery Algorithms in High-Energy Physics and the Conflict Between Model-Independence and Robustness
Building responsible AI: a trilateral framework integrating ethics, design and regulation

items.abstract: Abstract The rapid ascent of decentralized prediction platforms such as Polymarket signals more than a regulatory or financial controversy. This article argues that while prediction platforms represent a hyper-concentrated, automated case study, they instantiate a broader infrastructural condition of late technocapitalism: the hyperstitional collapse between representation and execution. Drawing on Nick Land’s accelerationist framework, the sociology of financial markets, and digital epistemology, we contend that prediction markets—much like conventional opinion polling, forward guidance, and algorithmic models—do not merely reflect probabilities but actively produce the futures they claim to forecast. However, whereas traditional polling operates through diffuse, human-mediated feedback loops (e.g., strategic voting and bandwagon dynamics), prediction markets intensify this operational logic by coupling real-time financial incentives, capital-weighted aggregation, and automated execution. We examine this hyperstitional condition across three registers: epistemological, ontological, and ethical.
items.title: Shaping the future as we bet

items.abstract: Abstract Emerging technologies pose various ethical challenges, including the need to assess their risks adequately. Still, the roles of different forms of rationality and power in assessing risks have not been fully scrutinized. To address this, we must differentiate forms of rationality to conceptualize power: instrumental, technical, and probabilistic. The latter has gained more power through the rise of artificial intelligence (AI), focusing mainly on optimization and accuracy. These forms of power and rationality lead to different conceptualizations of risk: real, hypothetical, and predictive risk. The ethical issues surrounding AI have not yet been fully scrutinized, since they are mainly approached through a lens of probabilistic rationality. I argue that optimizing algorithms to increase accuracy or engagement distracts from assessing whether AI-based systems are adequate for certain tasks. Furthermore, I discuss ways to govern AI-based systems through participatory processes and standardization that enable control and autonomous judgment in the deployment and use of such systems.
items.title: Beyond optimization: power, rationality and ethical risk assessment of AI
Toward understanding AI adoption in the Global South: an empirical study of creative practitioners’ experiences in Iran

items.abstract: I start by assembling three images, the first and third of which can be found online.
items.title: ‘Are there no foxes in the human soul?’ A Midgleyean Metaphysics for Mixed Communities

items.abstract: Abstract Scholarship about the Chinese Question has largely understood it as a “coolie” question, but what if it was reframed in terms of merchants? Well-studied US anti-Chinese laws like the 1882 Chinese Exclusion Act targeted working-class rather than elite Chinese, like merchants and students. But in 1921, the US-controlled Insular Government in the Philippines enacted a statute known as the Chinese Bookkeeping Act (Act No. 2972), marking a moment when US Chinese exclusion laws were directed toward businessowners. The act banned Chinese-language record-keeping and affected merchants ranging from small storeowners to multi-millionaire tycoons. A group of Chinese merchants in the Philippines sued the colonial government and appealed their case to the US Supreme Court, which ruled the Bookkeeping Act unconstitutional in 1926. For the “coolie” Chinese question, the US Supreme Court said “yes” to exclusion, but for the merchant Chinese question, the Court said “no.” The Court’s rejection of a merchant Chinese exclusion became part of the Philippines’ transformation into a US colony. In relation to a patriotic Filipino capital and unmarked Euro-American capital, Chinese capital won rights even as it was framed within US law as “alien” by American and Filipino judges and politicians and, surprisingly, by the Chinese merchants themselves.
items.title: From Exclusion to Protection: Chinese Merchant Capital in the Philippines Under US Law and Empire, 1921–1926

items.abstract: Abstract This paper presents a unified theory of the truth conditions and probability of indicative conditionals and their compounds in a trivalent framework. The semantics validates a Reduction Theorem: any compound of conditionals is semantically equivalent to a simple conditional. We obtain Stalnaker’s Thesis in full generality and generalize Adams’s p-validity into a criterion for valid uncertain inference. Finally, we show that Bayesian updating on an indicative conditional is tantamount to updating on the corresponding material conditional.
items.title: Probability for Trivalent Conditionals

items.abstract: This paper offers an original non‐consequentialist justification for the ‘bulk discount’ given to offenders who are sentenced for multiple counts in a single proceeding, a discount that is available in most jurisdictions. Existing justifications for this practice face serious objections. I propose a new account, ‘Lexical Local Justification’. On this account, imposing a long total sentence for a large number of minor offences is problematic because, in such a case, each individual sentence would materially contribute to depriving the offender of a high‐order good (such as the ability to pursue a meaningful life project) that a minor offence does not warrant taking away. One advantage of my account is that it preserves local punitive desert (the principle that the punishment for a particular crime should match that crime); it relies neither on non‐local punitive desert (the principle that the total punishment for a group of offences should match that group as a whole) nor on the claim that there is always an increasing returns relationship between the actual severity of a sentence and its length.
items.title: Why Bulk Discount for Multiple Offenders? A Lexical Local Justification
Codifying the Short Code

items.abstract: ABSTRACT In Chaoan He's “Farewell to the Modal Theory of Luck,” he constructs a Frankfurt‐style counterexample to modal theories of luck (LOTTERY*), and he argues that this counterexample obviates standard modalist responses to other prominent counterexamples in the literature. However, as I argue in this reply, the counterexample is not as decisive as He suggests. In section 1, I explicate (i) the modal theory of luck, (ii) He's counterexample, and (iii) a possible modalist response. In section 2, I argue that this response is a version of a strategy that He himself considers effective against non‐Frankfurt‐style counterexamples. If my argument succeeds, then the modal theory remains viable. I do not propose revising the modal theory; rather, I argue that, once we attend to the modal profile of the generating process, standard modal resources suffice to explain the intuition of luck in LOTTERY*.
items.title: Modal Combat: A Process‐Based Rejoinder to Luck's Farewell
Staging disease without illness: ethical issues of the Huntington’s Disease Integrated Staging System (HD-ISS)
The Weight of Reasons: A Framework for Ethics, written by Chris Tucker
What Should Individuals Do About Climate Change? A Debate, written by M. Hourdequin and D.C. Shahar
