items.abstract: Abstract In recent years, feelings of offense have taken on a starring role in multiple campus controversies. In this paper, I will argue that offense has important moral work to do, but it can only do its work if certain background conditions are met. I begin by sketching several cases of offense on college campuses. I then go on to highlight the central features of what might be described as our current culture of offense. While I think that the apparent rise of this culture of offense is regrettable, I also believe, taking a page from a prominent strand of thought in feminist moral epistemology, that feelings of offense can do important moral work. After sketching a tripartite account of offense, I defend a model of the relationship between feelings of offense, the offensive, and offense-based intervention which I call the Offense as Affective Answer Model. I argue that offense can do its moral work only if certain background conditions are in place, background conditions that are missing in the present culture of offense. Most importantly, a healthy moral culture will be one where assessments of offense in terms of its fit are central and disagreement about fittingness are hashed out through dialogical processes. If we are not willing to subject feelings of offense to these dialogical processes through which we acknowledge and recognize that some tokens of offense are unfitting, offense will not be able to do the important moral work claimed for it.
items.title: Putting Offense in Its (Fitting) Place (On Campus)

items.abstract: Abstract Collective harm cases are cases in which the actions of a number of people result in a morally significant outcome, but no individual’s actions seem to make a difference to the occurrence of that outcome. This paper argues against the “Instrumentality Thesis,” advanced by Nefsky, on which any successful approach to collective harm cases must be instrumental in the sense that the reasons which it gives against participating in collective harm must involve that action’s influence on the outcome. First, I argue that Nefsky’s own account of collective harm, based on the notion of a “non-superfluous cause,” does not succeed as an instrumental approach. Second, I argue that Nefsky’s objections to non-instrumental views fail, and that we have good reason to think that a successful account of collective harm problems will be non-instrumental in character.
items.title: Collective Harm and Instrumental Reasons

items.abstract: ABSTRACT This article examines the ethical shortcomings of selective apologies: cases in which a party apologises for one instance of injustice while refusing to apologise for others. Existing work on apologies has not addressed the particular kind of wrongdoing associated with the making of selective apologies. Apologising to one victim but refusing to apologise to another without good reason adds insult to injury. One is both failing to fulfil an existing duty, and adding an additional dimension of disrespect to one's extant moral failing. In addition, the making of a selective apology may undermine other apologies that one has made. Selectively apologising could only be permissible if one had well‐founded reasons to prioritise some cases over others. Determining if this is true necessitates an honest accounting and evaluation of the full range of one's past wrongdoing. The article develops this argument in three stages: first, by analysing contemporary examples of selective apologies, with a particular focus on the British state; second, by exploring the normative structure of selectively apologising, and third, by considering how the passage of time and the scale of political responsibility complicate the ethics of state apology.
items.title: The Inadequacy of Selective Apologies

items.abstract: Abstract The academic debate on the governance of neurotechnology has progressively shifted from proposals to create new lists of so-called neurorights toward the reinterpretation of existing human rights, with freedom of thought attracting particular attention, among a broader set of candidate rights. This article examines whether freedom of thought can currently perform that anchoring role in Latin American jurisdictions. Drawing on a comparative analysis of constitutional texts, jurisprudence, and the Inter-American human rights system, the article argues that freedom of thought does not yet possess a clear, strong, and autonomous normative content in Latin American domestic law and in its regional human rights system. As a complementary and, in the region, more operative anchor, it argues that human dignity, which in several Latin American constitutional orders functions as an absolute autonomous fundamental right of direct application with extensive jurisprudential development, constitutes a more operationally effective legal basis for absolute prohibitions on the use of people as instruments or objects, and can protect them from coercive neurotechnological interventions. The article proposes that human dignity supplies the absolute floor against instrumentalization and coercion, while freedom of thought, as its doctrinal development advances, can complement that floor with the protection of the forum internum . It further contends that any rights-based strategy is structurally insufficient on its own, because rights depend on judicial interpretation that is inherently contextual and contingent, and therefore supports a multilevel governance approach combining the interpretation of existing rights, soft-law principles, and potential specific hard-law provisions.
items.title: The Case for Human Dignity in Neurotechnology Governance: A Latin American Perspective Beyond Freedom of Thought

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Beginning with a recent high‐profile case in mainland China, this paper argues that the current prohibition on social egg freezing for single women cannot be justified from a Confucian ethical perspective. We first explain why Confucian ethics provides a normatively appropriate and socially salient framework for evaluating reproductive policy in the Chinese context. We then articulate a theoretical model that we term Confucian familist virtue ethics . A central contribution of the paper is to distinguish between Confucian ethical ideals and its minimal standards. While the ideals—such as timely marriage and childbearing within an intact family—are properly the objects of moral aspiration and voluntary cultivation, only violations of the minimal standards warrant legal prohibition. On this basis, we develop three lines of argument to show that although social egg freezing by single women may fall short of Confucian aspirational ideals, it does not violate the ethical minimum. Accordingly, it does not justify coercive state intervention. Finally, we examine the predictive concern that permitting social egg freezing would undermine marital norms or substantially increase single motherhood. We argue that such negative effects are empirically uncertain and in principle manageable through regulatory design. They therefore fail to provide sufficient grounds for a categorical prohibition.
items.title: Why Social Egg Freezing for Single Women Should Not Be Prohibited: A Confucian Perspective

items.abstract: ABSTRACT This response examines Joel Cox's proposal to reconceptualise fetal moral status as “imminent personhood.” While welcoming Cox's effort to move beyond static potential/actual personhood binaries, it argues that the concept of imminence remains metaphysically suggestive but institutionally under‐determined. Legal systems cannot operate on continuously variable metaphysical properties; they require discrete and administrable allocations of rights, duties, and powers. To address this gap, the paper proposes an institutional incidence framework, in which legal status is understood as the selective assignment of juridical incidents according to regulatory objectives without treating metaphysical classification as dispositive. On this view, the central question is not simply whether the fetus is a person (actual, potential, or imminent), but which incidents of legal status should attach at particular stages and for particular regulatory purposes. This reframes the legal regulation of abortion as a problem of institutional design rather than ontological determination. The paper argues that such an approach better explains existing legal practice, avoids threshold arbitrariness, and enables stable legal regulation amid persistent moral disagreement. While Cox's imminence proposal captures an important phenomenology of fetal development, an institutional incidence framework provides a more durable foundation for legal and policy architecture in pluralistic societies.
items.title: From Imminence to Institutional Incidence: Rethinking Fetal Status Beyond Metaphysical Classification
The Philosophy of Force: Violence, Domination, and the Ethics of Republican War. C. J.Finlay, 2025. Oxford, Oxford University Press. x + 330 pp, £119 (hb)

items.abstract: Abstract Given the rapid acceleration of the climate crisis, the IPCC has deemed Carbon Dioxide Removal (CDR) technologies as unavoidable to sufficiently mitigate the crisis. In this context, engineering biology (EngBio) is increasingly gaining traction in CDR research. While the deployment of EngBio is perceived by some as inherently high-risk for society, the economy, and the environment, the risks posed by insufficiently abated climate change are likely to be irreparable. Against this background, a pilot study was conducted, aimed at exploring experts’ perspectives on risk in decision-making regarding the use of advanced EngBio applications to develop CDR technologies. Our results show that EngBio experts are moderately or highly open to discussing, accepting, or taking the risks of using EngBio-based CDR. Our findings also indicate expert trust in the potential of rapid advancements in EngBio-based CDR technologies. While these findings do not entail an unconditional and uncritical acceptance of all risks arising from using EngBio for CDR purposes, they underscore a notion of risk as integral to environmental responsibility, namely as necessary to avoid the higher risk of insufficiently abated climate change. In our view, this notion of risk highlights the epistemic context in which ethical debates on CDR will unfold as the climate crisis intensifies, shifting the focus from traditional risk-risk analysis to how EngBio‑based CDR can contribute to environmental responsibility and to effective and ethical decarbonisation.
items.title: Expert perspectives on framing risk in engineering biology: anticipating ethical discourse about climate change mitigation

items.abstract: Abstract Thinking hard is hard. Cognitive misers like us are therefore inclined to seek extreme cognitive assistance : assistance that is ubiquitously available, highly substitutive, and relatively domain-general. Increasingly, we are being offered assistance like this as the default mode of cognition – it is being embedded in the infrastructure of our digital lives. But whatever its merits for adults, providing extreme cognitive assistance to children is pro tanto morally wrong. This is because the cognitive capacities that make a person self-governing are skills: they are built through deliberate, regular exercise and lost without it. Extreme cognitive assistance removes both the opportunities for that exercise and the incentive to undertake it. Maybe this won’t matter: in a future awash with extreme cognitive assistance, maybe persons won’t need or want to think for themselves. But people should decide for themselves how much of their cognitive self-governance to hand over; and doing that requires having the capacity for cognitive self-governance in the first place.
items.title: Cognitive enfeeblement by design

items.abstract: Abstract Healthcare professionals (HCPs) and the patients they treat would benefit from professional ethical guidance for the use of AI (PEG-AI) in healthcare. A proactive approach, asserting unified and standardised guidance covering all HCPs in the United Kingdom, would assert clear and authoritative standards for HCP practice to abide by. This rapid scoping review seeks to aid this goal by answering the question: What ethical principles, rules, or claims that can guide the use of AI in professional healthcare practice can be identified within the literature?. The literature search resulted in the inclusion of 124 items and generated 9 overarching themes comprising 33 distinct normative claims about the ethical use of AI in healthcare. This review captures current published thinking about principles to govern AI use in clinical settings across a wide range of peer-reviewed literature, grey literature, and formal guidance. This provides a baseline on which to build unified guidance across the healthcare professions.
items.title: Professional ethical guidance for AI use (PEG-AI) in healthcare: a rapid scoping review
From traditional to distributed responsibility: moral responsibility in generative artificial intelligence

items.abstract: Abstract What makes knowledge more valuable than mere true belief? This is the so-called value problem . Some epistemologists think that providing a solution to this problem is a key desideratum for theories of knowledge. One simple argument for this position starts with the claim that knowledge is intuitively more valuable than true belief. A more subtle and ambitious argument is rooted in the idea that theorists about knowledge must explain why knowledge is distinctively valuable, on pain of embarrassment; for without such an explanation, the thinking seems to go, epistemologists must confront the awkward possibility that they are spending time and energy on an unworthy subject. In what follows, I flesh out each of the arguments sketched above in a number of ways, and I argue that none of these versions succeed. The moral is that the value problem does not have the metaepistemological significance that is sometimes attributed to it.
items.title: Metaepistemology and the Value Problem

items.abstract: Abstract The UK’s Athena Swan Charter positions itself as a policy instrument, an award-based scheme for improving gender equality through self-assessment, evidence gathering, and action planning. I argue that this description overlooks the fact that Athena Swan is also a semiotic framework that governs gender through naming, iconography, and the public performance of institutional virtue. I defend three claims. First, the Charter’s mythic-inflected branding, acronym, and iconography frame the ideal of intelligible, respectable gender-equality practice that is in tension with emancipatory aims of loosening coercive gender norms and challenging credibility hierarchies. Second, insofar as Athena Swan operates by conferring public credentials, I elucidate how its semiotics function not merely expressively but also as instruments of legitimation that shape incentives, trust, institutional identity, and the handling of dissent. Third, I contend that the Charter’s credential economy is supported by audit feminism which abstracts equality into auditable artefacts (documents, metrics, and narratives) assessed as a basis for external recognition. The result is an audit regime that intensifies performativity, encouraging institutions to substitute appearances for substantive change and to commodify individuals as interchangeable units in a managed representational economy.
items.title: Innocence by Accreditation: Mythic Branding and Audit Feminism in Athena Swan

items.abstract: Abstract Hospital-based violence intervention programs (HVIPs) help survivors of violent injury to return to physical, psychological, financial, and social health by addressing a broad range of social determinants of health and reducing the risk of future injury. This work requires connections to a range of providers and services, which often requires the sharing of patient health information. While HIPAA gives providers more discretion to share information to address health-related social needs and care coordination than many providers realize, patients can and should be the ones deciding what health information is shared, with whom it is shared, and under what circumstances. Providers, patients, and programs like HVIPs would benefit from greater clarity on appropriate information-sharing practices. In this article, we consider the real and perceived barriers to information sharing to address social needs and we make recommendations for practice, research, and policy to improve how patient information is shared to address social needs, with relevance for a wide range of interventions.
items.title: Navigating Health Information Sharing to Address Social Needs: Practice, Research, and Policy Recommendations from Hospital-Based Violence Intervention

items.abstract: Abstract Words can have inherently multiple meanings; therefore, semantics can directly impact policies and behaviours. In regulatory practice, semantics refers to the specific, actionable meaning behind terminology, and attention to semantics can help ensure that legal frameworks are interpreted accurately. Refining semantics is not a purely theoretical exercise, but a subtle yet powerful element that has the potential to make the regulatory system more efficient in setting priorities and more reliable in meeting societal expectations and needs. When their intended purpose does not align with their true meaning, labels widely used in pharmaceutical regulation such as “breakthrough,” “orphans,” or “unmet medical need” risks undermining the clarity and precision essential to a sound regulatory framework. In addition, differences in definitions, scopes, eligibility criteria, and incentives can obstruct the efficient convergence of efforts in drug development and access. As pharmaceutical investments and clinical research increasingly transcend borders, the adoption of consistent terminology and regulatory definitions becomes crucial. This alignment can enhance cooperation among investors, governments, regulators, researchers, health care practitioners, and patients.
items.title: The Impact of Semantics in Medicines Regulation

items.abstract: There’s a lot to like about Respect and Loathing (not least the Hunter Thompson reference!): it breaks new ground by using empirical methods to investigate a theoretical concept; it is ambitious, taking on a key element of the current democratic crisis; and it is engaging and readable. It’s a real achievement and will inspire many young graduate students to emulate its methodology, leading to a useful rapprochement between political theory and political science. I also agree with a lot of the book: it is incredibly level-headed and sensible. I want to investigate two claims about which I wasn’t fully persuaded: first, is the liberal respect paradox really a matter of recognition respect? Second, is an egalitarian pluralist ethos the right response to the crisis of respect?
items.title: Does Contemporary Democracy Show a Crisis of Respect?
Linda M.G. Zerilli: A Democratic Theory of Truth. (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 2025. Pp. xiii, 189.)

items.abstract: Abstract Chapter 2 of On Liberty , titled ‘Of the Liberty of Thought and Discussion’, develops a well-known epistemic argument for free speech. While it makes a plausible case for open-mindedness and diversity of opinion, it also appears to encapsulate some of the flaws that critics attribute to ‘free speech ideology’. This paper defends On Liberty against this criticism and proposes a new interpretation of the chapter’s objectives and its contemporary relevance, the power-critical account. While I conclude that chapter 2 fails to show that it is always epistemically harmful to silence opinions, I defend the Millian idea that a robust principle of speaker immunity is required for the transition to an ideal, reflectively stable society.
items.title:
What Does Chapter Two of
                    On Liberty
                    Really Achieve? Introducing the Power-Critical Account
Reparations and redress for historical injustice
Disjunctures: Indigenous redirections in political theory
Talking with language models
The Claims of Our Hearts

items.abstract: Abstract According to Paul Boghossian’s ‘Inference Problem’, rule-following generates a regress because it involves inference, which itself involves rule-following. Boghossian claims the Problem leads to an ‘antinomy of pure reason’, showing that ‘we both must—and cannot—make sense of the notion of someone’s following a rule’. I argue that there is no antinomy by proposing a solution to the Problem based on the idea that following a rule consists in acting on a commitment to exercising one’s knowledge of how to follow it.
items.title: Competent rule-following

items.abstract: ABSTRACT This article examines a document that the ChatGPT interface made available during an exchange about capacity for saved memories. The response presented the reorganisation of writing rules for a narrative project as already completed, although my request concerned capacity alone, and no recorded prompt requested a file or specified the proposed hierarchy. Earlier, I had copied every visible saved memory entry verbatim into another document, allowing comparison in both directions to identify corresponding formulations and changes in their placement or prescriptive force. The phenomenological account follows my remembered reading and remains separate from those findings. In the linked document, rules appeared within a hierarchy not specified in my request and reading those formulations in their new positions changed how I understood decisions. Available records establish the limited request and the sequence through which the organised file became available without identifying the operations that produced the file. In this case, I formulated the rules without articulating their comprehensive relations, and recognising my formulations did not mean understanding what their new placement asserted. ChatGPT presented the organisation as already complete, whereas a human collaborator could have presented the same arrangement together with reasons.
items.title:
A Document Beyond the Request: A Phenomenological Case Study of
                    ChatGPT

items.abstract: Are stringent vaccine promotion policies associated with higher vaccine uptake? We argue policy stringency, which changes the costs and benefits of immunisation choices, can affect individual vaccination decisions. In a survey of G-7 countries, 22% of respondents ( n = 42,417) said they did not trust the Covid-19 vaccine, but half of them reported having at least one vaccination. We investigate factors associated with take-up. Our data indicate a high-stringency policy environment (with vaccine mandates and travel restrictions) is associated with increased uptake of the initial vaccination protocol (7 percentage points) compared to a low-stringency policy environment. Among those who did not trust the Covid-19 vaccine, a high-stringency policy environment is associated with increased uptake of the initial vaccine (16 percentage points) and the booster vaccine (20 percentage points). Our findings suggest high-stringency policies can promote vaccine uptake but raise questions about how to strike the right balance between persuasive and coercive policies.
items.title: Stringent policies were associated with greater Covid-19 vaccine uptake including among those who did not trust the vaccine

items.abstract: This article argues that the existence of financial institutions considered ‘too big to fail’ (TBTF) represents a systemic injustice requiring fundamental reform of the existing financial system. Drawing on and extending recent work on structural domination in republican political theory, the article develops the concept of ‘systemic institutional domination’ to capture the distinctive form of unfreedom that TBTF engenders. Systemic institutional domination is a reflexive form of domination, where the democratic state is subjected to uncontrolled power vested in identifiable financial institutions but grounded in the norms, rules and regulations of the financial system that the state itself enacts and upholds. Because the dominated public institution is at once the constitutive author of the system and the only agent capable of reforming it, TBTF confronts republican theory with a case of second-order domination: domination of the institution charged with securing nondomination. The article identifies four dimensions of systemic domination: effective compulsion to bail out failing megabanks; de facto legal impunity; the systematic subversion of tax enforcement; and background consolidatory pressure on public finances. The article concludes by discussing the democratic paradox involved in abolishing TBTF: namely, that the dominated institution – the democratic state – is the only institution that could reform the dominating system.
items.title: Too big to fail: On a systemic injustice of modern finance
Rethinking Ethical Employment Pathways for People with Intellectual Disabilities: A Systemic Nested Alliances Model

items.abstract: Abstract Many philosophers understand logic as a theory of truth preservation that is value-neutral and becomes prescriptive only when combined with external, non-logical rules. In this article, we develop an alternative view informed by recent work in the philosophy of scientific modeling. We argue that certain logical systems, in certain scientific and philosophical practices, are used as normative scientific models: they represent their targets by combining descriptive idealizations with assumptions adopted—and defended—on normative grounds. We propose a practice-based account of normative models in science, according to which the normative character of a model depends on its use in the relevant research practice, and apply it to the case of classical first-order logic, in its uses as a model of correct reasoning. Finally, we show how our proposal opens up a new perspective on several contemporary debates in the philosophy of logic.
items.title: Logic as Normative Modeling
Beyond blanket prohibition: generative ai, accountable authorship, and the genealogy of thought
The Aspiration of a Future Death Metal Fanatic
Reconsidering Charity in Relation to Social Justice: An Argument for Normative Complementarity

items.abstract: Abstract This paper develops an axiomatic framework for a non-referential theory of meaning by formally characterizing intra-theoretical synonymy through inferential and syntactic criteria rather than through reference or truth conditions. Building on formalist and inferentialist traditions, a series of axioms are proposed that satisfy basic semantic principles such as theory-dependence, semantic holism, and (restricted) compositionality. The resulting systems ( TS 0 and its extensions) satisfy these principles to progressively greater degrees, yielding a sufficiently fine-grained notion of synonymy. The framework thus shows that equality of meaning can be characterized in non-referential terms, while illuminating the limits of non-referential meaning.
items.title: Towards a non-referential theory of meaning: intra-theoretical synonymy

items.abstract: Abstract Some people are safe from harm yet remain in positions where things could easily go badly for them. Their proximity to worlds where something bad happens to them makes their situation ethically precarious. In some worlds, they are excluded, punished, or abandoned, which deserves attention in its own right. We argue that this is not just a matter of risk or harm, but about how people are placed within the space of possible worlds. We explain this through a modal account of difference-making and use it to highlight attitudinal responses fitting to fragility and introduce duties of modal security: moral reasons to protect one another from positions where small changes could lead to significant loss.
items.title: Fragile lives and moral duties: on the ethics of modal security

items.abstract: Abstract Metaphors in science communication do more than simplify complex ideas; they impose certain epistemic frameworks with the potential to steer public attitudes and behavior. In this paper, we investigate the effects of metaphorical framing on public understanding and evaluation of de-extinction, a field where dominant metaphors (“resurrection,” “bringing back to life”) have been criticized for mischaracterizing the technology and fostering undue optimism. We presented a nationally representative sample of the Spanish population ( N = 1,522) with popular science descriptions of de-extinction that varied only in metaphorical framing and assessed its downstream effects on misinformation, perceived scientific rigor, attitudes, funding preferences, and sharing intentions. Promotional metaphors increased misinformation relative to the neutral condition, while critical metaphors reduced it. These effects occurred without altering readers’ perception of the text’s scientific rigor—a dissociation we characterize as credibility without comprehension . Critical metaphors also reduced support for de-extinction, whereas promotional metaphors did not boost support above baseline levels in the neutral condition. Funding allocations and sharing intentions, though related to misinformation, were unaffected by metaphorical framing. We propose that metaphors function as epistemic conditioning devices : they influence downstream judgments not through direct persuasion, but by structuring the understanding upon which those judgments are formed. These findings bear on philosophical debates about the role of metaphors in science, the epistemic preconditions of democratic engagement with emerging technologies, and the limits of lexical precision as a remedy for public misinformation.
items.title: De-extinction, resurrection and biological Frankensteins: scientific metaphors and their impact on public perception

items.abstract: Abstract In the field of mental health, the role of Experts by Experience (ExE) has been gaining increasing attention. However, theoretical research on this topic remains limited, leaving it unclear how ExE can contribute to improving psychiatric research and services. In this paper, I propose two explanations for the contributions of ExE, drawing on perspectives from feminist philosophy of science. The first explanation focuses on the epistemic capabilities of ExE, grounded in standpoint theory. This approach highlights the unique individual potential of ExE as a factor that enhances psychiatric research and services. The second explanation underscores the epistemic diversity between ExE and professionals in research and/or service contexts, focusing on the value of epistemic diversity within teams and communities. The main difference is that epistemic capabilities focus on the individual, while epistemic diversity focuses on the collective. I argue that these two explanatory models should be chosen based on research design, but in the context of psychiatric PPI, considering ExE participation not only in terms of standpoint but also in terms of epistemic diversity may suggest a more inclusive approach to PPI.
items.title: Two explanations of experts by experience in psychiatry: epistemic capabilities or epistemic diversity

The House That Family Money Built: How Inequality Governs Debt and Wealth Management
                    . By Allison Anna Tait. Oakland: University of California Press, 2026.

Florian Couveinhes Matsumoto & Nathalie Clarenc Bicudo eds.
                    Le Rojava démocratique et le droit

items.journal: The Journal of Medicine and Philosophy: A Forum for Bioethics and Philosophy of Medicine
items.title: To Our Guest Reviewers: Thank You
Wellbeing Frameworks and Future Generations
From principles to practice: an Implementation Decision-Tool for Ethical AI in clinical governance
Giving voice without guardrails: lived experience and the ethics of epistemic mediation in public health
Structural realities and personal impact: how ethics teaching can prepare students for early clinical practice
Hobbes and Political Contractarianism: Selected Writings, written by D. P. Gauthier

items.abstract: Abstract The question who (or which things) are the agents has attracted a very wide range of different answers. For some, only humans can satisfy the necessary conditions for agency; others extend the concept to a wide range of animals or even plants; and some believe there are also agents outside the biological realm. Do these different answers constitute substantively different views about the same question? Or are the disagreements really terminological ones, at root, owed to different ‘definitions’ of agency? In this paper, I try to provide examples both of disputes which do, and disputes which do not seem amenable to this sort of terminological deflation. I then try to diagnose the difference, by offering a view about how we must think about the concept of agency if it is to play a role in genuinely substantive disagreement, combining Susan Carey’s idea that agency is a ‘core concept’ with an externalist account of how the concept must work, if it is to figure in thoroughly substantive disputes about who the agents are.
items.title: Who are the agents?

items.abstract: Abstract I argue that questions can be transmitted through asking just as beliefs are transmitted through testimony. Just as we rely on testifiers to assert only when their epistemic position is good enough, so (I argue) we rely on queriers to ask questions only if they are in a position to know that the question is sound, which guarantees that the asked question has an answer. Along the way, I argue against the view that we can only ask questions of people who (we know) know the answer to our questions. A recurring theme of the paper is that we learn about the norms for asking not just in those cases in which we straightforwardly comply with or violate them, but also by the ways we creatively deviate from the norms to accomplish our conversational goals.
items.title: Asking Questions Aloud: A Case for Interrogative Transmission

items.abstract: Abstract This Article investigates how law conceptualizes the temporality of migration, exposing a mismatch between the legal framework and migrants’ lived experiences. It shows that the dominant mode, which views migration as a sequential process, fails to capture the realities of migration. The Article argues that both epistemic and human rights arguments call for remedying this mismatch. In response, it introduces migration as simultaneity, which better reflects migrants’ experiences and the interplay between space, place, and time in migration and belonging. The argument proceeds in three stages. First, it examines migration as a sequence, the prevailing concept embedded in international, European, and domestic migration and citizenship laws. This sequential framework operates through linearity and temporariness, which function as primary mechanisms for governing inclusion and exclusion. Second, drawing on migration studies and anthropology, it critiques this model, showing its inability to account for how migrants perceive and experience migration and belonging. Finally, it argues that strong power asymmetries shaping the regulation of migration demand a temporal conception that better aligns with migrants’ lived experiences. To this end, it advances migration as simultaneity and suggests that this concept can inform legal frameworks regulating migration and belonging.
items.title: Everything Everywhere All at Once – From Migration as Sequence to Migration as Simultaneity

items.abstract: Abstract Modern shareholder primacy is commonly justified by reference to an equilibrium famously articulated by Milton Friedman: business may pursue profits provided it operates “within the rules of the game.” The legitimacy of shareholder–oriented governance thus depends on effective legal mechanisms capable of constraining harmful profit-seeking. This Article argues that corporate sanctioning regimes play a constitutive role in sustaining that equilibrium and in structuring the relationship between shareholder-oriented corporate purpose and stakeholder protection. Drawing on examples from EU competition enforcement, benefit–based attribution models of corporate criminal liability in the United States and Finland, and the organizational failure-to-prevent regime exemplified by the UK Bribery Act, the Article shows how sanctioning regimes institutionalize competing conceptions of the corporation as an economic instrument or as an organizational actor. Economically calibrated liability models reflect a conception of the corporation primarily as an economic instrument, framing compliance in instrumental terms and narrowing the boundaries of corporate accountability. By contrast, organizationally informed liability models embed responsibility in internal governance structures and preventive capacities. The Article conceptualizes this development as an emerging organizational turn in corporate sanctioning in which liability increasingly serves to shape internal corporate governance, encourage the prevention of harm, and protect stakeholders. It thereby conditions the legitimacy of corporate profit-seeking and redefines the institutional role of corporate sanctions in shaping corporate responsibility.
items.title: The Organizational Turn in Corporate Sanctioning Regimes: Rebalancing Profit–Seeking and Stakeholder Protection

items.abstract: Abstract Socio-legal scholarship increasingly conceptualizes legal consciousness as relational, yet research has focused primarily on how individuals’ understandings of law are shaped through interpersonal interactions and social relationships. Less attention has been paid to how broader cultural beliefs circulating within political-economic systems shape whether – and how – individuals invoke or refrain from invoking law when interpreting everyday experiences. We extend relational legal consciousness scholarship by examining how macro-level cultural beliefs structure meaning-making about digital data privacy in the United States. We analyze data from a survey experiment in which 600 respondents evaluated vignettes describing secondary uses of personal data by government and private corporations for different motives. Quantitative analyses of 2,555 vignette evaluations show that perceived acceptability varies systematically by both actor and motive. Interpretive analysis of open-ended responses reveals that participants draw on multiple cultural beliefs – including everyday expectations of legality, market logics, institutional trust, and narratives of technological inevitability – when evaluating these practices. By showing how cultural beliefs related and unrelated to law and legality work together to shape everyday interpretations of privacy encroachments, we extend relational legal consciousness scholarship beyond interpersonal relationships to encompass the broader cultural environment in which legal meaning-making occurs. We further demonstrate that this relational dynamic has political-economic consequences: a diverse range of cultural beliefs – not only narratives of commodification and technological inevitability – can normalize, conditionally legitimate, or challenge the data practices associated with informational capitalism.
items.title: Relational legal consciousness in the age of informational capitalism: how Americans make sense of data privacy

items.abstract: Abstract This article develops the concept of delegated gatekeeping to explain regulatory systems where a primary gatekeeper (the “principal”) delegates revocable roles of support withholder or provider to other gatekeepers (“agents”). Delegation requires that agents assume non-traditional gatekeeping roles such as reputational stewardship (safeguarding the principal’s reputational capital). To illustrate delegated gatekeeping concretely, this article conducts a detailed case study of the London Stock Exchange’s Alternative Investment Market (“AIM”). It argues that reputational incentives can partially alleviate agent gatekeepers’ conflicts of interest, and that these incentives have strengthened on AIM relative to historic levels.
items.title: Delegated Gatekeeping: A Study of the Alternative Investment Market (“AIM”)

items.abstract: Abstract Bernard Williams’s account of regret contains a lacuna with respect to the appropriate emotion for contributors to feel in response to faultless group harms. While he delineates ‘agent-regret’ for agents faultlessly causing harm and ‘spectator-regret’ for observers, neither suffices for individuals who unintentionally or unforeseeably contribute to harms resulting from group actions. This paper investigates the fitting emotion for such cases. I contend that contributors occupy ‘as-if positions’ in that they are quasi-agents in virtue of their own contributions and quasi-spectators owing to others’ roles. This dual standpoint generates a ‘biperspective’ that calls for a distinct form of regret, which is reducible to neither agent-regret nor spectator-regret but synthesises elements of both. I term this distinct form ‘biperspectival regret’. Taking the appropriateness of emotions to depend on their formal objects, I formulate the formal object of biperspectival regret as the ‘comparative disvalue of group harm to which one faultlessly contributed’. Because this formal object corresponds to the defining features of faultless group harms, I argue that biperspectival regret is the warranted emotion for contributors to experience in such scenarios.
items.title: Biperspectival Regret: The Appropriate Emotion for Faultless Group Harm

items.abstract: Abstract Disabled people continue to experience social exclusion and denial of meaningful belonging despite legal commitments to independent living and autonomy. This paper brings disability studies, legal scholarship and philosophical debates around a right against social deprivation into conversation. We argue that the concepts of social access needs and social contribution needs provide a valuable framework for identifying harms that existing disability rights and human rights approaches often fail to recognise or adequately address. At the same time, rather than simply applying the right against social deprivation to disability, we contend that disability offers a critical lens through which the right itself must be rethought. Drawing on critical disability studies, we foreground interdependence, care, relationality and vulnerability, while exposing ableist assumptions that may shape theorising in this area. Through engagement with disability law and rights frameworks, we explore the potential of this dialogue to reconfigure understandings of rights, responsibility and justice.
items.journal: International Journal of Law in Context
items.title: Disability, relationships and a right against social deprivation
The affinities between democracy and science
Abstraction and the Value Form
Ori Beck on reformed empiricism

items.abstract: Most of the discussion of adversarialism has taken place in the context of criminal justice and it is often assumed that family courts are not adversarial, particularly in child arrangements cases where the stated focus is the future welfare of children. Drawing on data from a recent study of child arrangements proceedings in England and Wales this article will argue that despite modifications to the adversarial process, adversarialism remains a structural barrier to safe processes and outcomes in cases where there are allegations of domestic abuse. It will be argued that the underpinning logic of adversarialism is fundamentally problematic in private family law proceedings given the high prevalence of domestic abuse in such cases reaching the family courts.
items.title: Adversarialism in the Family Courts in Child Arrangements Cases in England and Wales

items.abstract: ABSTRACT The determination of death by neurologic criteria (brain death) has increasingly become a topic of controversy. Here we address a question that provokes clinical ethics consultations and scholarly debate: “how should objections to the declaration of neurologic death be handled?” While much of the discourse on this question has focused on the legitimacy of the criteria for brain death determinations or the motivations of individuals' objections to declarations of death, our analysis addresses a deeper issue inherent in the conflicts in clinical settings. We argue that some objections to brain death cannot be explained away as grief, misunderstanding, or different religious beliefs. Rather, tensions between worldviews—fundamental standpoints or lenses through which humans experience and conceptualize the world around them—may drive conflicts around brain death. In what follows, we introduce the concept of worldview silencing as a means of recognizing the injustice that can occur when brain death objections grounded in alternative ontologies of death are unfairly dismissed or disrespected. Ultimately, we contend that the concept of worldview silencing offers moral guidance for just recognition of objections to brain death in practice, education, and policy.
items.title: Worldview Silencing: Recognizing Reasoned Objections to Brain Death

items.abstract: ABSTRACT According to a traditional conception, a fact is individuated by its constituents and the way these are structured. Lowe (1998) argues against this, claiming that there is no principled way to ascertain what the constituents of facts are and, therefore, there is no way to coherently individuate them. In this paper, I examine and reject Lowe's argument. It will be shown that there are different conceptions of facts, a fine‐grained and a coarse‐grained conception, and that both can coherently individuate facts. In my diagnosis, Lowe's argument arises from a conflation of both conceptions.
items.title: On the Identity of Facts: A Reply to Lowe

items.abstract: This article argues that the contemporary crisis of the public sphere cannot be adequately understood as a crisis of communication alone. What is at stake is a contraction of the horizon of the possible: a narrowing of the conditions under which alternatives can be imagined. Drawing on the Frankfurt School tradition, it develops a concept of imagination as a critical faculty grounded in Walter Benjamin’s characterisation of it as the “awareness of the de-formations of the future,” and traces its erosion through Marcuse’s analysis of one-dimensional society. The article proposes the model of Infrastructural Conditioning of Imagination (ICI), identifying three interdependent dynamics (filtering, familiarisation and anticipation) through which algorithmic systems pre-structure the field of the thinkable. Each dynamic bears on a distinct dimension of experience: filtering concerns the structure of access, familiarisation the structure of reception, and anticipation the structure of temporality. The article argues that this conditioning operates as a suppression of non-identity in Adorno’s sense, eroding the conditions of Erfahrung under which the preponderance of the object can function as a critical moment, at the level of the conditions through which subjectivity itself is formed.
items.title: The Contraction of the Possible: Algorithmic Infrastructures and the Erosion of Critical Imagination

items.abstract: Kristeva’s abjection theory is a popular framework for grappling with leaking bodies. Yet while exploring the significance of women's involuntary urination during sport, abject theory's insistence that pissing oneself must be identity shattering failed to convince us. Indeed, some women find pissing themselves to be identity forming as it marks the threshold beyond which one becomes a ‘serious’ athlete. Drawing on Sedgwick, we frame abjection as strong theory—able to explain some aspects of the experience well but unable to account for other aspects. To supplement our approach, we draw on sexuality studies for inspiration regarding how to approach involuntary urination during sport through weak theory. Rather than trying to proffer a totalizing explanation, weak theory foregrounds near and specific phenomena, allowing for variation and complexity. In this case, weak theory is analytically useful as it allows us to consider women's diverse responses to urinary leakages alongside mainstream cultural responses (disgust at the leaky body) and subcultural sporting norms (prioritization of sport performance). Further, weak theory allows us to attend to the gendered specificities of peeing in sport. Drawing on interviews with women strength athletes, we question what women's responses to their nuanced, specific experience of peeing themselves while resistance training tells us about women's place in sport and their bodily capacities. Ultimately, we argue that far from being abject, bodily leaks can be transformative, creating new subjectivities and new understandings of what women's bodies are capable of: namely, being simultaneously strong, beautiful, and leaky. This article contributes a grounded exploration of the limits of abjection theory by highlighting the necessity of considering cultural context and specific phenomena, arguing that weak theory is a useful lens through which to do so.
items.title:
‘Why are girls lifting that heavy if it makes
                    that
                    happen?’: From abjection to a weak theory of ‘pissing yourself’ in sport

items.abstract: Der Konsum von Online-Pornos, eine relativ weit verbreitete Praxis, hat im Vergleich zur philosophischen Diskussion über die abstrakte Natur der Pornografie und im Vergleich zur Ethik anderer Konsumentscheidungen vergleichsweise wenig philosophische Aufmerksamkeit erfahren. In diesem Beitrag argumentiere ich, dass die Entscheidung für den Konsum solcher Medien eine Mitschuld an zutiefst schädlichen Praktiken impliziert. Angesichts der weit verbreiteten Gewalt und Ausbeutung in der Pornografieproduktion akzeptieren Konsumenten ein erhebliches Risiko, dass das konsumierte Material gefilmten Missbrauch oder Vergewaltigung zeigt. Indem man dieses Risiko durch den Konsum von Pornografie eingeht, behandelt man andere auf eine Weise als Mittel zur persönlichen Befriedigung, die ethisch nicht zu rechtfertigen ist. Im zweiten Teil des Artikels, präsentiere ich ein weiteres Problem des Konsums von Online-Pornografie – unabhängig davon, ob sie gewalttätig ist oder nicht –, da der sexuelle Zugang zu anderen durch den Konsum dieser Medien eine Form sexueller Aktivität darstellt, die den allgemein anerkannten Standards einer sinnvollen (moralisch transformierenden) Einwilligung nicht genügt.
items.title: Sexueller Zugang aus der Ferne Sexual access from a distance
Corporate Social Responsibility in Negative Marketing Events: The Overlooked Role of Normative Ethics

items.abstract: Abstract The article compares two ways to think about the implicit structure of systems studied in pure mathematics. The first approach specifies implicit structure in terms of formal languages, relying on a model-theoretic notion of definability. The second approach defines the notion in terms of invariance criteria. The structural features of a given system are often considered to be properties which are invariant under specific transformations of the system. In the paper, I analyze these two approaches to implicit structure in terms of invariance and definability conditions by drawing to the field of finite geometry. I then explore their formal relationship in the framework of relational algebra, based on the concepts of Galois closures and Krasner algebras. Finally, I examine the equivalence of mathematical systems with respect to their implicit structure in terms of the model-theoretic notion of bi-interpretability.
items.title: Two Ways to Think About (Implicit) Structure
Complex Subjects: On the Natural Origins of Subjective Experience

items.abstract: Abstract Delusion is one of the most puzzling doxastic phenomena: on the one hand, the subject appears irrational, holding a delusion despite counterevidence; on the other hand, the subject appears otherwise rational, apportioning their non-delusional beliefs to the evidence. Leading theories of delusion, despite their strengths, still face notable limitations. This article argues that they may benefit from a new empiricist approach. Drawing on insights from Hobbes and Locke, it proposes that the subject may have a distinctive kind of compelling experience that is phenomenologically analogous to, and can effectively be more compelling than, the Cartesian ‘clear experience’. How the experience may, in various ways and to varying degrees, compel domain-specific irrational belief in the face of counterevidence will be articulated.
items.title: Delusions and Compelling Experiences
Background Information as a Key to Resolving the Gettier Problem: Insights from Bayesian Confirmation Theory
Infinitary Metainferences, Categoricity and the Structure of Logical Theories

items.abstract: Abstract Doxastic deliberation about how to doxastically relate to a given proposition p is said to be transparent, in that the central deliberative question of ‘Whether to believe p?’ is equivalent to ‘Whether p?’. I discuss four challenges to this thesis based on non-evidential epistemic reasons, deliberative dilemmas, self-effecting attitudes, and permissivist pragmatism. By employing recent insights from both the theory of epistemic normativity and the literature on practical deliberation, I argue that each of these puzzles can be squared with a properly limited and constrained version of the transparency thesis. Ultimately, I show that the claim that doxastic deliberation is after settling ‘Whether p?’ can only be understood as an approximation of a sub-question of the initial normative deliberative question concerning a very specific set of attitudinal options. Nevertheless, the resulting theory retains the core motivation and upshots of the transparency thesis: one is still able to explain why the deliberative norms of doxastic deliberation appear to be, for the most part, epistemic norms.
items.title: Doxastic Deliberation and the Puzzles of Transparency

items.abstract: Abstract We often support our moral judgements by appealing to independent considerations. According to some approaches in moral epistemology, the best way to understand this support is as evidential . However, it is unclear how some metaethical positions, like expressivism, can be compatible with such a view. For expressivists, moral judgements are desire-like states, which ostensibly are not the sorts of states which can be evidentially supported. In this paper, I argue that expressivists can indeed make sense of relations of evidential support for moral judgements. Drawing on a common sides-stepping expressivist strategy, I argue that expressivists should first focus not on evidential relations themselves but on our thought and talk of the form ‘ e is evidence for p ’. I then appeal to a form of epistemic expressivism, according to which such claims express complex non-cognitive attitudes or normative perspectives about standards that make it permissible to judge that p given e . This approach allows expressivists to reinterpret questions about what evidential relations between evidence e and moral judgements that p are as first-order normative questions about which standards not ruled out by acceptable normative perspectives make it permissible to judge that p given e . Responses to these first-order questions should be, in principle, compatible with expressivist second-order accounts of moral thought and talk. Finally, to show that this first-order interpretation is plausible, I outline a version of evidential explanationism along those lines.
items.title: Expressivism and Evidence for Moral Judgments
Indispensable Mathematics and Isolated Universes

items.abstract: Abstract Many authors who reject the vacuous truth of counterpossibles still adopt a strangeness of impossibility condition (SIC): possible worlds are always closer than impossible ones. Others doubt that SIC holds across the board. I situate the debate between linguistics and other disciplines. Then I weigh considerations of conservativity, systematicity and intuitiveness against counterexamples to SIC and purported theoretical benefits of abandoning SIC. My result is that neither the supporting nor the opposing evidence so far is compelling. The most plausible hypothesis is that SIC holds for a ‘standard resolution’ of the vagueness of counterpossibles, but that it can be overridden by context and pragmatic considerations even when counterpossibles are assessed ‘out of the blue’.
items.title: Strange Days Have Found Us
Digital restraints: when AI may override human decisions

items.abstract: Abstract In philosophical work on the ethics of video games, ludic amoralists argue that acts players perform in games are beyond moral scrutiny. This is chiefly supported by the following arguments: the fictional harm argument, the consequentialist rebuttal, and the moral exploration argument. The fictional harm argument supports ludic amoralism in principle: if all game actions are fictional, none can be immoral. The consequentialist rebuttal supports a defeasible default: if violent games do not reliably produce harmful outcomes, amoralism is the default position. The moral exploration argument provides an aesthetic reason for amoralism: play is beyond moral criticism insofar as the player engages with the game in an aesthetic, exploratory way. Drawing on Waltonian theories of fiction, I argue that players often imagine themselves as performing the fictional acts represented in games, ranging from heroic exploits to morally abhorrent deeds. When players do this, they can come to identify with, to varying degrees, their fictional exploits. Strong identification occurs when players interpret their fictional actions as satisfying real desires, such as the desire to harm others. Using examples from players of violent extremist games, as well as mainstream violent games, I show how such identification can arise in practice. Most importantly, I show that in cases of strong identification, all three justifications for ludic amoralism fail.
items.title: Imagining evil: from violent imaginings to violent extremist video games
Parental reason-giving obligations in pediatrics: who owes what to whom and why?

items.abstract: Abstract Even if state-led biodiversity conservation projects can result in the displacement, exclusion, and impoverishment of former reserve residents, they are often presented as responding to the public interest. The core idea of these projects, I argue in this paper, is that nature and people should be separated, because people are too dangerous to be part of the landscape. However, this narrow perspective fails to acknowledge the numerous wrongs caused by conservation-induced displacement. That is, considering the interdependent relationships between human and non-human entities at the core of several Indigenous approaches to biodiversity conservation, I show that the conservation-induced displacement of some Indigenous groups can cause three interconnected wrongs: territorial, epistemic, and identity-based.
items.title: Why Conservation-Induced Displacement is Wrong
Against the Anti-History Principle

items.abstract: Abstract Business ethics increasingly explains corporate duties through failure-based theories. The Market Failures Approach (MFA) limits profit-seeking by reference to competitive efficiency, while the Justice Failures Approach (JFA) bars firms from benefiting from unjust background conditions. This article argues that both leave a distinct class of corporate wrongs under-theorized, namely the degradation of relational goods through which corporate authority becomes legitimate and social cooperation remains stable. The article develops a Relational Failures Approach (RFA), according to which firms are relationship-constituting institutions whose permission to exercise discretionary power depends on sustaining relational goods. Drawing on sociology and organizational research, the article defends an empirically grounded and non-perfectionist account of these goods and shows how firms can commit efficiency-compatible, justice-compatible, and institutionally corrosive wrongs. The argument clarifies why familiar corporate pathologies, including disposability regimes and fear-based cultures, are not adequately captured by efficiency or justice alone in contemporary corporate ethics debates.
items.title: Business Firms and Relational Failures: Situating Relational Goods Beyond Market and Justice Failures

items.abstract: Abstract This article draws on the cross-disciplinary literature on risk, uncertainty and precaution to address a central dilemma put forward against precautionary principles. According to this dilemma, weak versions of precautionary principles, which hold that policymakers can justifiably adopt precautionary measures even when they lack certainty of impending harm, fail to justify adopting any precautionary measures. Conversely, strong versions of precautionary principles, which hold that policymakers must adopt precautionary measures whenever they face significant risks of harm, yield contradictory policy prescriptions. The article argues that the proffered defences of precautionary principles provide only a partial solution to this dilemma. The article then demonstrates that a meta-precautionary approach, which applies precautionary reasoning to the prescriptions of precautionary principles, can resolve the dilemma and successfully address further prominent objections put forward against precautionary principles.
items.title: A meta-precautionary solution to the dilemma of precaution

items.abstract: Abstract Autobiographical memory and the self are closely connected. Autobiographical memories provide the information needed to form and maintain a stable self-model (memory-to-self). The self, in turn, modulates the construction of autobiographical memories during retrieval (self-to-memory). Past research has mainly focused on the former direction of influence. However, self-to-memory dynamics are being increasingly investigated both in neurotypical and neurodivergent individuals. We contribute to this line of research in two ways. First, we elaborate on the self-memory system framework focusing on self-related processes involved in autobiographical memory retrieval. In particular, we distinguish between long-term and situationally activated aspects of the self, as well as between its representational and agentive aspects. Second, we propose a general framework for understanding self-to-memory dynamics in major depressive disorder based on four dimensions of the self: self-coherence (comprising self-coherence proper and self-congruence); self-valence; self-knowledge; and self-control. Based on the characteristics of the self in depression, we propose an outline of the self-to-memory dynamics in individuals with depression, drawing on existing empirical evidence. Additionally, we suggest that our framework, adjusted as needed, could be employed to describe self-to-memory dynamics in other mental health conditions.
items.title: Varieties of self-to-memory dynamics in autobiographical memory: the case of depression
Towards a PDL Framework for Reasoning About Causality
Fairness Interventions in Classification: A Study on AI Explainability
Capacities-First Philosophy as First Philosophy

items.abstract: Abstract Debates about the extended mind and extended cognition typically focus on the boundaries of cognitive processes and the mechanisms responsible for their realization. This paper develops a different perspective, one that foregrounds the role of dispositional properties such as beliefs, capacities, and abilities. According to the dispositional hypothesis, cases of cognitive extension share a common structure: an entity is credited with a dispositional property whose manifestation is realized by a mechanism that extends beyond the boundaries of that entity. This provides a unified way of understanding otherwise disparate cases of cognitive extension. The dispositional perspective also sheds new light on several familiar issues in the active externalist literature, including cognitive bloat and the criteria used to evaluate putative cases of cognitive extension. More generally, it draws attention to the importance of disposition ascription and the identification of disposition bearers: whether a mechanism qualifies as extended depends not simply on whether it crosses an organismic boundary, but on whether it extends beyond the boundaries of the entity credited with the relevant dispositional property. The resulting framework provides a common basis for understanding both natural and artificial forms of cognitive extension.
items.title: Beyond Skin and Skull: A Dispositional Approach to the Extended Mind

items.abstract: Abstract This paper aims to show that a neo-Aristotelian version of capacity-first philosophy of mind is fruitfully applied to a question which is specific to philosophy of psychology, namely: What counts as an adequate explanation in psychology? Drawing on Kenny, Glock and Schellenberg, the paper argues that the neo-Aristotelian capacity view is built around a set of criteria for the classification of capacities. All capacities are classified according to (1) possession-, (2) exercise-, (3) vehicle-, (4) opportunity-, (5) enablement- and (6) successful employment- criteria. These classification criteria are used to reconstruct the process of de-intellectualizing explanations of psychological phenomena. De-intellectualization targets theoretical assumptions about the circumstances in which the various criteria for classifying capacities are satisfied. The capacity approach offers a tool for regimenting the process of de-intellectualization. It also illustrates the contrast between de-intellectualization and Dennett’s homuncular functionalism. Rather than offering nothing more than conceptual clarity for debates about the metaphysics and epistemology of mind, the neo-Aristotelian capacity view explains why de-intellectualizing explanations is a feature of adequate explanations in psychology.
items.title: Capacity-First Philosophy of Psychology
Discrimination Without Phenomenal Difference in Schellenberg’s Capacitism
Abduction by Analogy in Bio-Medical Inquiry

items.abstract: Abstract Computational or machine ethics examines how morality could be implemented in machines and represented computationally. In the cognitive sciences, different architectures (rule-based and connectionist) have been proposed. Nevertheless, such approaches have limitations when incorporating ethical claims. With the rise of artificial intelligence, new ways of simulating moral expertise seem possible, where chatbots can serve as dialogue partners for moral orientation. However, as I will argue, such systems lack a theoretical grounding in metaethics, as do the former approaches. In order to align such systems ethically and ground them conceptually, a topography of moral competence must be developed. By outlining this topography, I will show some directions for further research and how such systems might enhance us morally.
items.title: Limitations of Computational Morality: Can We Morally Enhance Ourselves via AI?
Ethical and safe by construction: a unified assurance pipeline for physical AI

items.abstract: Abstract This comment assesses the evidence from four papers on the development process for four breakthrough drugs or treatments. The comment notes that the papers show all the key breakthroughs in the development process were financed either through the National Institutes of Health or various foundations or charities, not drug companies looking to be compensated through patent monopolies. It argues that this evidence suggests patent monopolies are an unnecessary distortion that results in high drug prices and creates perverse incentives. Expanded public funding could replace patent monopolies, allowing new drugs to be sold at free market prices, ending the problem of high drug prices blocking access.
items.title: What Have We Learned About Incentive Mechanisms?

items.abstract: Abstract This paper examines the role of public interest litigation in promoting accountability for AI and automated decision-making (ADM) in Australia. Since ADM regulation faces political and geopolitical headwinds, effective governance will have to rely on the enforcement of existing laws. Drawing on interviews with Australian public interest litigators, technology policy activists, and technology law scholars, the paper positions public interest litigation as part of a larger ecosystem for transparency, accountability, and justice with respect to ADM. The paper explores the tactics and strategies of what one participant described as “retrofitting” old laws to ADM. These go beyond creative legal argumentation to encompass practices of community-building, collaboration on theories of change, canny selection of clients and causes of action, and careful alignment of the interests of stakeholders in litigation. Naturally, the paper also contends with the limits of these strategies, and of the Australian legal system. Where limits are, however, capable of being overcome, the paper presents findings on urgent needs: the enabling institutional arrangements without which effective litigation and accountability will falter. The paper is relevant to law and technology scholars; individuals and groups harmed by ADM; public interest litigators and technology lawyers; civil society and advocacy organizations; and policymakers.
items.title: Retrofitters, pragmatists, and activists: public interest litigation for accountable automated decision-making
Worthy of freedom: indenture and free labour in the era of emancipation
When did China have law? A genealogical approach to Chinese legal history

items.abstract: Abstract This article examines the significance of what Edmund Husserl calls “the paradox of human subjectivity” for the metaphysical realism‐idealism debate in transcendental phenomenology. I distinguish two plausible interpretations of the paradox that are relevant to this debate. I term the first a vicious circle of mutual dependence: the world is characterized as being ontologically dependent on one causally dependent part of the world. I term the second a paradox of bodily self‐constitution: the transcendental subject is defined in such a way that it would be impossible for it to constitute itself as an empirical subject, and yet, in order to constitute the world, it must undergo such a process of self‐objectification. I focus on one prominent version of phenomenology from each side of the realism‐idealism debate, treating them as counterparts insofar as they share three core commitments. I argue that while the main accounts of the subject available to this idealist version generate at least one such paradox, the realist version can explain how one and the same subject is both transcendental and empirical without generating either paradox. My argument therefore provides a substantial prima facie reason to favour this realist version of phenomenology over its idealist counterpart for those who accept their shared commitments and take transcendental phenomenology to have metaphysical implications for the realism‐idealism debate.
items.title: Realism, Idealism, and the Paradox of Subjectivity in Transcendental Phenomenology

items.abstract: In this motivational article, I employ Michel Foucault’s ideas about genealogy, power, and the subject to provoke a new problematization of the subfield of bioethics. By drawing on the claims of feminist abolitionists, the challenges of Foucault’s work, and the lessons of historical epistemology, I reiterate and expand my earlier argument—an argument that merges Foucault studies, feminist philosophy, and  philosophy of disability, as well as complicates them—that the field of bioethics is a strategy and mechanism of neoliberal eugenics that must be abolished. To support this expanded version of my argument for the abolition of bioethics, I introduce genealogical work that should compromise the notions of autonomy and self-determination, both of which notions are foundational to the field.
items.title: Notes for a Feminist Abolitionist Genealogy of Bioethics

items.abstract: Abstract Editorial policies increasingly require authors to disclose substantive uses of generative AI, but such requirements commonly focus on whether, where, and how a model was used. Even function-specific disclosure may locate a model in the research or writing process without showing how its outputs entered scholarly judgment, how they were evaluated, or whether contributors can reconstruct the relevant reasoning and defend resulting claims without treating those outputs as sufficient justification. Drawing on research ethics, AI disclosure policy, human–model interaction, and researcher formation, this article argues that disclosure documents model use, whereas responsible use requires claim-level authorial warrant: a contributor’s capacity to understand, justify, and defend claims within their contribution. The article distinguishes cognitive delegation, in which model outputs shape substantive choices, interpretations, or justifications, from routine delegation, which does not ordinarily bear on the substance of judgment. Its conceptual contribution is to link the epistemic role of outputs that shape judgment to the function-appropriate evaluation required to justify decisions and retain warrant for resulting claims. It then repurposes disclosure categories as a claim-sensitive ex ante heuristic, mapping six recurrent research functions to risks, forms of oversight, and formative questions for recognising cognitive delegation and selecting function-appropriate evaluation. The article contributes to the ethics of information technology by clarifying when AI-supported scholarship remains under responsible human judgment and when cognitive delegation threatens the epistemic basis of authorship.
items.title: When disclosure rules are not enough: authorial warrant and judgment in ai-supported scholarship

items.abstract: Abstract Political protests are almost always collective endeavours, in which many people come together to jointly express some claim or demand. The power of those protests lies, in part, in their collectivity. But this collectivity also means that we may end up protesting alongside others who, though they endorse the shared claim the protest is expressing, also make other claims which are deeply unjust or harmful during the protest. This paper explores whether protesting alongside such others makes one complicit in the promotion or expression of those unjust or harmful claims, and whether we therefore have a duty not to participate (or to cease ongoing participation) in such protests. I identify two moral risks involved in protest which may ground such a duty – that we inadvertently amplify those views, and that we are unable to engage in effective counterspeech in response to them – and submit that when these risks are especially high, protestors have a pro tanto duty not to participate. However, I also show that the resources provided by different organisational forms protestors may use can help mitigate these risks.
items.title: Protesting Together
Weatherson on knowledge and inquiry
The recognition problem for theories of hedonic states
Synopsis of Good as Usual: Anti-Exceptionalist Essays on Values, Norms, and Action
Against the Arrow

items.abstract: Abstract The development and ubiquitous availability of large language model based systems (LLMs) poses a plurality of potentials and risks for education in schools and universities. In this paper, we provide an analysis and discussion of the overreliance concern as one specific risk: that students might fail to acquire important skills, or be inhibited in the acquisition of these skills, because they overly rely on LLMs. We use the distinction between local and global goals of education to guide our investigation. In our view, the harm of LLM overreliance is specifically that it severs the connection between local educational goals (e.g., successfully solving a specific kind of math problem) and global educational goals (e.g., acquiring general skills for mathematics). Based on this analysis, we sketch three possible responses to the overreliance concern: preserving both local and global goals while making minimal changes to educational practice (a conservative approach), changing global and local educational goals (a revisionary perspective), and preserving global educational goals while changing local goals (an in-between view). Since different types of responses have different benefits and weaknesses, we think that it is likely that an optimal response ultimately combines elements from all three types.
items.title: Learning alone: language models, overreliance, and the goals of education
Digital mayflies: transient personhood of AI companions

items.abstract: Abstract ‘Corrubedo’ is one of many stories Ben Judah tells in This is Europe: The Way We Live Now . It follows Graña, a fisherman from the titular Galician town who, faced with the erosion of his community, is forced to answer what Martha Nussbaum terms a ‘tragic question’ and joins the crew of Kunlun , a vessel sailing to Antarctica to poach Patagonian toothfish. Given the ubiquity of European law, in this article we interrogate its role in shaping the choices available to him and his everyday. We critically examine the Common Fisheries Policy and the IUU Regulation, highlighting their disconnect from the complex social and ecological contexts they seek to regulate, as well as the ensuing forms of alienation. These, we argue, hinting at the principle of subsidiarity, could be overcome through a reflexive law and policy that attends to the voices and lived experiences of those it most directly affects. We thereby hope to contribute to a collective inquiry into the law of the everyday in Europe, revealing the everyday as the site where the costs of governance accumulate and where ‘tragic questions’ are lived rather than resolved.
items.title: Against the tide: law, illegality and the everyday in Corrubedo

items.abstract: Abstract Large language models produce assertion-shaped outputs that often bring their users to true belief. I argue for two conclusions of different strengths: that on the best current evidence, these systems do not transmit testimonial knowledge and that hearers are not now positioned to accord their outputs testimonial uptake, which does not wait on the first. From Burge, Williamson, Goldberg, Faulkner, and Lackey, I derive a Tracking Minimum: a source transmits testimonial knowledge that p only if the truth of p , or the evidential support for p , figures in the explanation of its producing that assertion, and does so in virtue of the source’s own production process rather than of a proxy on which that process depends. It is this endogeneity requirement, not any modal profile, that the five accounts share and current systems fail.
