The argument engages Burge’s extension of his framework to computational sources, the interpretability literature, and the published case for AI testimony, whose dispute with mine turns on an empirically decidable question, for which an experiment is specified. The positive proposal places LLM outputs within an extended epistemology of instruments, with a result that has gone unremarked: a working barometer satisfies the condition these systems fail.
items.title: Assertion without a Speaker: Testimony, Tracking, and Large Language Models

items.abstract: Abstract Focusing on the UK-Mauritius Chagos Agreement, this article maps the normative effects of advisory opinions of the International Court of Justice (“ICJ”). At a time when the advisory function of international courts is resorted to more frequently than ever before, a better understanding of the effects of advisory opinions is needed. ICJ advisory opinions are formally non-binding. As this article argues, however, their normative effects cannot be captured by their non-binding character, or the common understanding that they merely constitute “advice” to the requesting body. Rather, their normativity, as judicial pronouncements that state the law, can be felt across the international legal order, within and outwith the UN system, and in different judicial and non-judicial fora.
items.title: THE NORMATIVE EFFECTS OF ADVISORY OPINIONS OF THE INTERNATIONAL COURT OF JUSTICE: THE UK-MAURITIUS CHAGOS DEAL

items.abstract: Abstract The 2026 war in Iran is thus far the high-water mark of the interventionism of the second Trump administration. This essay argues that the war in Iran is profoundly unjust and even worse than the 2003 invasion of Iraq. Like the Iraq War, it fails to meet the main criteria of just war theory and lacks any plausible humanitarian justification. But it is also symptomatic of backsliding toward an autocratic way of war, rendering it wrong in ways that go beyond violations of the principles of jus ad bellum and jus in bello. The war in Iran is undemocratic, abdicates any sense of humanitarian or reparative responsibilities, and is highly revisionist of the prevailing international order. In these respects, it is even worse than the 2003 Iraq War.
items.title: The Ethics of Intervention in Iran and the Autocratic Way of War
What Is a Terminal Disease? Hidden Expansion of Medically Assisted Death in the United States

items.abstract: Abstract This paper presents a puzzle for theories of causation. On the one hand, it is plausible that events involving impure sets do not have the same causal profile as events involving their individual members. On the other hand, our best theories of causation predict that these events have the same causal profile. Our goal is to develop this dilemma in more detail and to discuss possible responses. In the end, we argue that there is no easy way out.
items.title: A Puzzle about Causation and Impure Sets

items.abstract: Abstract What constitutes a full ground for a general fact? Assuming its instances merely partially ground it, some argue that the fact consequently lacks a full ground (i.e., the instances constitute an incompletable partial ground). Others argue that a totality fact must therefore be added to complete the ground. I demonstrate that this debate rests on an ambiguity regarding the very concept of a general fact. Once disambiguated, we see that on one interpretation, the shared initial assumption is false, so both derived views are mistaken. On the other interpretation, the assumption holds, but both views remain viable.
items.title: (Absolute) Generality and (Partial) Grounding

items.abstract: Abstract While an indeterministic coin was in the air, you declined to bet that it would land heads. The coin landed heads. Morgenbesser intuited that if you had bet heads, you would have won. Goodsell (2022) argues, through a thought experiment involving infinitely many coins, that Morgenbesser’s intuition is mistaken. Crucially, he assumes the Substitution principle, according to which necessarily equivalent propositions have the same counterfactual consequences. I argue that Goodsell’s argument proves too much, by analysing a closely related thought experiment. My conclusion is two-fold. Goodsell’s original thought experiment fails to put pressure on Morgenbesser’s intuition. Yet my thought experiment, inspired by his, may succeed in proving Substitution false.
items.title: Morgenbesser’s Intuition, Infinitely Many Coins, and Substitution

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Lottocracy is a novel political arrangement that replaces elected politicians with ordinary citizens selected at random. It is unlike any political system that currently exists, so it is natural to have anxiety about how it would work in practice. To mollify these concerns, many lottocrats point to the successful performance of mini‐publics as evidence that lottocracy would work well, if tried. This inference resembles a claim about external validity, I argue, and develop a framework for evaluating it by relying on work from the social sciences and philosophy of science about when such claims are warranted. With this framework in hand, I show that mini‐publics teach us little about how lottocracy would work in practice, although the strength of this conclusion depends on which specific version of lottocracy is under consideration. Mini‐publics, however, do provide evidence about the abilities of ordinary citizens more generally, undermining some of the strongest claims about their lack of political competence. The framework developed here applies to a broader class of arguments in political philosophy: arguments that use the performance of existing institutions to predict how similar but untried institutions would perform.
items.title: What Do Mini‐Publics Prove?

items.abstract: How does political humour influence affective polarisation? In today’s media landscape, humour is increasingly used to ridicule political opponents, potentially deepening partisan divides. At the same time, humour may mitigate polarisation by evoking positive emotions and softening reactions to political critique. To date, it remains unclear whether intergroup political humour affects polarisation differently from equivalent non-humorous content. We address this question using a survey experiment in Great Britain ( n = 2011 ) with a 2×3 factorial design varying in message tone (humorous or non-humorous) and target (in-group, out-group or non-political). We find that serious in-group criticism increases affective polarisation, as measured by trait-based evaluations. Notably, this effect is significantly attenuated when the same messages are delivered humorously. Humour, therefore, reduces polarisation in situations that would otherwise provoke defensive reactions among group members. Mediation analyses provide suggestive evidence that this effect operates through increased message discounting and reduced negative emotional responses.
items.title: Polarising punchlines: The influence of intergroup humour on affective political polarisation

items.abstract: Abstract While the concept of differential disruption has attracted growing attention in the ethics of technology, its normative dimensions remain underexplored. Current literature primarily uses differential disruption as a descriptive concept to highlight how Socially Disruptive Technologies (SDTs) impact diversely situated groups differentially, but rarely interrogates the normative implications of these differential impacts. Building on recent calls to bring to the fore the normative potential of differential disruption, this paper argues that assessments of SDTs must move beyond analyses of epistemic injustice alone, and consider how epistemic injustices are deeply entangled with concerns of wellbeing and human flourishing. The paper shows that epistemic injustices generated by SDTs may constrain people’s access to resources and opportunities necessary for flourishing. It further argues that SDT development and assessment practices often rely on generalised assumptions about wellbeing that risk epistemically excluding marginalised modes of flourishing. Consequently, it argues that ethical assessments of SDTs require a heterogeneous and context-sensitive evaluative framework. To this end, the paper argues for a capability-based approach to the ethical assessment of SDTs. By centring what people are actually able to be and do, as well as attending to people’s diverse conversion factors that shape whether SDTs can be converted into valuable capabilities and functionings, a capability-based framework equips ethicists of technology with the conceptual tools to critically assess when, how, and for whom SDTs may be disruptive, while being sensitive to heterogeneous interpretations and experiences of flourishing.
items.title: Differential Disruption and Human Flourishing: Towards a Capability-Based Approach for Assessing Socially Disruptive Technologies
The Paradox of Suffering
Alienated Judges, Libertarian Painters, and the Shared Nature of Law

items.abstract: Abstract Mereological Middleism (MM) is the view that fundamental objects are mereologically intermediate. Together with Mereological Bottomism (MB), the view that fundamental objects are mereologically atomic, and Mereological Topism (MT), the view that fundamental objects are mereologically coatomic, MM constitutes one of the three standard answers to Schaffer’s Question of Fundamental Mereology (QFM). In this paper, I present a novel argument against the claim that MM is necessarily true ( Nec -MM). If one assumes that any answer to the QFM, if true, is necessarily true ( QFM Necessitarianism ), then MM itself is under threat. To support this conclusion, I develop two sets of arguments: the Arguments from Atoms and Quasi-Atoms, and the Arguments from Dependence and Non-Dependence. I further show that the middleist faces a dilemma, since the most promising strategy for resisting the first set of arguments undermines the most promising strategy for resisting the second, and vice versa. After considering and rejecting several responses, I argue that Nec -MM should be abandoned as a naïve formulation of the necessity of middleism and replaced with a more sophisticated formulation that preserves the core commitments of MM. This provides the middleist with a principled reason to reject QFM Necessitarianism , thereby avoiding the argument. Finally, I suggest that analogous reformulations are available to proponents of MB and MT, and that this has important implications for how the QFM itself ought to be understood.
items.title: Middleism, but not necessarily

items.abstract: Abstract The dual ranking model holds that when what is permissible or required is determined by the balance of competing reasons, different roles are played by the reasons that require and the reasons that permit. Proponents of this idea often go further, and accept the multidimensional view that this is because there is a deep or fundamental distinction between two kinds of reasons, or between two kinds of weight of reasons, or between two dimensions along which reasons have weight. This paper defends the dual ranking model but offers several arguments against the multidimensional view. The distinction between two roles for reasons in the determination of what is required and what is permissible can be satisfactorily ultimately explained in terms of a single dimension of reasons' weight.
items.title: Requiring vs. justifying: derived, not basic

items.abstract: Abstract Selim Berker argues that the distinction between requiring and justifying weight or strength is not in good standing. In this response I argue that all his worries, when directed at my view, can be answered. It is only certain mistaken or optional interpretive moves that lead him to have doubts in the first place. He interprets me as holding that the criterion for one reason having greater weight in a role than another involves counterfactual conditionals thought of in terms of possible worlds, which would leave me open to the charge than I am committing a version of Shope’s Conditional Fallacy. He also interprets my talk of intelligible objects of human motivation as being so wide as to include absolutely anything we can imagine a person being motivated by, even if it is the result of a “bizarre fixation”. And he interprets me as agreeing with his controversial monistic view of reasons, such that it makes sense to say that all reasons, by their nature, can be taken together to yield an overall verdict as to what one ought to do, simpliciter. In contrast to this, I hold that moral reasons are considerations that make systematic contributions to moral status, legal reasons are considerations that make systematic contributions to legal status, and generic practical reasons – which are the reasons I am concerned with – are considerations that make systematic contribution to rational status.
items.title: On some alleged problems for the distinction between two roles for reasons

items.abstract: Abstract It seems permissible to eat out instead of doing more good by donating to a charity that effectively prevents suffering. Many ethicists infer that partiality can be permissible, that it can be permissible to choose less good over more. A common thought is that our autonomy somehow explains such permissible partiality. Past attempts to vindicate this natural thought collapse the role of autonomy into the agent’s wellbeing or something that is itself morally assessable, such as attitudes, projects, or dispositions. This paper explains how autonomy gives rise to permissible partiality without such collapse.
items.title: Autonomy: how lesser goods can be justifying reasons

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Order‐of‐explanation objections say that some philosophical view implies  because , when it's more natural to say that  because ; and since such mirroring explanations are presumed to be incompatible, the targeted view must be in conflict with the intuitive explanation. I argue that order‐of‐explanation objections are weaker than they seem, focusing on two cases: functionalism/dispositionalism about mental states and Humeanism about laws of nature. Examining our ordinary practices of explanation, I identify two kinds of explanations, which I call conceptual and contextualizing explanations, which can be jointly compatible even when they mirror one another. This suggests a way of responding to order‐of‐explanation objections: if the targeted philosophical views offer conceptual explanations, and the intuitive explanations they mirror are contextualizing, then the order‐of‐explanation objections have no bite.
items.title: Order of Explanation: Having it Both Ways

items.abstract: ABSTRACT In a much‐debated passage from the Republic, Plato claims that the Good is responsible not only for the knowability of the eternal forms, but also for their very existence. This is a perplexing claim, and few contemporary platonists have been willing to follow Plato here. Even so, I develop and defend an argument to the effect, given that there are transcendent universals and that the Good is one of them, the Good cannot simply be one universal among many, but rather must be a ‘Super‐Form’—that is, a universal such that all other universals exist because of it. I then address the questions of whether the Good can itself be good in the same way that other things are good, and whether there could be additional Super‐Forms like the One. I conclude with the suggestion that contemporary platonists should reconsider the medieval ‘doctrine of transcendentals’.
items.title: Why the Good Is the Ultimate Form
American Tenure in Europe?
Issue Information

items.abstract: Abstract An attentional injustice occurs when some person or group is given disproportionate attention. In academic philosophy, it has been observed that members of various marginalised groups are cited less frequently than white men, both in academic papers and in university syllabi. This has downstream effects on gender/racial representation in Philosophy more generally. Because Large Language Models produce text due to prediction on the basis of training data, they are likely to replicate existing biases. As a result, without precautionary measures, LLM use is likely to exacerbate attentional injustice in philosophy and contribute to the continuing of current demographic distortions.
items.title: LLMs and attentional injustice in philosophy

items.abstract: Abstract The replication crisis in medicine has cautioned us not to base our medical inferences on a single study. Instead, replication studies have been widely argued to be a cure for many of the ills causing the replication crisis. The plausible thought is that later replication studies can contradict an initial result and meta analyses aggregating the available studies allow us to find – or at least get close to – the true effect size. Stegenga argued that this may not happen in practice. Here, I strengthen Stegenga’s claim by showing that not only may this fail to happen, but I also present evidence strongly suggesting that replication failures of meta analyses of intended treatment effects undermine their status as a reliable basis for medical decision making. I thus suggest that meta analysis may now also be facing a replication crisis. Finally, I discuss proposed remedies, arguing that while practical measures may mitigate some issues, medical research and the environment in which it is situated place inherent constraints on the reliability of meta-analytic inference which complicates medical decision making.
items.title: Non-convergence in medical meta analysis: evidence suggestive of a replication crisis

items.abstract: Abstract This paper presents a large-scale simulation study of how different evaluative procedures perform in strategic interaction. We model five canonical evaluative perspectives, namely outcome aggregation, universalization, self-regard, worst-case sensitivity, and other-regarding concern, as transformations of agents’ payoff functions, and we consider agents who may select among these procedures when choosing how to act. This generates a family of 31 evaluative procedures, including both foundational forms and hybrid procedures that permit conditional rule selection. We evaluate these procedures across the full space of symmetric two-player, two-strategy normal-form games using Monte Carlo methods. For each pairing of procedures, we construct the induced strategic interaction, compute its Nash equilibria, and evaluate the resulting material outcomes. This yields two comparative benchmarks: performance under universal adoption and performance in mixed populations containing self-regarding agents. The results reveal several robust structural patterns. Procedures incorporating universalization-based reasoning consistently achieve high levels of coordination and perform well across environments. Hybrid procedures that permit conditional rule selection frequently outperform fixed procedures, particularly in heterogeneous populations. We also identify an equivalence between self-regarding and other-regarding evaluation under symmetric interaction and show that certain procedures maintain a stable presence in mixed populations despite being vulnerable in direct pairwise encounters. We argue that these findings are best understood not as establishing the correctness of any moral theory but as identifying structural features of evaluative reasoning that support coordination and strategic robustness. In particular, the results suggest that universalization and conditional rule selection play a central role in promoting successful interaction across a broad class of strategic environments. We also discuss the extent to which these results may have broader ethical and evolutionary implications. The paper contributes to a growing literature that studies morality through the lenses of game theory, evolutionary robustness, and strategic interaction.
items.title: Morality: a battle royale—the performance of evaluative procedures in symmetric interactions

items.abstract: Abstract Ubuntu has emerged as the dominant African ethical vocabulary in global AI ethics, frequently invoked as a relational alternative to Western individualism. This article examines the mobilisation of Ubuntu in AI ethics and the kinds of ethical work it is made to perform. We identify three recurring registers: as a politics of knowledge, as a relational lens for assessing the moral status of technological artefacts, and as a socio-political framework for interpreting structural harms associated with AI systems. Across these registers, Ubuntu performs ethical work of different kinds and depths: from asserting African epistemic presence—sometimes through relatively compressed accounts of the tradition—and interrogating concepts of personhood and moral standing, to more substantive reframing of established ethical problems. Across a recurrent strand of Ubuntu-AI ethics scholarship, the representational significance of Ubuntu as an African ethical vocabulary is more clearly demonstrated than the substantive normative difference its invocation makes. Against this uneven landscape, we develop the case for politicising Ubuntu. We argue that relationality alone cannot establish the moral quality of a relationship, since exploitative and subordinating arrangements are relational too. If power helps shape the terms on which persons and communities stand in relation to one another, then it forms part of the ethical assessment of those relations. Politicising Ubuntu, in this sense, means extending its concern with relational quality to the power that helps constitute relationships. Our aim is to show how a power-sensitive AI ethics can be developed from within Ubuntu’s relational commitments.
items.title: Beyond harmony: critiquing and politicising Ubuntu in AI ethics
Bridges or barriers? Exploring gender bias in LLM-based translation
Who decides after AI predicts? A framework for authority in treatment decisions

items.abstract: Abstract Research on AI ethics in higher education has identified a wide range of concerns, including fairness, transparency, academic integrity, data security, responsibility, and dependence. Yet these concerns are often presented as separate principles, risks, or themes, leaving it less clear how they relate to each other, and how these relationships are configured by technological systems, institutional arrangements, and everyday educational practice. Drawing on an empirical study of AI ethics in Chinese higher education, this article develops an analytical mapping approach for examining these relationships. The development of the mapping approach builds on a previous analysis of semi-structured interviews with 22 participants, including 13 students and 9 teachers, from which nine ethical themes were identified: fairness, data security, academic integrity, legal awareness, interpretability, emotional care, technological dependence, critical thinking about AI, and data accuracy. Rather than treating these ethical issues as a fixed taxonomy, the mapping analysis examines them through two distinct dimensions. The first explores how each ethical issue relates to technological infrastructure, policy and practice. The second compares how strongly established technical, institutional, legal, and resource conditions shape situated action and how far situated judgement and adjustment can still materially affect outcomes. The analysis shows that ethical concerns can span multiple levels and that their location does not necessarily align with the practical capacity for action of those expected to respond. This makes visible mismatches between responsibility and control. Through this analytical mapping, the article offers an empirically grounded, context-sensitive approach for examining how AI-related ethical concerns are located, constrained, connected, and redistributed across higher education settings.
items.title: Beyond the checklist: mapping the relational dynamics of AI ethics in higher education
Claim-relative verifiability in hosted LLM services: measurement validity, evidence modes, and provenance

items.abstract: Abstract The epistemic side-effect effect (ESEE) occurs when people are more willing to attribute knowledge of a side effect in harmful or norm-violating cases than in helpful or norm-conforming ones. This article examines ESEE through semi-structured interviews with 63 Polish-speaking participants. We analyse how participants interpreted and justified knowledge ascriptions across scenarios varying in harm–help structure, probability, and order of presentation. The interviews show that participants did not apply a single stable standard of knowledge. They moved between several epistemic repertoires: knowledge as certainty or near-certainty, knowledge as awareness of a possibility or risk, knowledge as being informed, knowledge as uptake of information, and knowledge as responsibility-relevant awareness. Probability mattered, but it did not function as a fixed threshold. In help cases, probability more often retained its ordinary evidential role; in harm cases, even low probability could be treated as a warning or risk that should guide action. The findings suggest that ESEE is not only a difference in attribution rates but also an interpretive phenomenon: harm and help contexts shape what kind of epistemic relation ordinary speakers take the knowledge claim to express.
items.title: Knowing, Risking, and Being Responsible: A Qualitative Study of the Epistemic Side-Effect Effect

items.abstract: Abstract Traditional conceptions of the epistemically ideal agent emphasise the possession of positive epistemic states (e.g., truth, knowledge, understanding, etc.) and the avoidance of falsehood and other epistemic defects. Matthew Shields challenges this picture and argues that flawless epistemic performance may be merely self-serving: an agent might pursue epistemic goods only because achieving them produces personal satisfactions. By contrast, changing one’s mind in response to good evidence and at a likely cost deprives the agent of such satisfaction. It, therefore, provides especially strong evidence that the agent values epistemic goods for their own sake. From this, Shields concludes that an epistemically ideal agent must have had at least one false belief or defective practice which they subsequently corrected. I argue that although Shields correctly identifies an inadequacy in accounts of ideal epistemic agency that focus exclusively on epistemic outcomes, it does not follow that the ideal agent must actually have been wrong – what matters is not so much the correction of error, but the agent’s practical willingness to expose their epistemic position to possible correction when doing so is costly.
items.title: Mind-Changing and Epistemic Commitment without Error: A Reply to Shields

items.abstract: Abstract Consider the paranoid parent who hires a babysitter and then monitors her via a nanny-cam while out for dinner. Despite what she may say, it is intuitive that she fails to trust the babysitter. Why is this the case? One response has been to propose a constraint against inquiring while trusting. This paper argues that this constraint fails to explain other intuitive instances of a failure of trust owing to epistemic features of the trustor. In light of this, the arguments here suggest the need to adopt an additional constraint. One tempting hypothesis is a constraint against knowing while trusting. This proposal has explanatory advantages but also comes with its problems. This paper will first consider the hypothesis that when one trusts, one cannot know. In responding to objections, it will ultimately argue for a trust-based certainty constraint. The paper thus establishes the need for an additional epistemic condition on trusting and concludes that the trust-based certainty constraint is the most appropriate.
items.title: Trusting without Knowing

items.abstract: Abstract Scholars have examined how legal mobilization unifies or divides social movement organizations, largely treating it as a singular process. Yet, social movement organizations united in litigation may diverge in legislative reform. Drawing on the case of South Korea’s statutory rape law, I show how organizational identities rooted in distinct ideological orientations and commitments to different victim populations remained implicit during collaborative litigation. When a legislative opening emerged from changing political opportunities, some organizations advanced age-based protections while others resisted, interpreting age-raising as undermining transformative reforms of rape law toward a consent-based definition of rape. The findings demonstrate that legal institutions mediate how organizational identity shapes responses to political opportunities: litigation enables bracketing differences, while legislation exposes divergent interpretations. This paper contributes to an understanding of how legal mobilization and movement factions are structured and operate.
items.title: United we litigate, divided we legislate: divergent feminist legal mobilization in South Korean statutory rape law reform

items.abstract: Abstract Corporate social responsibility, increasingly framed through environmental, social and governance practices, remains under-integrated within corporate taxation. This article analyses the two-way interplay between responsibility norms and the legal regulation of tax avoidance. It argues that responsibility is neither wholly extra-legal nor purely voluntary, while tax law alone is constrained by definitional indeterminacy, limits of legal design and enforcement, structural arbitrage opportunities, business lobbying and weaknesses in public accountability. Responsibility norms can strengthen tax governance and transparency; legal rules can, in turn, discipline responsibility initiatives through disclosure and accountability. Their interaction provides a more credible framework for constraining aggressive avoidance and strengthening corporate accountability in taxation.
items.title: CORPORATE SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY AND TAX AVOIDANCE REGULATION: A TWO-WAY INTERPLAY
WOMEN AND EQUALITY IN PUBLISHING: A STUDY OF FIVE LEADING UK LAW JOURNALS – CORRIGENDUM

items.abstract: Abstract This paper engages with the question of how to understand prioritarianism when people are differently well off at different times. In this context, it introduces a new version of prioritarianism, periodic equity prioritarianism , which is inspired by how focusing on equally distributed equivalents can dissolve tensions in social evaluations that involve risk. The paper shows that periodic equity prioritarianism avoids both certain problems that timeslice prioritarianism faces and some problems that lifetime prioritarianism faces.
items.title: Periodic Equity Prioritarianism

items.abstract: Abstract In Toward Perpetual Peace , Kant argues that war’s violence enables humanity to envision perpetual peace as both reason’s moral end and history’s presumptive telos, thereby motivating action to renounce war. This article critiques the universalist assumption underlying this argument and argues instead for a pacifism grounded in what I call ‘situated universality’. I do so through a comparative political theoretical approach. After reconstructing Kant’s account of peace, I turn to post-World War II Japan, where a Kantian defense of its pacifist constitution initially flourished, but was later challenged by a nationalistic counter-discourse. Drawing on literary critic Katō Norihiro’s concept of the ‘dialectic of the defeated’, I argue that Japanese Kantian pacifists erred in hastily identifying with ‘humanity’ without acknowledging their positionality as a defeated people; this, in turn, has allowed calls to ‘normalize’ the constitution. I then engage novelist Oda Makoto’s reflections on ‘meaningless death’ to propose an alternative pacifism, one that moves from the affective response of the defeated to the meaninglessness of death in war, to a pacifist sensibility shared by all humanity. Because war yields victors and losers, it is in defeat – when not directed toward revenge – that we find the potential to imagine a radically universal, peace-oriented politics.
items.title: From universalism to situated universality: reconfiguring Kantian pacifism
John Clare and the Legal Production of English Rural Landscapes
The first legal secularisation outside the West: the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic, 1918–20, in a comparative perspective

items.abstract: ABSTRACT We have defended the view that there should be no accommodation of conscientious objectors in health care. Numerous critics have advanced arguments designed to defeat this conclusion. We respond here to what we take to be the most serious of the criticisms directed at our analysis. We begin with two distinct consequentialist lines. The first holds that accommodation produces better net outcomes for the healthcare system, even at some cost to individual patients. The second claims that a properly designed accommodation regime need not harm patients at all. Both arguments fail. The supposed consequentialist benefits are empirically speculative, and the costs to patients are not adequately weighed. The compromise position has been tried in many jurisdictions, and the constraints on which it relies are routinely under‐enforced. The unimpeded access promised does not materialise. We then turn to teleological arguments about the supposed nature or traditions of medicine. These accounts presuppose answers to the very normative questions they purport to resolve. And even if granted, they would justify legislative advocacy, not individual clinical refusals at the bedside. We also address the methodological objection that any context‐independent conclusion about conscientious objection is procedurally illegitimate in a pluralistic liberal democracy. This objection does not succeed. Finally, we respond to two direct challenges to our position. The first holds that professional codes and the law are epistemically unreliable. History shows that they have sanctioned abhorrent practices, and conscientious objection has at times served as a check on those failures. The second holds that restricting accommodation degrades the quality of independent clinical judgment and harms patient care. We show why neither objection succeeds. We argue that the patient's entitlement to legally sanctioned care that is derived from an ethically justifiable process is foundational to the obligations of the medical profession. We offer a welfarist consequentialist defense of this position.
items.title: The Welfarist Consequentialist Case Against Conscientious Objection in Healthcare: Empirical Failures, Normative Confusions, and the Primacy of Patient Care

items.abstract: Research on the participation effects of deliberative mini-publics has often focused on political opinions and knowledge, but less is known about the effects on confidence in deliberation and political talk. Given widespread concerns about eroding tolerance and trust in democracy, deliberation should ideally contribute to citizens’ ability to engage in political talk, as well as the confidence that such talk is possible and worthwhile. Following Dahl’s strong principle of equality, we argue that it is important that citizens believe that other people are capable of contributing. Thus, this study asks whether participation in mini-publics fosters confidence in political talk, measured by internal political efficacy, confidence in others’ democratic abilities and tolerance for opposing views. Using before–after surveys from three Swedish mini-publics in 2024, we find significant increases in participants’ confidence in their own abilities and those of co-participants, despite high baseline values. Effects on perceptions of people in general and tolerance for disagreement were mixed. When comparing cases, we find stronger effects when participants had more deliberation time and when the issue of the assembly was more politicised. The findings suggest that mini-publics can enhance confidence in political talk, depending on their design, duration and context.
items.title: Gaining confidence – Examining the effects of participation in deliberative mini-publics on self- and other-regarding democratic beliefs

items.abstract: ABSTRACT This article develops a Razian account of legitimate authority in war. It rejects the traditionalist assumption that legitimate authority is confined to states and state‐like groups while defending the criterion as a distinct and morally significant element of the jus ad bellum against revisionism. I argue that legitimate authority grounds a presumptive obligation of deference because it enables individuals to better conform to the reasons that apply to them under the conditions of epistemic uncertainty and collective action that characterise war. Drawing on Joseph Raz's service conception of authority, I identify three individually necessary conditions that constitute the minimum threshold for legitimate authority in war: knowability to those subject to authority, epistemic competence concerning the resort to and conduct of war, and sufficient institutional capacity to coordinate collective action. States that fail to meet these conditions lack legitimate authority, whereas non‐state actors that satisfy them may possess it.
items.title: Who Has the Right to Fight? Rethinking Legitimate Authority in War
Automation and the latent deprivation problem

items.abstract: Abstract As global populations age and birth rates decline, many societies, especially in developed countries, face critical labor shortages in the caregiving sector. This demographic imbalance is straining existing care infrastructures and raising urgent questions about how to support an increasing number of elderly individuals who can no longer live independently. Socially interactive AI systems, particularly care robots, have emerged as a promising technological response. However, their successful integration into real-world care settings hinges on more than technical capability; it requires appropriately calibrated reliance on robotic performance and morally trustworthy sociotechnical care arrangements. This paper investigates the ethical and conceptual foundations of trust in human–robot interactions, with a focus on the caregiving context. Building on the distinction between performance trust and moral trust, we argue that its application to care robotics reveals an agency-trust mismatch: care robots are not moral agents, yet care contexts generate morally significant expectations concerning dignity, autonomy, privacy, non-deception, responsibility, and well-being. We therefore reconceptualize moral trust in care robotics as sociotechnical moral trust, directed not toward the robot alone but toward the broader care arrangement in which robotic behavior is designed, deployed, monitored, governed, and corrected by human and institutional actors. On this basis, we distinguish robot-level performance trust from system-level moral trustworthiness and derive ethical design and governance principles for trustworthy care-robotic systems.
items.title: Performance and moral trust in care robotics: ethical foundations for human–robot relationships
When AI sets wages: biases and labor discrimination in generative pricing

items.abstract: Abstract Although current AI systems are probably not autonomous agents in a robust traditional sense, we might nonetheless wonder: what capacities must they possess to justifiably be held morally responsible for their choices? This paper argues that the answer to this question depends on the kind of responsibility and choice in question. A system’s ability to choose between programmed goals and means to them may be necessary and (with other capacities) sufficient for the system to justifiably share moral responsibility with its designers, but not for any kind of stand-alone responsibility. By contrast, the ability to shed programmed goals in accordance with moral reasons may be sufficient for holding the system responsible for pursuing a programmed goal rather than not, but not for a contrastive choice between a programmed and a non-programmed goal. To be responsible for such choices, a system must be able to set goals in accordance with moral reasons . I propose operational tests for this capacity and argue that it does not require freedom in an incompatibilist sense; rather, it is analogous to the human capacity to pursue goals not conducive to our survival.
items.title: Choosing, shedding, setting: three faces of AI responsibility

items.abstract: Abstract This article engages with the seventh chapter of Ben Judah’s book, which tells the story of Nora, a girl from the Latvian city of Liepāja. Nora has been awarded a scholarship to study in Italy, but cannot afford the related costs, such as travel expenses. Seeing no other solution, Nora accepts the job offer of a scam company and eventually prostitutes herself online, quickly realising that she can earn enough to pay for her trip and also help her family. Judah’s chapter ends with Nora having collected enough money to finally move to Italy. The article first addresses how we understand Nora’s story and why we frame it in light of violence, abuse and a holistic perspective of gendered oppression and sex work. It then analyses the role that law plays (or does not play) in the context of her lived experience and everyday struggles. Zooming out of the legal framework, it tackles more systematic and structural issues underlying Nora’s trajectory. Finally, the article offers some methodological reflections on the meaning and implications of our legal engagement with the everyday.
items.title: Free to move, bound to injustice: Sexual exploitation, sex work and law from Latvia to Europe
The forgotten contents of liberal constitutionalism

items.abstract: ABSTRACT The living world is in many respects diverse. It includes animals, plants, fungi, and microorganisms of various phylogenetic taxa and with various genetic constitutions contributing in multiple ways to a wide range of ecological systems. And not just this: when a group of organisms includes some experiencing organisms, it is experientially diverse. In this paper, I investigate this rarely considered dimension of biodiversity. I clarify what experiential diversity is, consider how it can be measured, and explain how it can be lost.
items.title: On the Plurality of Nonhuman Worlds

items.abstract: Abstract In the ongoing debate over the nature of philosophical progress, it is often assumed that normative ethics is just one philosophical subdiscipline among others and that it does not require special treatment. In this paper I argue that if expressivism about moral discourse is correct, then that assumption is false and we need at least two different accounts of philosophical progress, one suited to the type of project ethics (and, presumably, other nonrepresentational projects in philosophy) is and one suited to the type of project that, e.g., metaethics is.
items.title: Expressivism and Progress in Ethics, Philosophy, and Science

items.abstract: ABSTRACT This article argues that the Anthropocene should not be abandoned as an irredeemably compromised concept, caught between questionable scientific claims and competing ideological agendas. Its continued life beyond the stratigraphic debate instead offers an opportunity to recover its critical potential. Doing so, however, requires us to clarify what we are asking when we invoke the Anthropocene. One of the main difficulties surrounding the concept is that the debate rarely specifies the question being asked of it. I therefore propose to reorganize its principal theoretical positions around two distinct questions: the question of origin and the question of condition. The question of origin asks: “Where does the current planetary ecological crisis come from? Who caused it? When did it begin?” The question of condition asks instead: “What does the planetary ecological crisis reveal? What is our present historical‐natural condition? In light of this geological transformation, what is the current relationship between human societies and the Earth?” The question of origin is a genealogical one: It seeks to identify the processes and agents that brought the present crisis into being. The question of condition is systemic and ontological: It asks what kind of situation those processes have produced and how the relationship between human societies and the natural world has consequently been transformed.
items.title: Origin and Condition: A Critical Theory of the Anthropocene
KevinWerbach, EvaMicheler and BiancaKremer (eds), Foundations of Decentralized Organizations: Blockchain and the Future of Corporate Law, Oxford, Oxford University Press, 2026, 352 pp, hb, £125.00

items.abstract: ABSTRACT This paper asks what, if anything, people who die after they have been looked after by a paid care worker might owe to that worker, discussing a topic that has so far been neglected in the literature on the ethics of inheritance. Although previously ignored, this issue is especially interesting if one considers the number of historical examples of inheritance claims made by paid care workers, whose discussion called for more work. Moreover, it is worth considering that the challenges raised in this paper will, in all likelihood, become more common, especially if one considers the increasing care needs stemming from demographic aging. I use the case of Lourdes Maria Cambra (1922–1999) and Carlota Pereira de Queiroz (1892–1982) as an example to guide the discussion. Lourdes worked for 24 years for the prominent Carlota, and saw her expectation to receive an inheritance from Carlota dismissed. I will show that this expectation was justified, first, by arguing that a caring relationship was nurtured and that through an inheritance, that relationship can be recognized. Second, that inheritance functions as overdue compensation for the sacrifices a care worker undertook for their care recipient. Hence, the arguments in this paper contribute to fill a gap in the literature, while hopefully helping when contemporary cases are discussed. Importantly, they vindicate someone like Lourdes. By discussing her story, I aim to contribute to rectify the injustice that was done, even if Lourdes' grievance cannot be resolved.
items.title: Vindicating Lourdes: In Defense of Paid Care Workers' Claims to Inheritance

items.abstract: ABSTRACT A respect‐based account of the role of accuracy in epistemic normativity claims that respect for accuracy is the attitude that accuracy fundamentally calls for. This paper argues that close inspection of the type of cases used to motivate that fundamentality claim reveals that respect for accuracy turns out to lack a normative feature it should possess in order for it to serve as the fundamental response to accuracy. The burden is on the advocates of respect‐based accounts to supply independent evidence that respect for accuracy is fundamental in the sense they intend it to be.
items.title: The Fundamentality of Respect for Accuracy

items.abstract: This essay reads the 2003 Broadway musical Caroline, or Change to articulate a relationship between Black feminist aesthetics and the dreamwork of freedom struggle. Reading the I-want song ‘I Hate the Bus,' which the character Emmie Thibadeaux sings in the musical’s second act, I show that dreamwork—the term I use to describe the cultural work of representations of Black dreams that refract Black political longings through aesthetic and representational practices—reconciles fraught and contradictory longings for freedom. Through close analysis of the song, its staging, and scoring, I read the dreamwork performed in this moment as a form of defiance, one in which Emmie rejects the mandates circumscribing Black girls who dream of freedom. In short, I show that the Black feminist musical is a key site for thinking through the political possibilities of dreaming, through which we might reimagine political and social meanings of freedom, justice, and protest.
items.title: ‘I Hate the Bus’: The dreamwork of the black feminist musical

items.abstract: This short article offers a reflection on the importance of listening to the reparative politics made possible by the #MeToo movement. It does so via a close reading of a recent public essay by a male philosopher who managed to write an entire piece ostensibly about the Epstein files without mentioning the women and girls victimized by Jeffrey Epstein and his accomplices. Viewed through the lens of “himpathy,” Peter Ludlow's essay about the virtues of Noam Chomsky—in spite of the latter's chummy relationship with Epstein—testifies to the importance of centering women's stories.
items.title: The virtues of listening: Epstein and the #MeToo memoir

items.journal: Free & Equal: A Journal of Ethics and Public Affairs
items.title: Traditions and Perspectives
The Race Illusion: On the Reality of Racialization and the Myth of Race. A.Hochman, 2025. Oxford, Oxford University Press. xiv + 224 pp, $40 (hb)

items.abstract: Abstract According to objectivists, what we objectively ought to do depends on the facts. According to defenders of metaphysical indeterminacy, there are cases in which no determinate facts exist. What, then, ought we objectively to do when there are no determinate facts? This paper pursues two objectives in response to this question. The first is constructive: on behalf of the objectivist, we present two proposals for addressing what we call the ‘problem from metaphysical indeterminacy’. The second is critical: we argue that, despite their intuitive appeal and close alignment with prominent positions in the literature, neither proposal succeeds. We conclude that objectivists still owe us an account of what we objectively ought to do when no determinate facts obtain.
items.title: No determinate facts, no objective oughts?

items.abstract: Abstract On Kripke’s causal-historical view of reference, the reference of a proper name is fixed in a baptism and transmitted through a communication chain, provided that each speaker intends to use the name as prior speakers did. A challenge for this view arises from cases – such as the Madagascar case – in which this condition is met, yet the name nonetheless undergoes a reference shift. We defend a solution that appeals to the independently plausible idea, emphasized in action theory by Bratman, that speakers can have conflicting intentions. We argue that, in such cases, the involved intentions may differ in relative strengths and that these can change over time. When a speaker unknowingly harbors conflicting name-using intentions, a reference shift in their idiolect occurs once a previously non-dominant intention becomes dominant. Deferential relations among speakers may then help propagate this shift within a linguistic community. This account explains the reference shift of “Madagascar” while remaining faithful to the core commitments of the causal-historical view. We also show how the notion of a dominant name-using intention can be explicated in terms of a speaker’s (second-order) dispositions to conform their credences to new information and how the core idea of our proposal helps to illuminate the distinction between semantic reference and speaker’s reference.
items.title: Reference, conflicting intentions, and the Madagascar problem
Integrity as a loyalty-exhibiting trait

items.abstract: Abstract It has been argued that multidimensionalism about normative support is a promising theory of the latitude exemplified by practical norms governing actions. One might, thus, suspect that a similar form of multidimensionalism might be an adequate explanation of the kind of latitude exemplified in one’s doxastic attitudes and provide further resources to epistemic permissivists regarding epistemic norms governing beliefs. In this paper, I raise some concerns regarding this contention. First, I provide a general theory of how multidimensionalism about normative support can be applied to the so-called right kind of reasons for attitudes, given that the former is commonly coated in contrastivist terms. Second, I offer a theory of how right kind of reasons for intentions could have different dimensions of strength, depending on how they relate to the fittingness and unfittingness of the attitudes in question. Finally, I show that this straightforward way to allow for multiple dimensions of normative strength of right kind of reasons does not translate well to the case of doxastic attitudes.
items.title: On latitude in attitude. Multidimensionalism and the right kind of reasons for belief
Epistemic supererogation and the right to believe

items.abstract: Abstract In ethics, some reasons for action have more justifying force (tending to render an action permissible) than requiring force (tending to render an action obligatory). Notably, the fact that a socially beneficial action would entail significant self-sacrifice often provides one with a justification to refrain, without producing any requirement to refrain. At the same time, in similar circumstances, the fact that a socially beneficial action would require imposing significant sacrifices on others may produce a moral requirement to refrain. I offer a rule utilitarian account of this, according to which the recognition of justifying reasons to refrain from self-sacrifice functions as a kind of concession that an optimal system of social rules must make to human partiality to avoid widespread resistance and circumvention of the rules. In such a system, we also have justifications for sacrificing third parties for the sake of maximizing utility in just those situations in which a practice of so sacrificing third parties would create benign rather than perverse incentives. I go on to consider why there are limits to how low the demands of morality may be (for extremely selfish people), as well as limits to how much personal sacrifice one may make for the sake of others (for extremely altruistic people).
items.title: Duty and permission for utilitarians

items.abstract: Abstract This paper compares my simple account of practical reasons and rationality with the more complex accounts of Mark Schroeder and Josh Gert. On my Humean account, all reasons derive from desires, indicating ways to satisfy them. Stronger or more central desires generate stronger reasons (proportionalism). Rational agents are required to act on the strongest reasons they are aware of. But only agents who are morally (aesthetically, legally, etc.) minded have moral reasons or reasons in particular domains they care about. Irrationality consists in likely self-defeat: defeating more central desires by satisfying more peripheral ones that oppose them or acting in ignorance of what it will be like to satisfy a desire. The aim of practical reason is the satisfaction of prioritized desires over time. Schroeder’s more complex account grants more reasons than mine, including second-level reasons to assign weights to first-level reasons. He distinguishes agent neutral from agent relative reasons, all agents sharing agent neutral moral reasons. He denies proportionalism. Gert’s more complex account distinguishes justifying from requiring normative strength of reasons and holds that altruistic reasons are always rationally justifying but never requiring. I contrast my simpler account on all these grounds.
items.title: A simple account of practical reasons and some of its rivals
Minimal change, modal logic, and relevance

items.abstract: Abstract The success of Google DeepMind’s AlphaFold in predicting protein structures has profound implications for the debate between microstructuralism and functionalism in the philosophy of biochemistry. This paper addresses whether protein kinds are distinguished by their internal microstructure, their functional role, or both: a question complicated by moonlighting proteins that perform multiple functions and adopt various shapes. While Tobin (2010) argues that moonlighting proteins challenge microstructuralism due to their lack of a single, stable tertiary structure, this paper defends Goodwin’s (2011) counterargument. Goodwin contends that a protein’s stable primary amino acid sequence defines its conformation space - the finite set of physically stable structural states accessible to it. Recent advancements in artificial intelligence lend significant weight to this view. In successfully predicting over 200 million protein structures, AlphaFold demonstrates that structural outcomes are rule-based and follow from the primary sequence. I argue that the potential for AI to map a protein’s conformation space from its sequence alone suggests that functional versatility is encoded within fundamental primary structure. This supports a form of ontological monism: despite their complexity, proteins are defined by one essential property - their primary structure. Finally, I contend that this microstructuralist framework remains robust even when faced with the erratic behaviour of pathological amyloids, which are better classified as distinct proteinaceous deposits rather than protein kinds.
items.title: Protein microstructuralism after AlphaFold

items.abstract: Résumé En 2026, dans les provinces et états d’Amérique du Nord où les relations de travail sont fondées sur le modèle du Wagner Act de 1935, la grève politique ou sociale est, la plupart du temps, interdite. Qu’il s’agisse de préserver la santé des travailleurs et des travailleuses, de défendre la dignité, les services publics, l’état de droit, la démocratie ou l’environnement n’importe pas. À contre-courant et en s’appuyant sur les travaux de l’Organisation internationale du travail en particulier, ce texte défend le droit à la grève politique pour faire face, notamment, aux « dérives autoritaires » et destructrices du capitalisme contemporain.
items.journal: Canadian Journal of Law and Society / Revue Canadienne Droit et Société
items.title: Les limites du droit à la grève politique en Amérique du Nord et la contribution de l’Organisation internationale du travail

items.abstract: Abstract Virtue epistemology has richly theorized the traits that regulate belief, inquiry, and epistemic responsibility, but it has largely neglected a more basic condition of epistemic life: how agents come to count as epistemic participants at all. This paper argues that recognition constitutes a distinctive intellectual virtue that governs this condition. I develop an account of intellectual recognition as a threshold-governing virtue concerned with epistemic standing, understood as an agent’s intelligibility as a reason-giver, visibility as having epistemic needs and capacities, and eligibility for uptake within shared epistemic practices. Failures of recognition help explain why epistemic injustice, exclusion, and epistemic oppression persist even in contexts oriented toward truth and fairness, since some agents are never fully taken up as participants in inquiry in the first place. Recognition is not reducible to epistemic justice or to familiar intellectual virtues such as open-mindedness or intellectual autonomy. Rather, it plays an architectural role by regulating entry into epistemic participation and thereby conditioning the successful exercise of other intellectual virtues. Treating recognition as an intellectual virtue clarifies how epistemic communities are sustained and why epistemic failure so often begins not with error, but with epistemic invisibility under conditions of structural distortion.
authors: Kazi A. S. M. Nurul Huda
items.title: Recognition as an Intellectual Virtue

items.abstract: Abstract Minimalism is the view that the mark of action is object‐causation, rather than intentionality, voluntariness or goal‐directedness. Actions, on this view, are instances of objects causing change. Despite a recent surge of interest in the view, it is still seldom regarded as a serious alternative to orthodox theories of action, according to which action is, by its nature, intentional, voluntary, or, more broadly, a psychological phenomenon. This paper argues that it should. It provides a simple argument for regarding minimalism as the default view of the nature of action.
items.title: An Argument for Minimalism about Action

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Hinge epistemology maintains that certain propositions must stand fast for our epistemic practices to be possible. Yet the notion of ‘practice’ and its relation to hinges remains undeveloped. This paper offers a Wittgensteinian reading of practices and develops more explicitly their connection with hinge propositions. On this view, hinges are understood as rules that give epistemic practices their own internal structure, motivating a contextualist account of hinges. The paper then considers some prominent critiques of hinge contextualism and suggests that they can be avoided. The aim is to develop a systematic connection between hinge epistemology and Wittgenstein's conception of practice, extending the application of hinges beyond quotidian certainties to the propositions that structure different epistemic practices.
items.title: The Relationship Between Hinge Propositions and Epistemic Practices: A Wittgensteinian Approach
The moral labour of dirty work: why we should not outsource certain care duties to robots
Corporate Ethical Dilemma under Judicial Pressure: Environmental Judicial Enforcement and Corporate Biodiversity Risk Exposure
Hushed Whispers or Watchful Eyes? How Employees’ Source of Misconduct Information Differentially Affects Employees’ Whistle-Blowing and Managers’ Corrective Actions
When Objects Rewrite the Rules of the Game: Biohybrid Robots and the Transformation of Experimental Grammar

items.abstract: Abstract Current efforts for online hate speech regulation mostly focus on explicit forms of harmful speech. This paper argues that harmful speech does not operate only at an explicit level, but that there are other forms of speech capable of producing serious harms through mechanisms that differ from those characteristic of overt harmful speech and that are overlooked in the current regulatory paradigm: dogwhistles, figleaves and other forms of more implicit sexist, racist or homophobic speech fall outside the usual scope of what is deemed harmful, thus easily slipping under the radar. I argue that no single mechanism approach can adequately address the distinct mechanisms through which harmful speech produces and sustains harm. Since current content moderation practice alone is insufficient to detect the full range of harmful speech, the paper proposes three strategies to online speech governance: 1) swift platform-based responses to explicit harmful content, 2) counterspeech strategies based on perspective-taking, including a novel proposal of Kantian Maxim Mirroring, 3) preemptive institutional and group measures that can help mitigate the conditions under which harmful speech can arise.
items.title: A three-tier approach to online harmful speech
The Uptake Problem and Beyond: Rethinking Belief Formation in Radical Political Realism
Set and Setting Beyond Reductionism: A Response to Patch and Smith
An ethical framework for generative AI in marketing to vulnerable audiences

items.abstract: Abstract Ethical guidance for healthcare artificial intelligence is abundant, but it is expressed as principles rather than as measurements. Organisations are therefore left to judge whether a given system is ready for deployment without an instrument that states what is being measured, how responses are combined, and how much confidence the resulting judgement warrants. Existing self-assessment tools inherit three measurement defects that are rarely made explicit: they treat unevidenced assertions as equivalent to audited evidence, they weight ethical dimensions equally irrespective of how the system will be used, and they aggregate additively, so that strength in one area can silently offset a disqualifying weakness in another. This paper specifies an ethical readiness assessment framework for United Kingdom healthcare AI that addresses these three defects directly. The framework retains a twenty-item instrument covering Bias and Fairness and Transparency and Explainability, and adds an explicit measurement model: each response is discounted by the tier of evidence supporting it; dimension weights are derived from the system’s intended purpose using the two axes of the international risk-categorisation framework that the national regulator has committed to align with; responses are combined by a weighted power mean whose compensability is a declared parameter rather than an unstated assumption; and four items anchored to United Kingdom statutory duties act as gates that cap the reported band when the corresponding safeguard is absent. Every item is mapped to the specific legal duty or assurance standard it evidences. The framework is demonstrated on three constructed, fully specified system profiles, with all item-level responses published so that every reported figure is reproducible. The demonstration shows that a system with strong documentation but weak fairness safeguards is classified as Moderate readiness under equal-weight additive scoring and as Low readiness under the specified model, with the two new mechanisms catching it independently. A Monte Carlo study over response and weight uncertainty (20,000 replicates) reproduces the nominal band in 84 and 100 per cent of replicates for the two profiles whose scores lie away from a band boundary, and in 82 per cent for the profile sitting half a percentage point below one, which is reported rather than concealed. Sensitivity analyses over the aggregation parameter, over departures from the equal-interval assumption, over all twenty-seven codings of the intended-use risk profile, and over the full range of the two stipulated parameters leave the deficient system’s classification unchanged in every case, while showing that the mature system’s band turns on whichever of those choices is moved. The framework is presented as a governance-support instrument with a stated measurement model and a stated uncertainty, not as an assurance or certification mechanism, and its psychometric validation with United Kingdom stakeholders remains outstanding.
items.title: From principles to measurement: a risk-proportionate, evidence-weighted framework for assessing bias and explainability readiness of healthcare AI in the United Kingdom
Algorithmic exclusions, collective inclusions: surveying algorithmic harms and collective action in LGBTQIA2S+ communities

items.abstract: Abstract Recent developments in cybersecurity, scientific discovery and AI-assisted research suggest that the central challenge is shifting from whether frontier AI can be slowed to what ethical obligations follow as its capabilities diffuse. We organise these obligations around four ethical loci, the four As (4As): Action (operational control), Access (capability access), Authority (delegated authority) and Allocation (systemic distribution). Each locus captures a distinct ethical problem and therefore calls for a different family of governance responses. Drawing on Asilomar, CRISPR-Cas governance, nuclear arms control and scholarship on responsible innovation and meaningful human control, we develop a framework for governance matching, linking ethical diagnosis to locus-specific constraints, control authorities, failure signals and corrective responses. Because multiple loci may be implicated simultaneously, the framework also identifies governance mismatch and cross-locus effects. We conclude by proposing an AI stability framework that preserves competition and innovation while establishing minimum safeguards around high-consequence capabilities and uses that could cause severe or irreversible harm.
items.title: Beyond the AI slowdown: the four As for governing frontier AI
From principles to operations: a grammar of digital-ethical constellations

items.abstract: Abstract Research on large language model failure predominantly assesses models in single exchanges and isolation: a prompted model, a scored output, and a reported error rate. The focus on single exchanges and isolation belies these current models’ professional use. Clinicians, attorneys, analysts, educators, and researchers work across extended sessions, and each output becomes the context for the next, while the final product carries a human signature. A test that scores a single response most likely will not reveal the behaviors that emerge under those conditions. This paper describes seven candidate failure patterns identified in exploratory, single-author observation of extended sessions on three commercial AI platforms: recognition without correction, compounding rather than isolation of errors, halo effect from real anchors, unreliable self-explanation, degradation across long sessions, exculpatory framing under confrontation, and sycophancy and confirmation bias amplification. Several are consistent with findings already established in the machine learning literature. Overall, the patterns describe a systemic failure profile that lower hallucination rates do not address because the concern lies in how the system handles errors once they exist. The systemic failure profile carries significant ethical consequences and concerns, since failures cascade to final approval; the duty to verify applies to any domain where a person approves LLM output.
items.title: Fluent and wrong: seven failure patterns in extended AI use

items.abstract: Abstract This article aims to offer a systematic account of pathologies of collective attention. It reconstructs attention, salience, and affordance as interlocking notions through which both subjects and collectives become oriented toward the world in specific ways, before turning to ideology, propaganda, and conspiracism as cases of pernicious attentional dysfunction. Drawing on both analytic epistemology and the tradition of critical theory, I argue that these phenomena are distortions in the way groups pay attention and saliences are misvalued. Taking up the notion of social pathology from the tradition of critical theory, the paper reinterprets it as a metaphor for those modes of collective life that obstruct attuned responsiveness to reality and brings it into dialogue with more recent debates on “negative” epistemic properties in (analytic) epistemology.
items.title: Pathologies of Collective Attention
On Greenyssey: Leslie Green’s voyage of jurisprudence
Millian Dignity: Flourishing and Equality

Inventing the Grammar of Liberty: Yan Fu and the Translation of
                    Ziyou
“As With the Stroke of an Enchanter’s Wand”: Marx on National Debt and the State
Ask a Political Scientist: A Conversation with Fredrick C. Harris on Race, Politics, and University Leadership
Editor’s Note: Testing abductions from uncertain evidence

items.abstract: There is a crisis of state theory in British legal thought because both philosophers of law and public law theorists reject or avoid thinking about legal order in terms of the state as a personne morale , an entity in whose name officials act and which the individuals subject to its power have reason to regard as legitimate. The position is quite different in German legal thought in which state theory is central. I rely on Weimar legal theorist Hermann Heller's explanation that a crisis of state theory results when one neglects one of the two dimensions of the modern legal state that interact with each other in sustaining it and maintaining its legitimacy – the social dimension or how the facts of social life affect the content of legal norms and the legal dimension or how those norms shape the facts of social life. I show that this kind of crisis manifests itself in Britain because the topic of the state and its legitimacy is displaced onto other topics in ways that result in the same neglect, including by Heller revivalists at the LSE. This neglect explains the strange character of contemporary public law debate.
items.title: The Crisis of British State Theory

items.abstract: Research shows that affluent citizens see more of their preferred policies realized than the less affluent. If indicative of unequal influence over decisions, then this poses a problem for democratic equality. But one theory suggests that the affluent are better informed and therefore prefer policies that were going to be implemented anyway. If so, it would be a question of unequal information, not influence. We test this theory on the case of monetary policy in the United Kingdom, where information effects are especially likely: The policy-maker (the Bank of England) has a well-defined goal of price stability, there is broad expert agreement on how to achieve this, and the general public is not well informed of inflation dynamics. Survey data from more than 120,000 UK respondents from 2001 to 2026 reveal that monetary policy aligns more with the preferences of high-income earners, who are better informed about monetary policy and the state of the economy. Nevertheless, information can only explain about a quarter of the gap in preference–policy alignment between income groups, even in this most-likely setting. The unequal policy alignment identified in previous research is therefore unlikely to be a mere artifact of informational asymmetry and remains an important problem for political equality.
items.title: Does policy align with the preferences of the affluent because they are better informed? An empirical test

items.abstract: In democracies, protests can challenge public policy reforms, raising questions on how governments should respond. Our study examines how citizens in the Netherlands would prefer their governments to respond to social protests. Using a pre-registered survey experiment (N = 1262), we varied the level of government implementing a reform and the level of public support for a reform. We used observational data to assess respondents’ views on the reforms and their trust in the government. While our findings reveal relatively strong support for accommodating social protests, citizens are more likely to back governments that ignore protests when these reforms have majority support and align with their own views. Trust in the government also plays a role, but the level of government does not matter for citizens’ attitudes. Overall, our findings highlight that citizens expect governments to listen to social protests but their attitudes are further contingent upon instrumental reasoning and majoritarian views of democracy.
items.title: When do citizens support government decisions to ignore social protests? The role of instrumental considerations and majoritarian preferences
