items.abstract: Abstract In a recent essay, Anna Boncompagni (2024) argues that prejudices are hinges that play a normative role of evidential significance. This is meant to account for why prejudices are resistant to counterevidence and difficult to overcome, while clarifying their epistemic role in undermining testimonial justification. I argue that prejudices are not like hinges and motivate my own view of the epistemic role of prejudices. In §2, I discuss the view that prejudices comprise generic generalizations and illustrate two key features of prejudices: resistance to counterevidence and accommodation of counterevidence. In §3, I reiterate two virtues of the hinge account but then show that it suffers from explanatory redundancy. To explain why prejudices are resistant to counterevidence, either we accept that prejudices play a hinge-like normative role of evidential significance, or we appeal to the generic content of prejudices. To avoid explanatory redundancy and account for evidential accommodation, I argue that we should reject the thesis that prejudices play a normative role of evidential significance. In §4, I present my view that prejudices (as generic generalizations) are misleading evidence about properties of the relevant target group, while defending it against some objections. In §5, I present a distinct argument about the rational evaluability and epistemic criticizability of prejudices, to show that local de facto hinges and prejudices differ epistemically. The essay ends with some suggestions for applying the hinge framework to social phenomena.
items.title: Prejudices are not like hinges
Expressives, Expressive-Relativism, and assessment-sensitivity

items.abstract: Abstract The reliabilist sometimes, contrary to our intuitions, has to confer justification on beliefs acquired via brain lesions or clairvoyance. This is the problem of strange and fleeting processes. Here, I attempt to find a solution to the problem. After rejecting a few attempts that seemingly lead us astray, I posit that strangeness has to do with mysterious ascriptions of propensities to produce true beliefs. Then, once we adopt a more appropriate understanding of strangeness, I argue that fleetingness becomes a non-issue. If correct, the approach taken in this article allows the reliabilist to forgo adding a necessary condition on justification that specifies a reliable belief-forming process’s circumstances, the type of world it belongs to, or its evolutionary origins.
items.title: The problem of strange and fleeting processes
Are there too many reasons?
Making the invisible visible: a reflection method to uncover justice-related design choices in energy models with model developers and users
The Digital Demon: a Cartesian challenge for AI alignment

items.abstract: Abstract Using a legally obtained dataset of 34 copyrighted O’Reilly Media books (13,962 paragraphs), we apply the DE-COP membership inference attack to test whether OpenAI models show recognition of non-public (pay-walled) content they were not licensed to train on. Our main contribution is examining non-public books, which allows us to consider potential access violations and not just training inclusion. Our results suggest that GPT-4o, OpenAI’s more recent and capable model in our sample, exhibits patterns consistent with recognition of non-public books, with an AUROC score of 0.82 (95% bootstrapped CI: 0.60−0.96)—where above 50% is better than random chance. GPT-3.5 Turbo (trained two years prior) and the smaller GPT-4o Mini both score near chance recognition on non-public data (0.54 and 0.56, respectively). Results are robust to independent paraphrasers (Gemma and Qwen) and leave-one-book-out sensitivity analyses. We also test both GPT-4o and GPT-4o mini, with the same October 2023 training cutoff date, to ensure the model is not simply identifying language shifts over time. These findings support disclosure requirements for pre-training data provenance and formal licensing markets for training content. Results remain preliminary given the small book sample, possible contamination of post-cutoff controls, and differences across models in size, architecture, and training composition.
items.title: Beyond public access in LLM pre-training data
Subjectivity without a subject: structural agency and ethical attribution in artificial intelligence

items.abstract: Abstract Context While artificial intelligence offers transformative potential for disaster risk reduction, its ethical deployment raises critical concerns when life-critical decisions depend on algorithmic systems with varying levels of accessibility across responsible organizations. This study quantifies AI adoption disparities across Australian DRR stakeholders and identifies institutional factors driving the adoption gap between innovation and operational deployment. A mixed-methods approach combined systematic review of 217 global AI-DRR publications (1999–2024) with qualitative analysis of 14 Australian organizations across government, academic, and NGO/private sectors (February-March 2025). Semi-structured interviews and document analysis examined AI technique adoption, data integration, and downscaling applications, with implementation levels systematically coded on a 1–5 scale following an inter-coder validated protocol. Government agencies demonstrate lower AI adoption (mean score 2.1/5) compared to academic institutions (4.0/5) and NGO/private organizations (3.4/5), representing a 47.5% adoption gap between government and academic sectors (Cohen’s d ≈ 2.0, indicating large practical difference despite small sample size). While academic institutions deploy advanced techniques including GANs and hybrid AI-physics models achieving 45% accuracy improvements, government agencies remain anchored to traditional systems like ACCESS with minimal AI integration. Critical barriers include procurement constraints (18–24-month cycles), computational limitations (10x below requirements), and regulatory mandates for explainable decisions. Academic innovations in AI-based downscaling, improving spatial resolution from 60 km to 10 km, remain inaccessible to operational agencies due to absence of knowledge transfer mechanisms. The study reveals an ethical adoption disparity where organizations with greatest responsibility for community safety show lowest AI adoption, creating accountability voids and equity concerns in disaster protection. This misalignment raises fundamental ethical questions about algorithmic justice, distributive justice, and procedural fairness in public safety contexts. Bridging this gap requires ethical governance frameworks addressing transparency, accountability, and equitable access to life-saving technologies, alongside institutional reforms enabling cross-sector knowledge transfer.
items.title: The ethical implementation gap in AI-driven disaster risk reduction: empirical evidence from Australia’s multi-sector analysis

items.abstract: Abstract This article examines the dynamics of inquiry under conditions of oppression. It presents an account of unjust zetetic exclusion , which arises when prejudice limits access to inquiry and the epistemic goods it yields. Unlike other forms of epistemic injustice, unjust zetetic exclusion need not result from a prejudicial credibility attribution. Instead, it may manifest even if one is perceived to be a highly competent and trustworthy inquirer, or even if one makes no judgment whatsoever regarding one’s zetetic capabilities. Unjust zetetic exclusion may result from prejudicial evaluations concerning who belongs within specific communities of inquiry and who should have access to, or possess knowledge about, a particular domain. Theories of epistemic injustice must account not only for how prejudice impacts credibility attributions but also how it regulates access to inquiry and shapes the conditions under which knowledge and other epistemic goods are acquired in the first place.
items.title: Zetetic Exclusion

items.abstract: Abstract This article examines the relationship between judicial dissent, participation, and authority at the Inter-American Court of Human Rights (IACtHR) in the highly complex and contentious field of environmental and climate litigation, with particular attention to Advisory Opinion OC-32/25. It proposes the analytical category of “competence resistance” to identify dissenting opinions that challenge the Court’s authority to progressively develop new rights and conventional standards. Drawing on informational, attitudinal, and interest-group models, the article empirically examines the influence of amicus curiae participation. The analysis shows that broad, diverse, and technically specialized participation does not necessarily eliminate internal resistance within the IACtHR but can contribute to reshaping and moderating the argumentative and institutional conditions in which such resistance unfolds, thereby strengthening the Court’s judicial authority.
items.title: De la resistencia a la participación: El impacto de los amicus curiae en el litigio ambiental y climático interamericano

items.abstract: Abstract From 2020 to 2024, the European Centre for Law and Justice (ECLJ), a conservative NGO backed by US evangelical Christians, secured certain procedural reforms to the practices of the European Court of Human Rights. The rules and guidance governing the recusal of judges were elaborated, and third-party intervention was made more transparent. These reforms were intended to constrain judicial discretion and possibly limit the liberal human rights community’s influence over the Court’s substantive jurisprudence and the Council of Europe’s (CoE) policies toward its member states and the public at large. Given the liberals’ predominance in strategic supranational litigation and their institutional incumbency, this is a puzzling outcome. The challenge to Strasbourg’s democratic legitimacy took place in the teeth of a tightly closed political opportunity structure for conservative Christians. Relying on process tracing and abductive inference to the best explanation known, within an actor-centered institutionalist framework, we show how the ECLJ, acting as a norm entrepreneur, controverted certain possible conflicts of interest involving named judges and prominent liberal NGOs and their private donors. In the process, it mobilized conservative member state governments and delegates to national and supranational parliaments to prevail on the CoE committee system (comitology) and the Court to undertake limited reforms. These concessions demonstrate the potential of a new elite transnational network of ­conservative Christians to challenge Strasbourg’s incumbents against a political background of rising populism.
items.title:
Disrupting Strasbourg: Conservative Christian challengers
                    versus
                    liberal incumbents

items.abstract: Abstract How is progress in the academic discipline of ethics related to improvements in people’s ethical thoughts and behaviors? We propose that there is disciplinary ethical progress on some phenomenon to the extent that the discipline puts people in a position to increase their understanding of that phenomenon. Even though progress, thus construed, does not guarantee improved thoughts and behaviors, progressive ethical theorizing nonetheless enables these improvements. Our account thus has the resources with which to substantiate and shed light on concerns that academic work in ethics is too isolated, obtuse, or trivial.
items.title: Progress in Ethics: Out of the Ivory Tower

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Climate change is a 21st century problem, and we must be ready to adapt our practices in order to confront it. Current philosophical efforts to reconcile our obligations to make healthcare sustainable with important principles of patient care have been successful up to a point, but do not go far enough. We consider a specific novel intervention that could be adopted by doctors as part of healthcare systems' efforts to reduce carbon emissions, which is an extension of the Pendleton consultation model asking General Practitioners (GPs) to explore patients' Ideas, Concerns, and Expectations (ICE). Our model, which we call ICE2, includes wider questions in which GPs also ask patients about how they might adapt their lifestyle to reduce its environmental impact. We consider the moral‐theoretical underpinning of this new model and argue for its consistency with patient‐centred care. We also consider specific objections to the adoption of ICE2: that there will be a backlash from patients that will lead to their being hesitant to seek healthcare going forward; that it will open the door to doctors moralising about other issues that are inappropriate; and that clinicians do not have the training or expertise required to discuss climate change. We discuss our responses to these objections, finding that they all fail to provide a knockdown reason against at least embarking upon a trial of the ICE2 model in settings where an individual doctor deems it appropriate to discuss it with a particular patient.
items.title: General Practitioners Should Ask Patients to Reduce Their Carbon Footprints

items.abstract: ABSTRACT This paper aims to address a lingering misconception about an ethics of care: that it is simply a form of virtue ethics that includes the straightforward virtue of care. Care cannot be a standard virtue of character, I argue, because care is a necessary precondition of virtue. Virtue ethics sets itself apart from consequentialist or deontological ethical theories by explaining ‘the good’ in terms of virtues, as opposed to outcome or right action. Superficially, there would seem to be nothing very unusual about accommodating care within a virtue ethical framework. In ordinary discourse we talk of the virtuous person as being caring in the same way that we might talk of them as being charitable, kind, courageous or witty. Nevertheless, over the course of this paper I argue that care is not a virtue like courage or wit but something more ethically fundamental that makes courage, wit and other virtues intelligible.
items.title: Is Care a Virtue? A New Account of Care's Relationship With Virtue Ethics

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Thomas Nagel highlighted a puzzle in accommodating the subjective fact that I am TN within an objective, centerless conception of reality. He rejected the “semantic diagnosis,” which treats “I” as an indexical as trivial, and proposed instead the concept of the “objective self.” In this paper, I do two things: first, I defend the semantic diagnosis against Nagel's objections; second, I vindicate Nagel's positive proposal involving the objective self by demonstrating that it is not a genuine alternative to the semantic diagnosis but is recoverable from within a Lewisian centered‐worlds version of it. I show how the Lewisian framework, through factorizing centered content into objective, and subjective components provides the conceptual resources to model the phenomenology of first‐person thought Nagel describes.
items.title: The View From the Centre: Recovering Nagel's Objective Self

items.abstract: ABSTRACT ‘Propositions’ are or include truths and falsehoods—potential points of agreement and disagreement. On the question of when it's a case of different propositions, or instead a case of the same proposition differently expressed, conflicting philosophical positions are canvassed and a Fregean conclusion drawn.
items.title: Distinct Propositions/Same Proposition

items.abstract: In this virtual roundtable, scholars Victoria Hesford, Vivian Huang, Michael Hardt, and Natasha Zaretsky discuss Ramzi Fawaz's Queer Forms (New York University Press 2002).
items.title:
Queer forms
                    : A forum

items.abstract: Should care be understood exclusively as the work done to meet the basic needs of dependents such as children or as a broader set of practices in which people in different kinds of relationships partake? If the latter, what makes care distinctive and distinct from other values, ideals, and practices? Despite the growing attention of political philosophy to issues of care, I argue that we still lack an account of care suitable to address these questions from a political perspective. One of the problems is that existing proposals are either too narrow, as they exclusively focus on dependency care, or too broad, such that they fail to capture the distinctiveness of care. In this article, I address this challenge by presenting an account of care that captures a wide-ranging set of politically relevant practices of care while at the same time making sense of its distinctiveness. What makes care distinctive, I argue, is that it takes place in the context of relationships of care characterized by specific attitudes.
items.journal: Journal of Ethics and Social Philosophy
items.title: Care and Caring Relationships: A Political Account

items.abstract: People sometimes attempt to avoid blame with the following excuse: “I didn’t know I was doing anything wrong; I was just doing my job.” I argue that this excuse points towards a distinctive form of genuinely exculpatory ignorance. Complying with social role norms involves following deliberative norms that can explain agents’ claims of ignorance and mitigate their blameworthiness. My account of this experience makes a surprising contribution to the debate over when ignorance excuses. If we accept that nonculpable moral ignorance excuses, my argument highlights a novel form of ignorance that can be experienced by role occupants. On some views, however, what matters is being motivated by the right reasons (having a “good will”), so even nonculpably morally ignorant agents are blameworthy because they are not appropriately responsive to moral considerations. My account challenges the accepted view that having a good will just is responsiveness to moral reasons. I offer role occupants as a case study of moral ignorance with a good will. The fact that our social roles can lead to exculpatory ignorance in this ordinary and pervasive way opens up new territory for theories of moral responsibility.
items.journal: Journal of Ethics and Social Philosophy
items.title: Social Roles and Exculpatory Ignorance

items.abstract: The just savings principle is the centerpiece of John Rawls’s account of intergenerational justice. Yet it is hard to see why the parties in the original position could accept it, for it imposes net costs on the worst-off first generation. Many attempt to solve this “problem of the first generation” by offering explanations as to why the parties could accept Rawls’s principle. Here I take a different approach. I show that most of these attempts neglect a crucial consideration; there is an alternative savings principle that the parties should prefer to Rawls’s own. According to the compensated savings principle, the first generation should be compensated for the cost of their savings by younger generations with whom they overlap. I defend this principle as the most promising explanation yet of why the parties could rationally choose a savings principle that generates the accumulation required for a just basic structure.
items.journal: Journal of Ethics and Social Philosophy
items.title: Just Savings, Compensation, and the First Generation

items.abstract: Disability self-ascriptions could be treated as descriptive claims: assertions that one satisfies the conditions for counting as disabled. This article focuses on a different function that such ascriptions can serve. Drawing on Quill Kukla and Mark Lance’s account of gender ascriptions, we argue that first-person disability ascriptions often function as speech acts that position the speaker within social space. More precisely, we argue that self-ascribing disability can serve as a request or demand that the speaker not be held to certain capability norms, or norms about what people are expected to be able to do. Not only that, but these self-ascriptions often also serve as demands for access, specifically access to what the speakers need in order to manifest valued capabilities. We use this account to explain three common sources of ambivalence that individuals experience around claiming disability.
items.journal: Journal of Ethics and Social Philosophy
items.title: The Pragmatics of Disability Self-Ascriptions

items.abstract: Manipulation is widely regarded as a presumptively impermissible method of influence, in contrast to persuasion, which is usually presented as presumptively permissible. Calling something manipulative is typically a moral criticism; calling it persuasive is not. Although there is a flourishing philosophical literature on manipulation, that on persuasion is comparatively underdeveloped despite persuasion being one of the most common and important ways in which people influence one another. This article begins to remedy that situation. We present a novel account of persuasion, drawing on and explicating the distinction from manipulation. The aim is to show what persuasion is in such a way that explains why it is presumptively permissible, whereas manipulation is not. We first develop an account of manipulation by adapting an account recently defended by Robert Noggle. We then define nonmanipulative influence in general, then carve out persuasion therefrom. Throughout, we assume that persuasion is not manipulative. However, we are open to the possibility that there is in fact overlap between persuasion and manipulation, in which case the account we present is of specifically nonmanipulative persuasion, which we still take to be an interesting and important category of influence. We are also not concerned specifically with rational persuasion; our account allows for persuasion that need not be fully rational. The result is a holistic account that is useful in considering the nature and ethics of influence.
items.journal: Journal of Ethics and Social Philosophy
items.title: Distinguishing Persuasion from Manipulation

items.abstract: Suppose that you must choose between killing an innocent person or letting others die. Moderate deontology says that when the stakes are high enough in such a case, killing the innocent person becomes right, but the stakes must be very high for this to happen—much higher than standard forms of consequentialism take them to be. Critics object that moderate deontology is committed to arbitrary cutoffs, and this feature makes the theory arbitrary in a way that competing theories are not. I refute this objection.
items.journal: Journal of Ethics and Social Philosophy
items.title: Refuting the Arbitrary Cutoff Objection to Moderate Deontology

items.abstract: Abstract Across societies and over time, the social control of objects deemed “dangerous”—i.e., as threats to public order, morality, or physical and psychological well-being—varies, from regulation to prohibition, with implications for responsibility, potential harm, and affected communities. Drawing on U.S. Congressional hearings on the issue of cannabis regulation and prohibition (1906–1951), we examine how shifts in social control track changing configurations of discursive institutional work. Our work demonstrates how configurations of rationalization, moralization, and syncretization shaped the meaning of cannabis as a dangerous object: rationalization calculates the risk, supporting calibrated regulation; moralization absolutizes the danger, promoting prohibition; and syncretization balances these two. We refer to this reciprocal dynamic as an epistemic ratchet, whereby rationalization and moralization each weaken the epistemic foundations of the alternative regime, making movement between regulation and prohibition difficult in either direction. Our study makes three contributions: (a) it extends the organizing-of-risk account of how danger is rendered governable to the form and reversibility of control; (b) it adds to research on discursive institutional work by identifying epistemology, complexity, and responsibility as the object-level qualities through which discourse becomes consequential for governance; and (c) it contributes to debates on responsibility, ethics, and harm by showing how the discursive redistribution of responsibility shapes the scope and coerciveness of control.
items.title: Discursive Institutional Work and the Social Control of Dangerous Objects

items.abstract: This article addresses two related questions. First, what is it to have a gender identity? Second, what are gender identities, metaphysically speaking? In answer to the first, I defend a “doing” model: to “have” a gender identity is to engage in an ongoing act of self-interpretation. In answer to the second, I defend a social model: gender identities are shared social tools that individuals draw on and recreate in their acts of self-interpretation. This account of gender identity remains faithful to the operative concept of gender identity, giving philosophical substance to the idea of a “gendered sense of self.” It respects sincere self-ascriptions of gender, escaping the exclusion problems that plague other accounts of gender identity. It avoids circularity, and it has greater explanatory power than rival accounts. By emphasizing how interpretative resources are learned and shared through social interactions, it captures the sense in which gender identities are not wholly internal but are negotiated in dialogue with others, using resources made available by one’s social context. It can therefore explain how and why practices of self-ascribing gender change over time and across cultures. Moreover, it explains why individuals cannot exercise entirely free choice over their gender identities yet can exercise some limited agency over them. This article demonstrates that we can take gender identity to be deeply social without denying its first-personal character; we can allow for agency without conceding unconstrained choice. We achieve this by understanding gender identity in terms of an ongoing, socially mediated practice of self-interpretation.

items.title: The Metaphysics of Gender Identity

items.abstract: ABSTRACT The purpose of a first‐in‐human (FIH) clinical trial is to gather safety, side effects, and (potential) dosage information, which is to say, information about how an intervention affects and interacts with the human body. Although participants in FIH trials may personally benefit, the primary goal is to obtain participant baseline human safety knowledge or knowledge of intervention efficacy. Some FIH clinical trials carry significant foreseeable risk to participants with little to no foreseeable participant benefit. As the potential risk is high and personal benefit unlikely, there is consensus that participants in risky FIH trials should consent to participate, which entails that children should not be included in a risky FIH trial that could enroll only adults. We take aim at this view and argue that risky FIH trials planned for adults should be open also to including children in some circumstances. Specifically, and focusing primarily on solid organ xenotransplant research, we argue that considerations of generalizability, fair inclusion, differential risk‐benefit, parental authority, and children's interest are ethically salient, and that concerns of exploitation, instrumentalization, and upper‐limits of harm can be effectively addressed.
items.title: The Case for Pediatric Participation in Risky First‐In‐Human Clinical Trials

Garland, sociological criminology, and the United States’ penal exceptionalism

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Algorithmically managed platform labor transforms the organization of employment, but the lived experience of this emerging form of labor has not yet received much attention in the philosophy of work. Starting from the assumption that work shapes individuals as citizens and therefore needs to be evaluated from a democratic perspective, this article explores how delivery riders in Buenos Aires experience this form of employment. Based on qualitative research, it explores two dimensions of the riders' perspective: to whom they ascribe agency and responsibility, and whether they experience spaces for deliberation in the context of their work. We show, in particular, how their ascriptions of responsibility for structural problems often focus on customers, while the company disappears behind the technical affordance of the app, and how the organizational model of platform work minimizes opportunities for deliberation. Our discussion sheds light on the interplay between subjective experiences of work and the broader structural forces shaping contemporary labor markets, and thereby the conditions of democratic politics.
items.title: “… You Realize How You Can Use the App and Not Let the App Use You.” The Moral Universe of Latin American Delivery Riders From the Perspective of Democratic Citizenship
Issue Information

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Suppose some uncoordinated group of agents causes tremendous harm, but none of the individuals could have meaningfully changed this result by acting differently. These “collective harm” cases have been the subject of extended philosophical discussion, but this paper argues that there are really two different, if connected, puzzles presented by such cases: (1) a puzzle about how to characterize the moral injury to those who suffer this harm (the “wrongness puzzle”) and (2) a puzzle about why agents may do something wrong in participating in producing this harm (the “participation puzzle”). This paper elaborates these puzzles, defends the idea that they are different from each other, and offers solutions to them both. The core idea is that an application of the distinction between ideal and nonideal theory can shed light on both puzzles; the injury experienced by the victims of collective harm is to be understood in terms of the shortfall they suffer from how they would fare if ideal circumstances obtained, and participation in collective harm is wrong when it involves reasoning that fails to appropriately apply ideal moral rules to nonideal situations.
items.title: Solving the Dual Puzzles of Collective Harm
Issue Information

items.abstract:
Private rights have returned to play a central role in public law. In the last few years alone, courts have invoked private rights to elaborate the elements of Article III standing, interpret the scope of 42 U.S.C. § 1983’s cause of action, articulate the limits of the administrative state, and give meaning to enumerated constitutional rights. But unlike private law—which has confronted a similar fall and rise of private rights with wide-ranging discussion over their meaning—public law has not been subjected to a fulsome debate about what exactly private rights are. Both proponents and critics of the return of a private rights model of public law adjudication share a basic understanding of private rights rooted in William Blackstone’s eighteenthcentury writings. But Blackstone’s view fails to capture the full significance of private rights in the common law. Overemphasizing it muddles the stakes of the return of private rights in public law.

This Article articulates the historical and doctrinal limits of the default Blackstonian view of private rights. Blackstone’s conception of private rights was based on an underlying view of liberty as noninterference that was controversial even when he was writing in the 1760s. Instead, the dominant view of liberty in the common law at the time was the republican view of liberty as independence. That view of liberty supported a distinct republican conception of private rights, which has coexisted in the common law tradition alongside the Blackstonian conception.

After outlining the oft-elided republican conception of private rights and tracing its influence on legal discourse, rhetoric, and case law, this Article illustrates its possible implications for public law doctrine. Recognizing the distinction between these two conceptions of private rights casts new light on Article III standing, damages, Section 1983, and adjudication outside Article III courts. This distinction also provides a corrective to the scholarly debates over private and public rights: Just as it is a mistake to suppose there was a single unified historical conception of private rights, it is also a mistake to dismiss private rights altogether as inherently confused or obfuscatory.
items.title: “Private Rights” in Public Law

items.abstract:
Federalism has long been celebrated for its ability to foster policy innovation, transforming states into “laboratories of democracy.” Yet, federalism discourse has largely neglected Indian tribes, the third sovereign in the American constitutional order. Tribes regularly implement novel policies. However, tribal policy innovation is hindered by uncertainty over whether tribes or states govern Indian country activities.

The most influential framework for determining the scope of tribal versus state regulatory power in Indian country is derived from the Supreme Court’s opinion in California v. Cabazon Band of Mission Indians—the case that launched Indian gaming. Cabazon held that tribes cannot permit an activity if the surrounding state prohibits it, but they can permit an activity if the surrounding state regulates it. For example, tribes in California can authorize gaming because California regulates it. However, Utah’s gaming ban prevents tribes within its borders from permitting casinos. The distinction between regulatory and prohibitory is often ambiguous; thus, state specificity invites endless litigation that stifles tribal policy experimentation.

To remedy this uncertainty and fully integrate tribes into the federal system, this Article proposes a “Cabazon-plus” paradigm. Under Cabazon-plus, if any state regulates an activity, all tribes would have exclusive regulatory authority over that activity. This paradigm provides the jurisdictional certainty vital for tribal self-determination and policy innovation. Furthermore, this Article argues Cabazon-plus will ignite tribal economies and benefit state economies, validating tribal sovereignty as a feature—not a bug—of a dynamic federal system.
items.title: Tribal Federalism: Expanding the Indian Gaming Paradigm

items.abstract: A murder is an intentional killing, but some killings happen by mistake or accident. Although mistakes and accidents are unintended parts of an action, some jurisdictions prosecute unintended homicides as murder crimes in at least three patterns of cases. Together, these propositions present a puzzle that undermines a fundamental principle of criminal responsibility: An agent must unify the elements of a crime as a matter of their agency for criminal responsibility to attach. I examine five insightful ways to interpret this principle in the literature, and I argue that none can account for all three case patterns. Primarily, I offer a solution to the puzzle based on the intentional causation relation. According to this solution, although intentionally acting does not involve the intent to cause every change one makes as part of the action, it does involve intentionally causing all such changes, including the mistakes or accidents.
items.title: Unintended murder

items.abstract: This paper addresses a question that has been overlooked by the growing body of literature on private law formalism: how are formalist private law categories constructed? I read Ernest Weinrib’s treatment of unjust enrichment in chapter 6 of his Corrective Justice not as a substantive theory of that doctrine but rather as an instance in which a formalist jurist appears to be constructing a private law category. I argue that in developing his account of unjust enrichment, Weinrib follows three consecutive methodological steps: compilation, characterization and determination. The article first distils these steps from Weinrib’s work and subsequently examines them in depth, proposing them as the building blocks of a preliminary theory of category construction within formalist private law theory.
items.title: The construction of formalist categories

items.abstract: ABSTRACT This article considers the prerogatives that parents have to shape their children's identity by adopting a dietary regime that gives expression to the conception of the good embraced by parents. It examines Matthew Clayton's recent claim that respect for the independence of children requires that parents set aside religious, aesthetic, and gastronomic reasons to control the food that children eat and that parents wrong their children if they impose on them comprehensive views about what they should eat. Against Clayton, I argue that a modest form of parental perfectionism is consistent with respect for children's independence. On this view, parents may provisionally privilege a dietary regime in raising their children. Moreover, privileging a dietary regime does not involve the kind of comprehensive enrolment into a conception of the good that Clayton views as objectionable. A suitable form of privileging can contribute to autonomy development in children and manifests respect for them.
items.title: Food, Families, and Parental Perfectionism: A Rejoinder to Clayton

items.abstract: ABSTRACT In recent years, many political philosophers have made the case for thinking that achieving a fully just society will require some variety of mandatory civilian service. However, there is widespread agreement that mandatory service schemes are in significant tension with commitments to freedom of occupation. Correspondingly, support for mandatory service schemes is also taken to be in deep tension with the liberal tradition, with its emphasis on the fundamental importance of protecting basic liberties. The purpose of this article is to argue that there is far less tension between mandatory service schemes and freedom of occupation than this widely accepted picture supposes. Though liberalism does contain the resources to mount a case against mandatory service in certain circumstances, that case will not be a straightforward matter of principle, but rather a complex matter of balancing difficult empirical considerations. Moreover, liberalism may, in some circumstances, actually be committed to some forms of moderate mandatory service, not in spite of but, in part, because of its commitment to the special status of liberty.
items.title: Forced Labour for Liberals: Mandatory Service, Social Equality, and Freedom of Occupation
“AI psychosis” in context: how conversation history shapes LLM responses to delusional beliefs

items.abstract: Abstract This study examines how Responsible AI (RAI) principles are translated as they move from ethical discourse into governance, standards, and national policy contexts. Drawing on comparative analysis of influential AI ethics guidelines, policy syntheses, and technical glossaries, the research traces how widely cited principles are reformulated across domains, using transparency and fairness as cases of how institutional translation operates in practice. It shows that while these principles originate as broad normative commitments, they become progressively institutionalized as policy categories, procedural requirements, and measurable technical properties. The comparison shows that the underlying mechanism generalizes across principles, while the resulting institutional forms remain principle-specific. Focusing on national AI strategies as a key site of institutionalization, the study analyzes how RAI principles are embedded within state agendas, regulatory approaches, and oversight mechanisms. This analysis reveals variation in how principles are prioritized and operationalized, reflecting differences in governance priorities, administrative capacity, and political context. The findings highlight that principles most amenable to standardization and measurement tend to dominate policy implementation, while more expansive ethical concepts are less visible. By mapping these shifts across institutional settings, the paper contributes to a deeper understanding of how AI ethics is reconfigured in practice and offers insights for policymakers seeking to balance technical feasibility with normative ambition in the governance of AI.
items.title: When principles become policy: the institutional translation of responsible AI in national AI ​strategies
What a rule base cannot say: a semiotic analysis of ontology-based legal reasoning in Vietnam

items.abstract: Abstract Control over the information ecosystem and the public narrative is a hallmark of authoritarian governments. In the digital age, social media created new vulnerabilities within information ecosystems that can be exploited by different actors to undermine democracy: particularly the ease of deploying disinformation at scale, and the economic weakening of independent media. This article documents how the government of Gustavo Petro in Colombia exploited both vulnerabilities simultaneously and systematically through four tactics: the opaque use of state-funded influencers, the political mobilization of institutional social media accounts, the redirection of government advertising spending to the detriment of independent media, and editorial control over public radio and television. The article argues that, together, the simultaneous and systematic exploitation of these vulnerabilities can be characterized of authoritarian tendency. Finally, the article identifies several areas for intervention to mitigate these risks in the future.
items.title: Cuando el Estado desinforma: Prácticas autoritarias en el ecosistema de información de Colombia y América Latina When the State Disinforms: Authoritarian Practices in the Information Ecosystem of Colombia and Latin America

items.abstract: ABSTRACT This article addresses the question whether arguments about the badness of death can offer useful analogies for understanding the badness of extinction. The two main lines of argumentation, the Epicurean approach and the deprivation view, are analyzed from this perspective. The analogies offer some interesting viewpoints to killing and anthropogenic mass extinction, for example. Nevertheless, we conclude that the analogy to death fails to explain badness of extinction. As the major (Western) moral theories also seem to fail on this task, we propose that the badness of extinction should be understood as a tethered concept: extinction is then bad as a loss to someone who understands and experiences that loss.
items.title: On Associating Extinction with Death: Fatal Implications for Conservation?

items.abstract: Abstract In this paper I will offer a detailed analysis of Bayesian species delimitation methods and the oversplitting problem. I will argue that when discussing oversplitting, two issues should be kept separate: the inference problem concerning the discovery of population structure and the labelling problem surrounding the classification of different lineages as distinct species. Understanding oversplitting as a methodological problem of Bayesian inference is the consequence of not separating the inferential problem from the labelling problem. While there is no intrinsic flaw with Bayesian inference of population structure revealed by oversplitting, treatments of the inference problem can benefit from some of the lessons learned in earlier discussions of Bayesian phylogenetic inference.
items.title: Oversplitting and Bayesian Inference
Minds in skilled performance: cognitive science and the wild west

items.abstract: This article examines the first use of section 35 of the Scotland Act 1998, which prevented the Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill from receiving Royal Assent. It argues that the 2023 Order is constitutionally significant because it operationalised a previously unused form of executive control over devolved legislation. Section 35 permits intervention where the Secretary of State has reasonable grounds to believe that modifications made by a devolved Bill would adversely affect the operation of reserved law. It therefore separates legislative competence from legislative effectiveness: a Bill may fall within devolved competence yet be prevented from becoming law following a prospective ministerial assessment. Drawing on the statutory framework, the Statement of Reasons, and the Court of Session's judgment, the article characterises section 35 as a preventive executive power constrained by statutory conditions, parliamentary annulment, and judicial review, but one which affords substantial latitude to predictive ministerial judgement. It develops this arrangement as a statutory form of conditional autonomy, building on earlier accounts of politically conditioned devolution, and situates the provision within a broader pattern of UK executive constitutionalism. Its longer‐term significance will depend on whether section 35 remains exceptional or becomes a more regular instrument of territorial governance.
items.title: Section 35 of the Scotland Act 1998 and Executive Control of Devolved Legislation

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Feminism opposes the unjust inequality and subjugation of women. Core feminist projects morally critique people, institutions, social practices, norms, and behaviors that contribute to or constitute the subordination of women. But such projects confront individual women and groups of women who participate in and endorse the practices being critiqued. A common response to this tension is to posit adaptive preferences in the form of “deformed desires” among participating women. But a standing alternative holds that participating women engage in trade‐offs among goods in nonideal situations. Here, I extend this “tradeoffs” alternative by arguing that simple ideas from game‐theoretic models support the possibility of trade‐off explanations that respect and illuminate the agency of participating women while allowing for feminist critique. And trade‐off accounts can avoid substantive assumptions regarding human flourishing or the nature of the good. Both features make trade‐off accounts normatively preferable to adaptive preference accounts of participation in unjust social arrangements.
items.title: Participation Without Adaptive Preferences

items.abstract: Today, it is commonplace to claim that liberalism created the modern world. This paper examines how and why the rise-of-liberalism narrative first emerged by examining textbooks and surveys on the history of political thought published in Britain and the United States between 1890 and the 1990s. In doing so, it shows how, in the interwar period, a new conception of “liberalism” was invented, imagining it as a secular emancipatory movement that shaped the modern world in its image. Second, this paper highlights how this master narrative was created by liberalism’s self-professed enemies—by Marxists and conservative thinkers—as much as by its friends, to serve different polemical purposes. Finally, this paper offers some reflections on the implications of this account of the historiography of liberalism for its contemporary defenders. It concludes that liberals themselves might have good reason to relinquish overblown claims about the importance of liberalism in the making of the modern world.
items.title: The Invention of Liberalism

items.abstract: Positions that link rights to sentience face an insect challenge: insects are plausibly sentient, yet recognizing individual insects as rights-bearers would problematize public health, veterinary, and agricultural benefits obtained by harming them. The most obvious responses seem inadequate. Indian animal ethics, which has always taken the idea of insect sentience seriously, is a promising place to look for further options. Of particular relevance is the idea of ahimsa (nonviolence, noninjury), but ahimsa in its ancient form has metaphysical commitments that secular animal ethics should not accept. More promising still is the progressive ahimsaism developed by Gandhi in the 1920s, on which duties of nonmaleficence can be overridden by duties of care, provided the duty of care is adopted, interpreted, and exercised in accordance with the guiding ideal of ahimsa. This article provides an exposition and analysis of the view and relates it to the insect challenge.
items.title: Ethics for a Large Sentient World: Insects, Ahimsa, and Gandhi’s Progressive Ahimsaism

items.abstract: Jonathan Birch's 'Ethics for a Large Sentient World' presents a novel approach to the challenges associated with granting sentient insects direct moral concern. The Gandhian-inspired ethic that Birch develops takes insect sentience seriously while maintaining that insects have no right not to be harmed when harming them is necessary to secure human and nonhuman animal health and agricultural benefits. This paper offers a critical response to Birch's framework. I begin by arguing that Birch misinterprets the challenge facing a robust rights-based theory. I then show that his Gandhian alternative is not a genuine departure from a robust rights-based view but rather a specific, and ultimately unappealing, version of it. I show that Birch's view is unattractive because it holds that duties of care can function as exceptions to rights, which has problematic implications for all sentient beings, including humans.
items.title: In Defence of Robust Rights for All Sentient Creatures

items.abstract: In his ‘Ethics for a Large Sentient World: Insects, Ahimsa, and Gandhi’s Progressive Ahimsaism’ Jonathan Birch attempts to provide a solution to one of the most difficult problems in animal ethics: the insect challenge. If insects are sentient, and if sentience is sufficient for the possession of robust rights not to be harmed, then much of our behavior is seriously wrong since it harms insects on a vast scale. Birch’s solution is based on Gandhi’s idea of Progressive Ahimsaism (PA). In this paper I argue that PA is unsuited to answer the challenges of animal suffering. First, though it emphasizes avoiding wrongdoing, the moral ideal proposed by PA makes it difficult to do positive good, tends toward antinatalism, and offers no pathway out of natural suffering. Second, PA’s duty of care model is incompatible with largescale beneficent action and precludes us from moving toward a genuinely harm-free world. Finally, I conclude by briefly suggesting that we could solve these problems by seeing humanity as a collective agent with a moral duty to care for all sentient beings and individual human actions as justified insofar as they are compatible with this mission.
items.title: Ethics for a Tragic World: Humanity, Insects, and Doing Good

items.abstract: The recognition of invertebrates as ‘plausibly sentient’ raises significant ethical questions in contexts where they are harmed. In response to Jonathan Birch’s presentation of Gandhi’s ahimsaism (nonviolence) as a potential means of navigating this ‘insect challenge’, we draw on fieldwork conducted at the Skanda Vale ashram to provide a comparative critique of, and potential alternative to, ahmsaism. For the community at Skanda Vale, the ethos of nonviolence cannot be separated from the wider metaphysical commitments of foundational South Asian religious traditions. Within such a context we come to question the prioritization of sentience as a marker of responsibility toward other living beings. Rather than seeking to justify harms to sentient others, we argue for an expanded circle of compassion that is more in line with traditional uses of ahimsa.
items.title: The ‘Insect Challenge’ – A Response to Birch

items.abstract: The three commentaries on ‘Ethics for a large sentient world’ raise several problems for a Gandhian approach to animal ethics. In my responses, I defend my position that granting robust rights to individual insects is untenable, pushing us to look harder at alternative options. I explain how Gandhi’s commitment to nonviolence allows him to avoid the unwelcome implications his principles might otherwise have. I consider his nuanced position on the interplay between general principles and embedded responses to particular situations. I explain why he should not be read as an antinatalist. That said, his framework undeniably presents an austere ascetic ideal that calls on us to rethink the meaning of ‘progress’. The framework condemns many aspects of modern industrialized economies, not just their treatment of nonhuman animals.
items.title: How to Live Nonviolently in a Large Sentient World: Replies to Pepper, Hurn and Badman-King, and O’Brien
CEO Religiosity and Corporate Philanthropy: Navigating Institutional Pressures
A Sophiological Analogy for Business Ethics Achieving Unity-in-Diversity through the Wasserstein Barycenter

items.abstract: Abstract Whenever you use apps, websites, or digital infrastructure owned by large platform companies, these companies collect data from your activity. They then use the data for various highly profitable purposes, e.g., by designing targeted advertising and selling it to third parties. This paper argues that such data collection should be considered a form of wrongful exploitation. We begin by defending the simple and relatively uncontroversial idea that to exploit is to extract excessive advantage from vulnerability. We then argue that platform companies’ data collection practices are exploitative in this sense. Many internet users are vulnerable because they have limited capacity to make an informed and voluntary decision about exchanging access to their data for access to the companies’ services, or because they have no reasonable alternative to doing so. Moreover, platform companies take advantage of these vulnerabilities to extract profits that they could not otherwise have extracted. The paper ends by discussing what governments and other third parties should do about this form of exploitation. We distinguish preventive measures, which remove or mitigate users’ vulnerabilities, from prohibition and regulation, which leave these vulnerabilities intact but block companies from taking advantage of them.
items.title: Is Data Collection from Internet Users a Form of Exploitation?

items.abstract: Abstract Inner speech is often said to be a by-product of motor control, the product of a forward model driven by an efference copy of a cancelled motor command to speak. The conscious auditory imagery of inner speech is said to arise when the product of this forward model becomes conscious. This conception of the genesis of inner speech founders on some basic questions about the consciousness of inner speech and about the interaction between inner speech and episodes of imagination. Further, the empirical evidence cited in support of this theory falls short. An alternative starts with a general conception of constructive imagination, which is our capacity to produce mental images (visual, auditory, etc.) in the course of practical problem-solving. Inner speech may be conceived as a species of constructive imagination in which we construct auditory images of episodes of speech. Inner speech is an imaginative representation of speech events that do not exist, which also represents the objects and events that the represented episodes of speech would represent if they existed.
items.title: The genesis of inner speech: forward models or constructive imagination?

items.abstract: Abstract In this paper, I discuss and explore two responses to problems that arise for a simple, weight monist version of reasons first in the practical domain. These responses—weight pluralism and threshold reasons first—attempt to provide a more nuanced account of reasons and all-things-considered deontic statuses. The first problem for weight monism is that it lacks the resources to predict the intuitively correct deontic statuses for the agent's options in cases of supererogation, of practical latitude, and of moral dilemmas. The second problem is that weight monism cannot distinguish requirements from oughts. I sketch how weight pluralists try to do justice to the problem cases, as well as to distinguish requirements and oughts, by introducing several independent dimensions of a reason's weight. However, as I argue, weight pluralism faces problems of its own—it cannot uphold the entailment from requirement to ought (on some variants); it problematically casts ought as an evaluative notion (on another variant); and it undermines the action-guidingness of reasons. In the end, I explore a more sophisticated weight monist alternative, threshold reasons first, that holds some promise to avoid all of these problems.
items.title: Quo vadis, reasons first? From weight monism to weight pluralism to thresholds
A pluralist account of mnemic accuracy

items.abstract: Abstract Despite increasing legal emphasis on accessible language in contractual information, individuals continue to encounter legal documents, such as terms and conditions, imprints, and privacy statements, that remain difficult to understand. The emergence of large language models (LLMs) offers a new opportunity to translate legal jargon into accessible language and to support ongoing efforts to provide legal documents in accessible and inclusive languages. However, the use of LLMs for this purpose raises distinct ethical concerns, including hallucinations, personalization risks, and jurisdictional bias. This paper presents a preliminary ethics framework for evaluating LLM-based legal translation tools, grounded in EU regulations and aligned with the EU High-Level Expert Group’s Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI. Building on the EU-funded AI4Pol project, which aims to develop an AI-powered tool for translating legal jargon into accessible language, we examine the ethical risks of such systems, focusing on their intended purpose and challenges related to technical robustness, privacy, algorithmic bias, and explainability.
items.title: The ethical dimension of AI systems in legal jargon translation: a preliminary assessment

items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is evolving from a collection of discrete applications towards a technology increasingly embedded in the infrastructure of medicine. This development may improve diagnosis, prediction, monitoring, and the use of clinical information, but technological adoption is advancing faster than the governance structures needed to accompany it. At the level of the individual patient, this transformation creates a specific ethical problem. Patient information enters computational systems and emerges as probabilities, classifications, predictions, or recommendations that may influence care. The black box provides a metaphor for the intervening computational process when clinically relevant elements cannot be sufficiently examined. Yet opening the black box does not resolve the entire problem: an intelligible and validated prediction does not itself establish that a proposed intervention will benefit a particular patient. I propose a Patient-Level AI Code of Conduct governing the transition from AI output to clinical action. The Code requires examinability, validation, patient-level applicability, independent clinical justification, and meaningful human responsibility before an AI output materially influences care. Its purpose is to preserve a fundamental distinction as AI becomes increasingly infrastructural to medicine: computational capability can inform clinical decisions, but it cannot by itself justify action on a patient.
items.title: When prediction is not explanation: AI and the ethical transformation of medicine
The conversation missing from the article: epistemic custody and authorship in human–AI writing

items.abstract: Abstract Scholarship on responsibility and autonomous technology has extensively examined responsibility gaps, distributed agency, and the obligations of developers, manufacturers, regulators, and human operators. Yet the prospective normative position of users across repeated engagement with partially automated systems, and its relationship to responsibility after harm, remains comparatively underdeveloped. This paper argues that users of SAE Level 2 partial driving automation systems occupy a normatively distinctive position that generates two forms of obligation which have not been adequately theorized. Drawing on Conradie and Nagel’s [1] framework of taking versus holding responsibility and the concept of extended responsibility developed by Mason [2], this paper makes two-part argument. First, users of SAE Level 2 systems bear prospective responsibilities arising from their continuing supervisory role, including sustained supervisory engagement, reasonable trust calibration, appropriate knowledge-seeking about system limitations, and readiness for control intervention. Second, where harm occurs and the user’s involvement is morally significant but the conditions for ordinary blameworthiness remain uncertain, users may nevertheless be positioned to take extended retrospective responsibility. Extended responsibility therefore supplements rather than replaces ordinary responsibility.
items.title: Taking the wheel: user-side responsibility and the ethics of SAE level 2 driving automation

items.abstract: Abstract Current generative AI systems increasingly elicit attributions of understanding, emotion, and even consciousness. This creates an evidential problem for AI sentience assessment, because the behavioural and linguistic markers that motivate these attributions may be generated by multiple underlying processes. One source of uncertainty is the gaming problem: AI systems may satisfy sentience indicators because they have learned the relevant behavioural regularities. A further observer-side concern is that anthropomorphic or socially responsive behaviour may influence how strongly these markers are weighted. This paper treats these as distinct sources of evidential uncertainty and focuses on the problem of evidential certification. Behavioural similarity and verbal self-report are not evidentially significant merely because they resemble human or animal expressions of sentience. Their evidential value depends on whether they can be connected to internal processes that causally explain why the relevant outputs are produced. Cross-validating multiple behavioural markers remains unreliable in the LLM case, since models may learn not only individual markers but also their patterns of co-occurrence. Moreover, even under controlled training conditions, verbal self-report remains vulnerable to alternative computational explanations. Since assessments of AI sentience may bear on questions of welfare and moral status, errors in evidential attribution can have ethically significant consequences. In response, I propose the Causal-Representational Corroboration Standard (CCS). The CCS directly evaluates whether behavioural or verbal markers are supported by a stable and causally relevant internal organization whose evidential role is not exhausted by training pressure that directly selects for the assessed marker. The corroborated mechanism becomes relevant to sentience if it also participates in an affectively structured organization and satisfies functional or architectural conditions independently motivated by a plausible theory of consciousness. Therefore, the CCS provides a more disciplined basis for managing the ethical risks of both over-attributing and under-attributing sentience to AI systems.
items.title: Beyond behavioural markers: causal-representational corroboration in AI sentience assessment

items.abstract: Abstract We offer a theory of contrarians such as Socrates, Martin Luther, and Thoreau, and explain how contrarianism can function as an epistemic virtue. On our view, contrarians don’t just dissent from orthodoxy, but from a specific ingroup, and in a specific domain. Contrarians must also have some independent perspective that animates their dissent rather than parroting others, and they must express their dissent publicly, which will often produce alienation or reprisals. Finally, contrarianism isn’t bloodless inquiry; contrarians are animated by contempt for conformism and herd-behavior. The virtues of contrarianism include the ability to disrupt epistemic bubbles and echo-chambers that have formed among our ingroup, and contributing an adversarial element to our social epistemology, familiar from the legal system. But our account also has the resources to explain how contrarianism can spill over into a vice, since it is a trait like kindness or skepticism that requires judicious application.
items.title: The Virtues (and Vices) of Contrarianism

items.abstract: Abstract How should sociolegal scholarship understand sovereign citizens who contest state authority while remaining deeply invested in law? This article examines how Dutch sovereign citizens construct, enact, and negotiate understandings of legality in lived experience and institutional encounters. Drawing on in-depth interviews with four participants and six courtroom observations, and combining legal consciousness scholarship with narrative and relational perspectives, we identify three interrelated narrative stances through which sovereign legality is constructed and negotiated: legitimacy under contestation, re-authoring the normative order, and strategic navigation of institutional reality. These stances show that sovereign legality is neither a coherent alternative doctrine nor a straightforward rejection of state law. Rather, participants reinterpret legal authority, relocate legality in alternative normative foundations such as consent, natural law, and humanity, and adapt claims and strategies in response to institutional constraints. We conceptualize this configuration as counter-nomic legal consciousness: a narrative and relational mode of legal meaning-making through which individuals contest state authority while remaining invested in law’s language, procedures, and symbolic force. This study of Dutch sovereign citizens thus extends legal consciousness scholarship by showing how sovereign legality cuts across conventional distinctions between compliance and resistance and serves interpretive, practical, and affective functions.
items.title: (Re)writing the fiction: how Dutch sovereign citizens narrate legality

items.abstract: Abstract Consent – the organizing principle of legal responses to sexual harms – rests on a yes-versus-no binary. Yet, ambivalence is pervasive in sexual life, often eluding binary simplicity. This article assesses the implications of ambivalence for sexual consent jurisprudence. Drawing on interviews with Israeli gay and bisexual men regarding their experiences in (semi-)public sexual venues, it examines a context in which sexual norms have historically developed outside dominant cultural scripts, where ambivalence is particularly salient. Through the men’s testimonies, the conditions under which ambivalence leaves individuals uncertain of how to name sexual harms, identify boundary violations, or assign responsibility are mapped. Grounded in these findings, alongside sociological theories of ambivalence and socio-legal theories of sexual consent, the article adopts dialectical sensibility to capture what binary consent models tend to flatten: the simultaneous presence of agency/coercion, empowerment/vulnerability, and pleasure/danger within a single sexual interaction. Ambivalence in these “gray zones” is therefore reconceptualized here as neither anomaly nor individual failure but as a structuring – and even productive – feature of sexual life, complicating theories that cast ambivalence as primarily suppressive. Finally, the analysis underscores the limitations of prevailing consent paradigms and surfaces new questions about how criminal law might respond to the indeterminate realities of sex.
items.title: The ambivalence of sexual consent: a socio-legal inquiry

items.abstract: Abstract This paper examines rights consciousness (RC) in hospitals during emergencies, drawing on interviews with bereaved relatives and healthcare workers from isolated COVID-19 wards in Israel. It reveals that neither group framed visitation as a formal legal entitlement but rather as a privilege, gift, or luxury. While visitation is a routine and expected practice in ordinary times, the crisis exposed its fragility, transforming it into a discretionary allowance whose availability depended on institutional priorities and frontline discretion. Family responses ranged from compliance to selective resistance, with rights awareness often emerging retrospectively and collectively. The analysis advances few theoretical insights. First, it conceptualizes visitation as a “fragile right” robust in everyday practice yet weakly anchored in law and easily erased in crisis. Second, it shows how “de facto rights” can re-emerge from within institutions through professional ethics, norms, and informal organizational diffusion. Third, it demonstrates that RC is relational and spatial, suppressed inside hospitals by clinical hierarchies, yet reconstructed outside them through collective comparison and shared experience. These dynamics suggest that strengthening such fragile rights may depend not only on legal reform but on bottom-up participation of patient/family in hospital policymaking during crisis, which can cultivate rights awareness from within care itself.
items.title: Fragile rights: rights consciousness in hospitals in times of crisis

items.abstract: Alexander Lewis-Ranwell killed three people while suffering a psychotic episode. He brought a claim against several defendants who failed to detain him prior to this tragic incident. Following the UK Supreme Court’s recent decision in Lewis-Ranwell v G4S Health Services , 1 his claim in negligence was barred for illegality. The case is significant because it is the first time the UK Supreme Court has confronted the effect of an acquittal for insanity on a tort claim for damages arising out of the crime. 2 Its answer to the question posed in the title of this case note – even if crime does not pay, does tort law? – was thus ‘no’.
items.title:
Crime does not pay, but does tort?
                    Lewis-Ranwell v G4S Health Services (UK) Ltd
                    [2026] UKSC 2

items.abstract: Abstract This paper investigates the concept of the commons in the context of the emergence of convenience-based delivery drone networks around the world. It contends that the drone-facilitated commodification of our skies constitutes a modern form of enclosure, facilitated by a legal architecture that centres around questions of ownership. Additionally, and consistent with more traditional land-grabs, expropriation of the sky is supported by its characterisation as a vacant and unused resource. Drawing on historical, doctrinal, and socio-legal perspectives, this paper explores the powerful, countervailing implications of identifying this strategy, and reconceptualising the sky as a commons – for law, governance, and society.
items.title: Reclaiming the commons of the sky: drones and the limits of property law

items.abstract: Abstract Since the enactment of Criminal Justice Act 2003, Sched. 21, the average minimum term for murder in England and Wales has risen by more than 60 per cent. Very lengthy determinate terms are now the norm, subject only, in effect, to the Secretary of State’s discretion to release on compassionate grounds. This article asks whether there should be a mechanism for revisiting such terms, and, if so, on what principles. Although Hutchinson v United Kingdom holds lengthy minimum terms compatible with European Convention on Human Rights, art. 3, it is argued that the principles animating the court’s jurisprudence – shifting penological justifications, the centrality of rehabilitation across Europe and legal clarity – sit uneasily with domestic law. Taking Canada’s former “faint hope” clause as an institutional model, the article imagines a judicial mechanism for late tariff review, separate from parole and calibrated to the gravity of murder.
items.title: REVISITING MURDER TARIFFS: MINIMUM TERMS, REVIEWABILITY AND COMPARATIVE LAW

items.abstract: Abstract Discrimination law is notoriously difficult to categorise. Depending on the context, discrimination law can be classified as human rights law, constitutional law or labour law. Notably, though, the UK Supreme Court has drawn significantly on the language of torts in its discrimination decisions. One prominent example is its use of the “but-for” test to determine the causative element of direct discrimination. This article explores the implications of relying on these tortious principles in discrimination jurisprudence. We argue that while the court’s use of the “but-for” test has been useful to claimants by removing the need for malice or intention to prove discrimination, it conflates factual causation with legal causation and misunderstands the analysis required to determine causation in a direct discrimination claim. As a result, the “but-for” test weakens the coherency of discrimination law, ignores its unique conceptual challenges and muddies its factual and normative inquiries.
items.title: CAUSATION IN DISCRIMINATION LAW: THE TORTIOUS “BUT-FOR” TEST

items.abstract: Abstract This article examines how Uzbek migrants become incorporated into Russian society under conditions of legal precarity, discretionary enforcement and pervasive informality. Drawing on multisited ethnographic fieldwork conducted between 2014 and 2026 among Uzbek migrants in Russia and their families and communities in Uzbekistan, it develops the concept of shadow legal integration to explain how social and economic incorporation can deepen without a corresponding movement towards legal security. The article argues that repeated encounters with migration authorities, police, employers, intermediaries and migrant networks generate practical legal knowledge that migrants test, revise and circulate over time. This process of legal adaptation enables migrants to navigate the interaction between formal rules and informal practices while rem aining vulnerable to detention, deportation and administrative uncertainty. Ethnographic analysis of deportation, migration bureaucracy, legal brokerage, document economies and changing migration governance after 2022 further demonstrates that such competence is not a fixed repertoire but requires continual recalibration as legal and enforcement environments change. Shadow legal integration thus identifies how learning to navigate the intersection of formal and informal practices can itself become a mode of incorporation. The article contributes to migration and socio-legal scholarship by showing that migrant integration and legal security need not develop in parallel.
items.journal: International Journal of Law in Context
items.title: Shadow legal integration: migrant legal integration, Russian style
Algorithms instead of adjudication: why?
All that it takes to be reasonable
Spatial Injustice and Political Placemaking in Slavery’s Wake

items.abstract: Abstract This article argues that Nietzsche’s rejection of the doer/deed distinction in the famous lightning-flash passage in On the Genealogy of Morality 1:13 is more radical than Robert Pippin’s influential expressivist interpretation allows. Nietzsche’s target is not merely the causal conception of agency, but a metaphysical picture according to which a bearer of a capacity subsequently actualizes it in action, and thus ultimately the ontological distinction between potentiality and actuality itself. The conventional distinction between strength and expression presupposes a bearer of a capacity that can remain unactualized; Nietzsche’s criticism of precisely this distinction, together with his identification of force with activity and his rejection of the capacity-bearing ‘substratum’, is also directed against the metaphysical structure required by the potentiality/actuality distinction itself.
items.title: Against the expressivist interpretation of Nietzsche’s lightning-flash analogy
BernardKeenan, Interception: State Surveillance from Postal Systems to Global Networks, Cambridge, MA, MIT Press, 2025, 275pp, pb, US$45.00, C$65.00
LewisGraham, Judicial Individuality on the UK Supreme Court, Oxford: Hart Publishing, 2025, 304 pp, hb, £85.00.

items.abstract: ABSTRACT The project of Moral Bioenhancement (MBE)—biomedical interventions causing individuals to have better moral beliefs, motivations, or behaviours—is controversial, particularly as MBE relates to human freedom. Proponents argue that MBE is utility‐promoting and compatible with freedom. Conversely, critics charge that MBE—particularly when it bypasses or replaces rational moral deliberation, or when it is imposed compulsorily—threatens freedom of thought and action. I argue that much of the disagreement on this topic is due to conflation and obfuscation, resulting in conceptual confusion. Accordingly, I draw a distinction between two types of MBEs: those that incline individuals to moral action, and those that prohibit immoral action, by invoking the higher‐order desires of Harry Frankfurt's freedom of the will. Importantly, this distinction runs parallel to, rather than tracking, the familiar distinction between voluntary and compulsory MBE. Ultimately, I argue that inclining MBE interventions may not infringe, and may even enhance, freedom by allowing individuals to translate sincerely held moral beliefs into desired moral behaviours, enabling freedom as moral self‐mastery. Conversely, prohibitory MBEs necessarily restrict freedom, though this does not by itself entail that they are impermissible in all circumstances.
items.title: Clarifying the Distinction Between Inclining Moral Bioenhancement and Prohibitory Moral Bioenhancement, and Their Effects on Freedom

items.abstract: ABSTRACT In this paper, we argue for the adoption of algorithmic bioethics , which uses algorithms, in the form of decision trees, to articulate, understand, apply, and evaluate bioethical arguments. Algorithms bring many benefits to the study of bioethics: they clearly, precisely, and transparently articulate the decision procedure and facts relevant to an ethical decision; furthermore, they can be used to systematically discover, map out, and compare different ethical decision procedures concerning a practical issue. We then also outline and tackle potential limitations of algorithmic bioethics, and explore future directions for using decision trees in bioethics. Throughout, we illustrate our points using a case study of ethical decision trees, created with the help of large language models, about conscientious objection in medicine.
items.title: Algorithmic Bioethics: A Defense and Demonstration

items.abstract: ABSTRACT In the mid‐20th century, there was a debate about whether the quantifiers in first‐order logic should be understood objectually or substitutionally. This debate typically focused on ontology and assumed that we could use only one of these two types of quantification. After Kripke and others influentially argued that the two kinds of quantification were logically equivalent, defenses of substitutional quantification were rare. Following Gottlieb and Field, I argue that Kripke was wrong and that substitutional consequence is language‐bound and non‐compact. While of no help with ontology, I also argue that so‐understood, substitutional quantification can be applied to help explain our grasp of a determinate notion of arithmetical truth.
