To argue for this, I give an account of the metasemantics of the substitutional quantifiers and prove that adding a single, very natural, mixed axiom to weak theories of arithmetic results in a categorical theory. This approach promises to explain arithmetical truth on a less controversial basis than appeals to either second‐order logic or the omega rule, thus making progress on the project of explaining our grasp of arithmetic in a naturalistically acceptable fashion.
items.title: Substitutional Quantification and Arithmetical Truth

items.abstract: ABSTRACT A popular indifference principle for self‐locating probability faces skeptical challenges, most notably a skeptical challenge concerning Boltzmann Brains. We examine the prospects for various views that prescribe some degree of bias in place of indifference. Although a bias view has attractive anti‐skeptical features, it turns out that bias leads to puzzles about deference to chance, reflection, and other related principles.
items.title: Bias Against Boltzmann Brains?

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Frankfurt's idea that bullshit is “fake,” “counterfeit,” and “phony” has been overshadowed in the later debate by his claim that the bullshitter is indifferent to truth. The former insight deserves to be taken more seriously. I begin by asking whether bullshit is a fake assertion and argue that it isn't. What makes it bullshit, rather, is that the speaker's performance is meant to raise the audience's credence in some proposition h by resembling genuine evidence for h , while simultaneously concealing that it lacks the features of genuine evidence. Bullshit, on this analysis, is best understood as a communicative act that the speaker intends to serve as “counterfeit evidence.” I then use the ideas of relevance theory to distinguish bullshit from plain lying. Since deception is a corollary of counterfeiture, it is also an intrinsic element of bullshit. This helps to contrast the present view with other accounts in the literature.
items.title: Bullshit as Counterfeit Evidence
Issue Information

items.abstract: Abstract Recent years have seen a decisive turn in neuroscience toward embodiment, shifting focus from a brain-bound view of the mind to a more holistic one where the body is treated as constitutive of self and consciousness. While this turn has yielded valuable insights through studies on interoception, multisensory integration and bodily ownership, it also carries significant theoretical and ethical risks. This essay identifies the body problem: the risk of collapsing selfhood into bodyhood, with troubling consequences when applied to bodies that are marginalized or that otherwise do not meet the status quo. Tracing historical debates on mind–body relations, clarifying contemporary notions of the self and examining empirical findings on embodiment, it is argued that strong formulations of the embodied self risk reviving old reductions whereby “less body” implies “less self,” not because such formulations explicitly assert the inference, but because they leave it available for others to make. Such reductions threaten to undermine the value of persons whose bodies diverge from normative assumptions. Rather than rejecting embodiment research, this essay calls for caution against its uncritical extension, underscoring the need to guard against theoretical slippage that may entail harmful social consequences.
items.title: The Body Problem: Cautionary Notes on the Embodied Self

items.abstract: Abstract Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can expose interpretable features in language-model activations, but public SAE resources such as GemmaScope and Llama Scope are trained on generic web text rather than cybersecurity evidence. CyberLens is a purpose-trained SAE and heuristic taxonomy-mapping pipeline for cybersecurity interpretability of an open-weight language model. Because cyber uplift is a foreseeable deployment risk, reasonable care requires developers of general-purpose language models to provide proportionate internal observability of cyber-relevant behaviour. We train a width-4096 JumpReLU SAE on layer 8 of EleutherAI/pythia-160 m, a 12-layer, 162-million-parameter model with a 768-dimensional residual stream, using 14,925 documents (approximately 1.85 million tokens) of MITRE ATT&CK descriptions and procedure examples, NVD vulnerability reports, CISA KEV records, CAPEC, malware reports, phishing emails, and Dolly-15k benign contrasts, with grouped splitting to prevent source-document leakage. The cybersecurity SAE achieves FVU 0.0435 (95.7% explained variance) versus 0.186 for a matched generic-text SAE—an absolute explained- variance gain of 14.2 percentage points on the reported activation sample. Its 4,096 feature rows are mapped heuristically to ATT&CK techniques and CISSP domains using local all-MiniLM-L6-v2 similarity, with confidence scores from 0.313 to 0.928; the top 50 remain pending hand-verification after a labelling pilot failed. Refusal is 0.000 in both arms (a Pythia-160 M base model without instruction tuning or RLHF). Suppressing 20 selected features increases keyword-flagged cyber content from 0.067 to 0.317 overall and from 0.050 to 0.800 for exploit items; phishing and malware are null, and 15 of 20 exploit placeholders contain “Exploit,” inflating this lexical metric. English-only, phishing-heavy corpus; one completed layer-8 width-4,096 SAE whose observed $$L_0=286$$ greatly exceeds the target 20; heuristic, unverified labels; keyword-based outcomes; a placeholder-heavy 60-prompt intervention set; no evidence about frontier models or effective cyber-content suppression. SAE weights, feature dictionary, loader, and an interactive demonstration are released for reproducible small-model research; scaling to larger models remains future work.
items.title: Cyberlens: taxonomy-mapped sparse autoencoders for cybersecurity interpretability of open-weight language models
The intelligent successor paradox: human knowledge, displacement narratives, and the ethics of knowledge production

items.abstract: Abstract The Gettier problem suggests that the core challenge for theories of knowledge lies in eliminating knowledge-undermining epistemic luck. In response, two major approaches have emerged in contemporary epistemology: modalism and explanationism. However, both approaches have limitations and exhibit an interesting theoretical symmetry: while modalism effectively handles environmental luck, it struggles with certain cases of intervening luck; explanationism faces the reverse difficulty. This symmetrical limitation suggests that any theory of knowledge relying on a single dimension is likely to be inadequate. To address this, this paper presents a new, integrated approach – Modal Explanationism (ME). ME requires that a belief counts as knowledge just in case it is explained by the truth of the believed proposition in the actual world, and that this explanatory connection is preserved across a range of nearby possible worlds. It is argued that ME offers a more successful solution to the Gettier problem than either modalism or explanationism alone.
items.title: A Modal Explanationist Solution to the Gettier Problem

items.abstract: Abstract The Article analyzes how gender markers on passports are used to bolster the digital racial borders of the European Union (EU). It traces the history of gender markers on passports, showing that they increasingly emerged in the EU and elsewhere as part of border digitalization processes from the 1980s onward. It further investigates how gender markers on passports increasingly serve border-related risk assessments by examining the ongoing expansion of Advanced Passenger Information, Passenger Name Records, and the Visa Information System in the EU. While this analysis shows that gender markers help to identify the “unwanted” migrant—a deeply racialized concept—the Article also interrogates whether abolishing gender markers would necessarily render borders gender- or race-neutral. It therefore explores how border governance that relies on big data and biometric tools, rather than gender markers, may equally reinforce cisnormative and racialized borders.
items.title: Gender Markers in Passports and the Digital Racial Borders of the European Union

items.abstract: Abstract This paper aims to advance current debates on gendered language reform by making explicit the assumptions in much of the philosophical literature, and by proposing a reorientation of how we theorize about pronoun reform and linguistic amelioration. While sympathetic to the normative aims of prominent proposals, I caution that prescriptions grounded in any single language risk overstating language-specific features and blurring the sources and dynamics of gender essentialism. Drawing on the case of Mandarin Chinese, where gendered pronouns were a modern invention, I clarify the limits of language-specific diagnoses and show how reform is mediated by social conditions of uptake. More broadly, I advocate a shift from language-specific proposals to a cross- and trans-linguistic perspective: cross-linguistic comparison identifies which claims generalize across languages, and a trans-linguistic lens highlights how reform ideas and practices travel across contexts and are reshaped through uptake and negotiation. This approach offers a more philosophically robust account of the prospects and limits of linguistic amelioration, and of language’s role in social change.
items.title: Pronouns and Linguistic Amelioration
Shmuel Nili, Beyond the Law’s Reach? Powerful Criminals, Foreign Entanglement, and Justice in the Shadow of Violence. (New York: Oxford University Press, 2024.)
Una reflexión a doce años de “Comparative Matters”, de Ran Hirschl

items.abstract: ABSTRACT This article develops a critical account of human rights through an encounter between Jacques Derrida and Jacques Rancière. Rather than treating their approaches as complementary components of a single theory, I argue that their disagreement reveals two irreducible dimensions of the politics of rights: the situated enactment of equality and the temporal non‐closure of every such enactment. Rancière shows how rights become political when those excluded from an existing distribution invoke their egalitarian inscriptions to stage a dissensus and enact themselves as political subjects. Derrida, through the distinction between law and justice and the temporality of the à venir, shows why no institutional or political articulation of equality can determine in advance the subjects and forms through which future claims may emerge. This reading rejects both the interpretation of deconstruction as an indefinite deferral of political action and the claim that Rancière fails to recognize the recurrence of exclusion through the politics/police distinction and le tort. Bringing these positions into tension, I argue that human rights require determinate legal and political forms while remaining contestable by claims those forms cannot anticipate. A deconstructive politics of human rights thus emerges in the interval between enactment and non‐closure: Equality must take political form without any particular form becoming its final horizon.
items.title: A Scene of Contention at the Limits of Sovereignty: Derrida, Rancière, and the Deconstructive Politics of Human Rights

items.abstract: ABSTRACT This article revisits Agamben's state of exception. Homo Sacer and State of Exception frame camps as spaces where law is suspended and life reduced to “bare life.” This decisionist paradigm underestimates the institutional and economic complexity of refugee management. This article proposes the concept of sovereignty by omission: Exclusion produced not by a decisive suspension of law but by legal ambiguity, bureaucratic deferral, and systemic inaction. Engaging Schmitt, Benjamin, Foucault, and Butler, the article situates omission within debates on sovereignty and rights and develops the argument through the case of Gaza. The argument rests on systematic analysis of legal, monitoring, and advocacy documents published between October 2023 and August 2025, each coded for acknowledgement, assignment, and execution. Gaza's blockade, siege, and overlapping legal regimes, invoked yet unenforced, exemplify omission, even as cultural and political life persists. Camps and enclaves are thus fractured fields of governance where abandonment and resilience coexist; sovereignty today manifests less in decision than in omission.
items.title: Sovereignty by Omission: Rethinking Agamben's State of Exception

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Daryush Shayegan (1935–2018), a major yet underrecognized Iranian philosopher, offers a compelling framework for rethinking the Islamic revolution and broader religious‐political dynamics. This article introduces his thought to Anglophone audiences, challenging traditional interpretations of the 1979 revolution. Rather than a return to tradition, Shayegan views it as a modern event, in which religious symbols act as unconscious psychological defenses against change. Through a process he terms “ontological shift,” political and religious realms become intertwined, each repressing the other. These hybrid religious‐political symbols, detached from their original contexts, gain power through misrecognition. The study also extends Shayegan's insights beyond Iran, arguing that various fundamentalisms and populisms reflect similar reactions to existential disruption. It concludes by examining the notable academic oversight of his incisive analyses, highlighting the research trajectories that his rediscovery might generate.
items.title: Reconceptualizing “Religious Revolutions”: An Introduction to Daryush Shayegan

items.abstract: Having a child by in vitro fertilisation (IVF) entails the creation of in vitro embryos, their transfer to a woman's uterus, a successful pregnancy, and live birth. Under the European Convention on Human Rights, using IVF principally engages the right to respect for private and family life under Article 8(1). The approach of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) to the embryo is part of its jurisprudence regarding prenatal life, which it has considered under Article 8(2), including regarding the right to life under Article 2. Since an embryo currently needs a woman's uterus to have any chance of born life, questions about what legal status and claims to life it may have, if any, involve consideration of a woman's autonomy and bodily integrity interests under Article 8(1), and thus the legal relationship between the embryo and the woman – the central focus here. This paper principally identifies and analyses several problematic features of the ECtHR's jurisprudence regarding prenatal life as this relates to a woman, with particular reference to the embryo. It also considers the implications of a heightened concern for the embryo in a minority of States’ IVF laws, and in debates about heritable human genome editing.
items.title: The Embryo at the European Court of Human Rights

items.abstract: ABSTRACT This article focuses on the question of how to understand the role and use of ethical theories in bioethics. Work in bioethics often involves uses of ethical theory, but methodological developments such as the empirical turn and the growing insights into the plurality and contextuality of moral considerations challenge a traditional view of ethical theories as providing moral input into the value‐neutral descriptions offered by empirical studies. Nevertheless, bioethics is characterised by a relative neglect of questions related to the use of ethical theories. The article develops a number of desiderata that any understanding of the role of ethical theories should be able to address; to accommodate moral plurality and contextuality, to motivate choices and uses of specific theories, to minimise risks of theory‐driven attention and blindness, to allow for theoretical plurality, to address relations between theories and theoretical integrity. It then presents some challenges for existing accounts of theory‐use in bioethics, thus paving the way for an alternative understanding of the role of ethical theories in bioethics. The suggestion presented here is that ethical theories should be understood as descriptions or representations of moral grammars , implicit normative structures of thinking and action that constitute moral considerations. Furthermore, in relation to problems in bioethics, it is suggested that ethical theories are used as heuristic tools to illuminate and clarify moral grammars as they appear in specific bioethical poblems or studies.
items.title: Reconsidering the Role of Ethical Theories in Bioethics: Ethical Theories as Heuristic Descriptions of Moral Grammars

items.abstract: Abstract One of today’s foremost counterfactual analyses draws many causal links where it shouldn’t—not only towards the future, but also towards the past. The root of these problems is that unlikely events are too modally fragile to ground reasonable causal claims. However, I will argue that these issues arise just as readily for likely events, spelling double trouble for this analysis. By recentring this approach around probabilities instead, causation tracks structure whose modal robustness justifies its name, sidestepping the old problems and the new.
items.title: Modal Fragility and Counterfactual Causation
Engineered hesitation: the ethics of unresolvable uncertainty in algorithmic systems
Who does the relational work? response-saturation and a Confucian role-ethical account of AI companionship
Who holds the judgment? Agentic AI, vendor custody, and the accountability gap
Beyond human oversight why AI ethics needs phronesis
Acting without asking: agentic AI, informed consent, and the erosion of patient agency in healthcare

items.abstract: Given the rapid rise of AI and its capacity to help firms customize consumer prices, price personalization has become a hot topic at the intersection of business ethics and technology studies. This article challenges the argument that price personalization would increase social welfare, addressing the claim that firms should charge more to people with greater willingness-to-pay (WTP), and less to people with lower WTP, because this will boost social welfare. I develop two reasons for doubt. First, preferences that influence WTP often do not conduce to consumers’ well-being. So, adjusting prices to preference-based WTP will not necessarily enhance social welfare. Second, firms’ long-term strategic agendas will often disfavor increased price personalization. If “ought implies can,” firms can morally be expected to do only what they reasonably can in competitive conditions.
items.title: Price Personalization in the Age of AI: Complicating the Defense

items.journal: Cambridge Yearbook of European Legal Studies
items.title: Preface

items.abstract: Abstract The debate between permissivists and impermissivists – which concerns the question of whether there is at most one epistemically rational doxastic attitude to adopt toward a proposition given a body of evidence – has been a focus of discussion in the literature. However, this debate has occurred almost exclusively within an internalist context. I aim to change that by introducing an externalist perspective into the debate. In particular, I will consider what a process reliabilist should think about the debate. Since process reliabilists do not typically talk about evidence, I will show how the debate can be translated into process reliabilist terms. In light of this translation, I will argue that process reliabilists should be permissivists. I will also argue that process reliabilism is a plausible version of permissivism because it can successfully respond to common objections to permissive views.
items.title: Process Reliabilism is Permissive (and Plausible)

items.abstract: Abstract The possibility of distinguishing good from bad reasoning – the precondition of any normative role for logic – has been challenged by a cluster of skeptical arguments in recent philosophy of logic. While much attention has focused on the gap between logical knowledge and ordinary reasoning highlighted by Harman and Russell, this paper identifies three additional arguments against logical normativity that have received insufficient scrutiny: one concerning the inherent limitations of formal evaluation methods, one concerning the pragmatic indeterminacy of illogical behavior in natural language communication, and one rooted in the early-twentieth-century doctrine of the ‘feeling of logicality’ directly opposed by Charles S. Peirce. The paper pursues two sequential aims: first, to show that skepticism about the logical normativity of reasoning is deeper and more historically entrenched than contemporary discussions suggest; second, to reconstruct Peirce’s theoretical framework – centered on the distinction between logica utens and logica docens , the tripartite account of good reasoning, and the method-based criterion of validity – and to demonstrate that it provides a unified response to all four skeptical challenges.
items.title: Can We Logically Tell Good from Bad Reasoning?
Research ethics in and out of crises: cluster randomized trials without consent
MAGA Constitutionalism: Originalist Intuitions and the Invention of Legal Doctrine

items.abstract: Abstract It is now widely understood that constitutions are interpreted and enforced by a broad range of actors—not simply courts. Much of constitutional theory has come to embrace this form of (what I call) “constitutional polyvocality,” or the idea of “polyvocal constitutionalism.” At the same time, there are several different versions of polyvocal constitutionalism. For instance, one set of polyvocal theories argues for collaboration among different constitutional actors and the importance of norms of comity, respect, and restraint in mediating any conflicts that arise in a process of polyvocal constitutional construction. Another set of ideas focuses on notions of accountability and the importance of judicial and fourth-branch impartiality, independence, and authority in the resolution of certain constitutional disputes, even in a polyvocal world. A final set of ideas focuses on the idea of contestation and disagreement among constitutional actors as potentially generative forces in a democratic constitutional system and as helping underpin the legitimacy of its outputs. Some theories also seek to balance these competing ideas in an open-ended way, whereas others seek to provide a more structured or “tiered” approach to balancing competing polyvocal constitutional ideas or values. This article explores these different understandings of the idea of polyvocal constitutionalism and how it helps us understand and situate a range of recent works in comparative constitutional theory. It further highlights the strengths and weaknesses of these different theories, especially their capacity to respond to the current political moment—in which many previously stable democracies are experiencing “abusive” constitutional change.
items.title: Polyvocal constitutionalism

items.abstract: ABSTRACT In this article I ask whether the main traditions of Western political thought, republicanism, conservatism, liberalism, and socialism, can supply an account of human flourishing capable of sustaining a broad antifascist movement. Each tradition defines full humanity as an achievement reserved for the mature adult and treats the child as a being in preparation, excluded from the sites of genuine political agency and human actualization. I refer to this shared framework as the metaphysics of maturity. The argument links the emergence of this metaphysics to a political economy in which the coerced labor of children generated the first surpluses, financed the enslavement of outsiders, justified the subjection of women, and furnished the material foundation for the philosophical ideals of virtue, piety, reason, and recognition. Each tradition thereby carries forward a structure of subordination that fascism shares and extends to whole populations, declaring races, classes, and nations permanently immature and therefore naturally governed and disciplined. Existing scholarship on fascism has identified its patriarchal core yet rarely goes deeper that then racialized and gendered forms of patriarchal rule. I conclude by pointing toward anarchist traditions that come closest to refusing the metaphysics of maturity, often by invoking Indigenous and other non western forms of political thought.
items.title: Antifa Theory: Beyond the Western Metaphysics of Maturity

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Discourse ethics rests on the assumption that validity claims fall into a closed triad: facts about the objective world, norms about the intersubjective world, and self‐expressions disclosing the subjective world. This paper challenges that assumption. I argue that the tripartite framework is not exhaustive, and that treating it as such generates a previously unrecognized form of exclusion: not at the level of access, power, or expression, but at the level of intelligibility itself. To make this case, I introduce “ecological truth” as a candidate for a distinct kind of validity claim. Drawing on examples from place‐based discursive practices, I suggest that such claims are plausibly neither factual, normative, nor self‐expressive, but exhibit a different structure of validity grounded in long‐term ecological relationships and practices of attunement. I then propose criteria for recognizing new kinds of validity claims and show that ecological truth plausibly satisfies them. The plausibility of ecological truth as a distinct validity claim gives us reason to think that the tripartite model should not be treated as closed. Instead, validity claims are better understood as forming a more complex conceptual space, within which additional forms of reason‐giving may exist. If so, discourse ethics must revise its foundational categories if it is to adequately account for the full range of meaningful contributions to deliberation.
items.title: The Closure Problem in Discourse Ethics: Ecological Truth and the Limits of the Tripartite Model

items.abstract: ABSTRACT There is an enormous theoretical literature on representation through parliamentary means, and a growing literature representation through extra‐parliamentary pathways. However, there is little philosophical literature on representation through the executive. This paper introduces two forms of executive representation—executive leadership and process executive—arguing that these form two different aspects of executive representation. Current theoretical literature discusses leadership executive in terms of symbolic representation but outside of public administration philosophers have ignored process representation. This is a major lacunae since the bulk of citizen interaction with the state are through the courts, police, welfare officers, tax officers, planning departments, teachers, and so on. Briefly reviewing the empirical literature, we argue that process executive representation requires a culture of empathetic leadership and deliberation, alongside descriptive representation. These ideas fit well with political theorists discussion of assembly representation arguing that these ideas need application to the executive as well as the legislature. We also briefly examine how new public management, digitalization, and AI threaten process executive representation. Our paper brings ideas and evidence to the attention of political theorists to inspire further work on executive representation.
items.title: Executive Representation

items.abstract: Abstract This paper pursues two aims. First, it develops a novel objection to metanormative constructivism, which I term the Duality Objection . Second, it proposes a dual‐role account of practical reason and argues that it can meet this objection. Constructivists like Korsgaard and Street maintain that normativity is constructed within agents' first‐personal practical standpoints, shaped by their evaluative input. Valuing is prior to, and metaphysically grounds, value. However, a basic feature of our normative experience is that our evaluative judgements also respond to and track pre‐existing normative facts. Thus, evaluative commitments appear to play two seemingly contradictory roles – creating and responding to normative reality. This tension forms the basis of the Duality Objection. I respond in two steps. First, I show how constructivists can reconcile their metaphysical commitments with agents' normative experiences by distinguishing between first‐ and third‐personal levels of explanation. Second, I develop a Korsgaardian dual‐role account of practical reason , which elucidates the passive‐responsive and active‐creative roles that practical reason plays within our first‐personal agential standpoint. Making sense of “responsive” normative experience within a constructivist framework has a further upshot. It allows us to reject recent “arguments from first‐personal deliberation and experience” by metanormative realists (cf. Enoch 2007, 2011; Kirwin 2024).
items.title: Creating Normativity and Responding to It: How Metaethical Constructivists Must and Can Have It Both Ways

items.abstract: Abstract Today, research on consciousness spans various fields, including neuroscience, philosophy, psychology, physics, and computer science. These studies focus on demonstrating the effects of consciousness rather than defining its essence. While consciousness is often used as an overarching concept in thought processes, its nature remains unclear and is expected to be more precisely defined in the future. Some theorists propose that consciousness resides within neurons or the cytoskeleton. Examining the history of science reveals similar concepts that were once widely accepted but later proven nonexistent. This paper argues that consciousness is akin to aether and phlogiston—once considered scientific truths but ultimately discarded. While debates persist on whether consciousness is a fundamental reality or an illusion, the paper asserts that consciousness is merely a term, neither real nor illusory. As our molecular understanding of brain function deepens, the concept of consciousness, like aether and phlogiston, will eventually fade from scientific discourse.
items.title: Rethinking the Concept of Consciousness
A Minimally Good Life: What We Owe to Others and What We Can Justifiably Demand, written by N. Hassoun
Why It’s OK to Be a Moderate, written by Marcus Arvan

items.abstract: This response to Michell’s article raises three main concerns. First, there is an important yet unexamined relationship between psychology’s reliance on inferential statistics (NHST) and the “missing corpus” of critiques of psychometricians’ a priori assumption that psychological attributes sustain quantitative structure. Second, framing the problem as one of “visible” (NHST) versus “invisible” (measurement) critiques may mask how commitment to NHST drove psychologists to assume measurement is taking place. Finally, Michell fails to account for the role political theory played in explaining the widespread adoption of psychometric methods, sans scientific evidence.
items.title:
The Analytic Cart Before the Ontological Horse: A Response to Michell’s “The Mystery of Missing Psychometric
                    Corpus
                    ”

items.abstract: Ulrike Kern (2016) unpacks the history of a concept, broken colors. Though it’s been in use since the early seventeenth century, and is even used today by painters, critics, and art theorists when discussing color, it hasn’t much influenced philosophy. Instead, it evolved independently, alongside the early modern philosophical discussions of color. This paper has two goals. First, work out a philosophical reconstruction of the concept whose early history Kern so ably traces. So, this paper is a philosophical contribution to the history of ideas. The paper’s second goal is to show how broken colors contribute to two contemporary issues. First, they help us understand the depiction of things as colored, and second, they can deepen our understanding of the nature of chromatic experience. Broken colors are thus relevant to contemporary philosophy of art and perception. Though there are historically informed contemporary accounts of color on the market—Adams (2016) stands out—they typically address the history of philosophical discussions of color. And there is comparatively little work in the philosophy of art about the depiction of things as colored.
items.title: Understanding Broken Colors

items.abstract: Can we offer a constitutive account of fittingness? Offering such an account has proven difficult because of the great diversity of fit-assessable responses—e.g., believing, desiring, fearing, blaming, apologizing, thanking, and laughing. Yet, when surveying such examples of fit-apt  responses, what's striking is that invariably each response-type has a job, a goal, an end, a telos. Believing, desiring, fearing, blaming, apologizing, thanking, and laughing are all plausible candidates for having proper functions. The account I aim to defend runs with this idea. Put roughly, fittingness is the relation that holds between a response and its object just when and because the object has the properties that an object of that response needs to possess for the response to non-deviantly fulfill its function.
items.title: A Function-Based Account of Fittingness

items.abstract: The concept of essence is a paradigm case of a putatively hyperintensional concept in metaphysics, a concept that can draw distinctions between necessarily equivalent propositions. Yet as several authors have recently emphasized, fine-grained distinctions in metaphysics come with a substantial risk of inconsistency, due to the Russell-Myhill paradox and its variants. This concern is especially pressing for hyperintensionalists about essence because the hyperintensionality of essence has been motivated primarily by examples. This paper presents a novel, more systematic case for the hyperintensionality of essence that shows that the relevant distinctions can be systematically modeled in a natural theoretical framework. I start by offering a general heuristic to motivate a range of examples of fine-grained essentialist distinctions. I then present a higher-order logical framework for regimenting essentialist statements and provide a general argument for hyperintensionality on the basis of minimal assumptions about the logic of essence. Finally, I address the question of consistency by developing a semantic framework that demonstrates that the relevant fine-grained distinctions can indeed be consistently drawn.
items.title: Essence and Grain

items.abstract: I propose a novel A-theory that attractively articulates our common-sense, pre-relativistic conception of time. This A-theory posits fundamental facts about how things were at a specific past times. It treats time’s passing by positing fundamental facts like: four hours passed from 8am today until noon. It allows fundamental cross-temporal relationships. I show that the presentism–eternalism dilemma does not embarrass the proposed A-theory. There are two notions of existence in play: existence at a time and ‘∃-existence’. Neither features in the fundamental facts. I define them up in a way that vindicates the claims of common sense. Past objects count as metaphysically ‘gone’, but there are fundamental facts about how they were. My account rejects presentism and eternalism (properly defined). I defend other aspects of the proposal elsewhere.
items.title: Escape the Presentism–Eternalism Dilemma: Towards A Common-Sense A-Theory

items.abstract: Human cognition and behavior are guided by a myriad of norms which enable us to successfully navigate our social environment and our interactions with others. Many of these norms might be hard for us to articulate (e.g. how far to sit or stand from a stranger on the bus), and some of them differentiate between different hierarchies and roles, reflecting patterns of injustice. This paper addresses the fact that social norms, including gendered, ableist, adultist, and racist norms, influence our perception of action possibilities, or affordances, making some actions possible for some agents and not for others. In particular, we propose an account of these interactions in terms of scripts, that is, expected sequences of actions that shape the landscape of the possible ways to interact with one another. Scripts can be learned implicitly, they are dynamic and flexible, and can regulate complex interactions by prescribing permissible actions and responses in specific situations. A script-based account can explain the way norms regulate which actions we perceive as possible in a representationalist way, and can help us explain how norm change occurs.
items.title: Seeing what to do: norms, scripts, and social affordances
The Penalty of Anticipated Motherhood in the Boardroom: Fertility Policy and Corporate Risk-Taking

items.abstract: Abstract Although a given mathematical theorem can typically be proved in many ways, only some of those proofs are regarded by mathematicians as explaining why that theorem holds. Furthermore, mathematicians routinely use non-deductive arguments to confirm conjectures before they have found proofs (or disproofs) of them. These two features of mathematical practice suggest that some confirmation in mathematics proceeds by “inference to the best explanation” (IBE). Furthermore, a mathematical theorem may exhibit a striking symmetry, and a proof of such a theorem would have to exploit a similar symmetry in order to explain why that theorem holds. This aspect of mathematical explanation reveals an important, heretofore unrecognized form of IBE in mathematics. In such a case, a conjecture is confirmed by some mathematical discovery partly because the conjecture “perfects the symmetry” in that discovery. This paper examines one historical example of such an IBE: Brahmagupta and Snell (independently) regarded Heron’s formula for the area of triangles as confirming a conjecture not merely because that conjecture generalizes Heron’s formula, but also because that conjecture perfects the formula’s symmetry.
items.title: Perfecting the symmetry: a variety of inference to the best explanation in mathematics

items.abstract: Abstract The concept of the self is the concept of what makes a person the person that they are. But how can a general, theoretical account be given of something that is, by definition, specific to each individual? Discussions of selfhood in the analytic tradition have focused on three different issues: (1) self-reference in language and thought, (2) the epistemology of self-knowledge, (3) the metaphysics/ontology of selves. These are all connected to each other and all important. But even if we had satisfactory answers to all of them, we would have at best an account of the formal conditions of selfhood, rather than of selfhood itself. Focusing primarily on ancient Greece, this paper explores an alternative approach to thinking about selfhood. Individuality, selfhood, can only be expressed within certain limits and certain structures. When we look at historical texts, if we seek to find an author’s conception of the self, we need to tease out how they frame those factors that constrain and channel the development, articulation, and expression of selfhood - as opposed, for example, to looking at whatever metaphysical account they might give of the mind or of personhood (or of the uniquely Greek concept of the psuchē ).
items.title: What would count as a theory of the self?

items.abstract: Abstract Deontological arguments, in the broad sense, are those that refer to properties of choice options other than their consequences, such as whether the option is an act or omission. These arguments are often used to justify public policies, such as those concerning vaccination. In principle, some of these arguments could lead to outcomes worse than those of utilitarian choices, i.e., choices designed to yield the best expected consequences. Arguments for deontological choices ought to explain why it is better to make outcomes worse. We suggest that political arguments attempting to do this are usually fallacious. We list several categories of such informal fallacies, and we report two demonstrations in which we ask whether people without special training can distinguish types of such reasoning. People seem generally weak at this task, although those who are more inclined to accept the standards of actively open-minded thinking (AOT) do better, possibly because both AOT and fallacy classification require meta-cognitive competence. Performance may also be improved by more thorough instructions about the task. The idea of requesting justification for making things worse is a new method for empirical research on moral judgment and for instruction in argumentation. It is also a new kind of thought experiment for philosophical argument.
items.title: Recognizing fallacious reasoning in deontological arguments
Joint aesthetic attention

items.abstract: Abstract This paper addresses a central phenomenological puzzle: how to reconcile the traditional view of compassion as an instance of suffering with contemporary neuroscientific findings characterizing it as being hedonically positive. Building on the attitudinalist framework, I argue that this conflict arises from a failure to see emotions as unfolding episodes. By thinking of emotions as felt readinesses to act, we can understand compassion’s valence not as a fixed hedonic tone, but as a dynamic trajectory within a structured affective space. The argument proceeds in three stages. First, I establish that positive and negative emotions are defined by their structural orientation, welcoming or rejecting value. Second, I apply this to compassion, arguing it is fundamentally a mode of taking displeasure in another’s suffering. Finally, I show that the “positivity” noted by scientists is the result of the benevolent action tendency being allowed to run its course, transforming initial distress into the expansive experience of relief and connection.
items.title: The Valence of Compassion
Criteria for the Evaluation of Analogies in Scientific Discovery
Can people challenge an AI decision? Measuring the contestability chain in law and corporate disclosure
The detection vacuum beneath the accountability vacuum: stigmergic convergence and spiral detection failure
Building AI-ethical competencies: an integrated framework for AI governance, organizational learning, and leadership education

items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the proliferation of conversational agents have brought transformative changes in education but pose challenges in ensuring the academic integrity of assessments. This article proposes ‘affirmation vivas’ as a potent response to reasonable doubts about the authorship of assessed student work. It draws on a case-study of the first affirmation viva conducted at the University of Glasgow, conducted after ChatGPT “confessed” to generating part of a student dissertation. During the viva, while acknowledging experimenting with AI chatbots, the student successfully demonstrated understanding and ownership of their work. The article reviews practical and ethical issues involved in responding to suspected AI misuse and develops a principled framework for affirmation vivas. We conceptualise these vivas as a means of affirming student understanding rather than detecting AI misuse or presuming misconduct. We derive five principles for their fair and proportionate implementation, including a high threshold for convening them, a presumption of innocence throughout the process and for marking to take place only after the viva, avoiding biases that derive from assuming a student’s guilt.
items.title: Presumption of guilt? AI chatbots and the role of affirmation vivas in assessing academic integrity

items.abstract: Abstract The rise of agentic AI and so-called AI companions introduces a shift in the modes of interactions between humans and machines. The exact contours of this shift remain unclear, but early signs of social, affective, and even romantic engagements demonstrate areas of potential benefit and potent harms to individuals and to the broader social fabric. A full appreciation of these benefits and harms demands a multi-perspectival account not only of technological innovation and emerging modalities of human-machine interaction, but also of the historical, socio-cultural, psychological, and ethical aspects of companionship. This essay provides such as account through a pragmatist perspective that considers the material, institutional, and psycho-social conditions behind the rise of AI. From this perspective, the essay broadens the notion of “alignment” as one between means and ends rather than the commonly accepted formulation between design goals and outputs. We argue that AI companionship blurs the boundaries between tools and social actors—a dynamic that emerges from the interplay of technical architectures, intentional design practices, user psychology, and political-economic forces. Given that interplay, a set of interrelated questions arise, which we address in three clusters (supply, demand, mediation), highlighting the emerging social and ethical dilemmas, and suggesting pragmatic interventions to inform public discourse and policymaking. In so doing, we hope to curtail the tremendous fallouts that have become evident in other domains such as social media only in retrospect, and ​to contribute to the creation of an environment conducive to social cohesion and individual wellbeing.
items.title: AI companions, human concerns: a pragmatic perspective

items.abstract: Abstract The choice of legal basis of EU legal acts is a constitutional question in EU law, determining the relevant competence, institutional role, voting rule, related procedures, and issues of judicial review. This article advances a legal basis critique of a corpus of EU legal acts adopted in the past decade. As it demonstrates, the legal basis case-law set out by the Court of Justice of the European Union, and the limits of what particular legal bases permit, remain formally undisturbed. The practice of EU law, however, has demonstrably shifted, requiring sustained constitutional attention.
items.journal: Cambridge Yearbook of European Legal Studies
items.title: Legal Basis of EU Legal Acts: Choice, Doctrine, and Practice

items.abstract: Abstract The lack of affordable prescription medicines is a global problem. But even as various governments, nonprofit organizations and pharmaceutical companies attempt to address the issue, agreements lack transparency. The absence of key details — notably, pricing, in some instances — makes it difficult to determine whether the deals will sufficiently succeed in providing needed medicines.
items.title: What Details? A Lack of Transparency Impedes Access to Medicines

items.abstract: Abstract This paper offers the largest empirical study to date of the rights of persons with disabilities in the Commonwealth Caribbean. Drawing on interviews, surveys, focus groups and consultations conducted across twelve jurisdictions between 2017 and 2022, it examines the persistent gap between the region’s formal commitments under the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and the lived realities of persons with disabilities. Deploying Martha Nussbaum’s capability approach, alongside intersectional theory, the paper argues that pervasive failures across education, health care, employment, social protection, accessibility and civic participation deprive persons with disabilities of the substantive freedoms necessary for human flourishing, with compounded effects for those experiencing multiple forms of marginalisation. Situating these findings within the region’s heterogeneous legislative landscape, and assessing Barbados’s Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2025 as the region’s most far-reaching statutory response, the paper contends that transforming disability rights from aspiration into substantive capability requires structural change that addresses the intersection of ableism with racism, sexism, classism and geography.
items.journal: International Journal of Law in Context
items.title: Disability rights in the Commonwealth Caribbean: a capability and intersectional critique

items.abstract: Abstract This article offers a comprehensive legal, linguistic, sociodemographic and psychological analysis of the phenomenon of mandatory fictitious paternity in civil status registration in Ukraine, as provided for in Part 1 of Article 135 of the Family Code of Ukraine. The study critically reassesses the Soviet legal legacy, which, through the prism of conceptual metaphors of ‘structural symmetry’, forces single mothers to enter non-existent data about the father, thereby creating administratively constructed paternal identities. Using a longitudinal analysis of this phenomenon from 2008 to 2025, the author demonstrates that the number of children at risk of administrative invisibility is approaching one million. Drawing on netnographic and autoethnographic methodologies, including cases of neurodivergent children, the article reveals the attendant psychosocial risks and critical barriers to the safety and mobility of Ukrainian refugee families in foreign jurisdictions during wartime. Based on these findings, the study conceptualises a model of moving beyond Soviet-era paternalistic registration practices in favour of documentary truth, advocating the introduction of the legal institution of the matronymic at the stage of primary registration.
items.journal: International Journal of Law in Context
items.title: Legal fictions in birth registration: linguistic manifestations and social implications of paternity attribution in Ukraine and comparative perspectives

items.abstract: Abstract The article examines the challenges involved in restoring the rule of law in Poland. Under the rule of the Law and Justice (PiS) party from 2015 to 2023, Poland faced a profound constitutional crisis, marked by serious attacks on judicial independence. This crisis first affected the Constitutional Tribunal and later extended to the National Council of the Judiciary, whose unconstitutional politicization cast doubt on the legality of thousands of judicial appointments. Following the 2023 parliamentary elections, a new governing coalition assumed power, facing the complex challenge of rebuilding the Polish judiciary. The article outlines the guiding principles for the process of rule-of-law restoration and examines and assesses measures taken by the coalition government to resolve the crisis in the Polish judiciary. It is based on the assumption that the process of rule-of-law restoration must itself comply with the rule of law. Moreover, it argues that effectively resolving the crisis surrounding the Polish judiciary would require a meaningful political compromise involving the adoption of constitutional amendments to eliminate the roots of the crisis and increase the resilience of the constitutional system.
items.title: Lessons from the crisis: Rebuilding the Polish judiciary after the rule-of-law crisis

items.abstract: Abstract Epistemologists have recently argued that there is such a thing as ‘epistemic blame’: blame targeted at purely epistemic norm violations. Leading the charge has been Cameron Boult, who has argued across a papers and a monograph that we can make sense of this phenomenon by building an account of epistemic blame off of Scanlon’s account of moral blame. This paper argues a relationship-based account of epistemic blame is untenable, because it eliminates any distinction between blameworthy and excused agents. Attempts to overcome this problem cannot succeed because of the important but unrecognized ways his account deviates from Scanlon’s, and because of differences in how our moral and epistemic conduct are affected by our attitudes and expectations.
items.title: Epistemic blame isn’t relationship modification

items.abstract: Abstract In this paper, I analyse how and to what extent social structures constrain their occupants. To do so, I propose a 4-fold taxonomy of constraints: normative, conceptual, practical, and bodily constraints. They are distinguished by the nature of their binding force and by their existence conditions. For each type of constraint, I also analyse the strength of the limit that they can exert on our agency and examine whether they can be said to render certain options unavailable, rather than merely ill-advised or socially costly.
items.title: Social structural constraints and limits in the social world

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Gestational harm occurs when exposures in‐utero, such as alcohol, lead to long‐lasting health effects in the child born of that pregnancy. Because the actions of pregnant people can bring about such harm, this has given rise to debate about whether pregnant people are morally obligated to prevent harm to their future children (call this ‘gestational responsibility’). The debate on gestational responsibility increasingly recognises the social context of gestational harm. To the extent that unequal structural conditions constrain pregnant people's ability to prevent harms to their future children, some scholars argue that collective agents, and not individual pregnant people, are primarily responsible for such harms. In this, the debate has neglected to seriously consider the question of individual gestational responsibility under conditions of structural inequality. To address this question, I develop a framework for gestational responsibility grounded in the concept of vulnerability. The concept of vulnerability has gained traction in feminist bioethics as a means of capturing relational autonomy and increased susceptibility to harm under unequal social conditions. Focusing on the context of foetal alcohol spectrum disorder, I argue that the metaphor of ‘layers’ of vulnerability can help to articulate the varying degrees of autonomy—and correspondingly responsibility—of pregnant people under conditions of structural inequality. The purpose of my argument is to demonstrate the differential degrees of responsibility that people (in this case, those who are pregnant) possess in contexts of inequality, and to show how inequality mitigates responsibility.
items.title: Gestational Harm and Responsibility: A Vulnerability Framework Approach
Introduction
Is consenting to digital duplication ethically distinctive? A bioethical analysis
When is treatment clinically appropriate? The Townsend v Epsom and St Helier NHS Trust controversy
Reciprocity, responsibility and the ethics of minimum service periods in the NHS
Cohen: Liberty, Justice and Equality, written by Christine Sypnowich, G.A

items.abstract: This article is about an internal contradiction within the ascendant philosophy of new materialism, namely that its ethical opposition to harm clashes with its ontology. In the first part, I summarize new materialists’ attention to material entanglements and rejection of hierarchies in nature. In the second section, I argue that diagnosing and addressing harm to ecosystems and individuals (almost) always depend upon a hierarchy of beings within that ecosystem and a set of pre-determined potentials/preferences of how individual entities should be, two principles that new materialists explicitly reject. In the conclusion, I suggest that new materialists’ contradictions surrounding harms mean that they can either maintain a concern over ongoing damage to ecosystems and beings or their opposition to immaterial potentials and a hierarchy among beings—but not both. My preferred option is to retain the former and to accept that we must have some hierarchy among and within beings to address ongoing ecological deterioration around us. I close by outlining how new materialism’s key insights might be put in dialogue with other voices on the relation between humans and the rest of the world.
items.title: New Materialism, Harm, and Hierarchies in Nature
Explainable long-document classification for predicting outcomes of individual applications to the C​onstitutional Court of Türkiye

items.abstract: Abstract Williamson (2007) has given a celebrated isomorphism or translation-invariance argument that an infinite sequence of heads should have zero probability. However, infinitesimalists who hold that such a sequence has non-zero infinitesimal probability are very likely to deny the translation-invariance (e.g., Weintraub, 2008). Thus, we give two new arguments that an infinite sequence of heads has zero probability, without relying on the full translation-invariance thesis. We also show that two of our arguments extend to the setting of primitive conditional probabilities such as Popper functions and to total comparative probabilities.
items.title: The probability of an infinite sequence of heads is zero
Revenge of the indifference objection to fine-tuning

items.abstract: Abstract Epistemic supererogation involves going beyond what epistemic rationality requires. If some beliefs can be epistemically supererogatory, then others are epistemically suboptimal yet still rational. In ethics, knowingly doing the suboptimal is commonplace—we often spend money on ourselves rather than giving it to charity. By contrast, existing accounts of epistemic supererogation deny that one could knowingly adopt an epistemically suboptimal attitude. I challenge this assumption and develop a commitment-based account of epistemic supererogation. I focus on cases involving religious, moral, practical, or interpersonal commitments, where the evidence allows more than one rational attitude. In these cases, a longstanding commitment can help explain why someone reasonably sticks with a belief that is epistemically suboptimal. I then consider two ways of explaining this: one on which the belief remains rational because it fits the evidence well enough, and another on which practical factors affect epistemic rationality. This account strengthens the analogy between ethics and epistemology by showing that, in some cases, we can knowingly—and rationally—decline to take the epistemically best option.
items.title: Knowing the better, believing the worse: a commitment account of epistemic supererogation

items.abstract: Abstract This paper is divided into two main parts. In the first part, I defend a non-descriptivist account of imperatives, based on Paul Portner’s idea that imperatives serve to manage speakers’ to-do lists. I show that, once we recognize the multiplicity of operations that can be performed on a to-do list, the account can explain weak uses of imperatives without postulating additional structure on the to-do list or another list alongside it. In the second part of the paper, I present a logical framework which integrates the dynamic forces associated with declaratives, imperatives, and rejections thereof. I use this framework to inferentially explain the meaning of deontic modals such as must in terms of imperatives. The resulting inferential expressivist account has the resources to explain performative uses of must and hitherto unaccounted for data about their occurrence pattern.
items.title: Imperatives and Deontic Modality: An Inferential Expressivist Perspective
Argumentative Injustice as Structural Pathology: A Theory of Collective Epistemic Vice
RichardBellamy, Defending the Political Constitution, Oxford, Oxford University Press, 2026, 368 pp, hb, £105

items.abstract: ABSTRACT We argue that time is the great enabler: it is that which makes causation and change possible. We develop this idea into a functionalist account of time that has some very nice features: (i) it differentiates time from space where needed, (ii) it illuminates time via its connection to causation and change, (iii) it accounts for the apparent multiple realizability of time, and (iv) it correctly classifies worlds that have time as such. We compare our account to three rivals: time as the great necessitator, time as the great informer, and time as the measure of change. We show that treating time as an enabler does better.
items.title: What Is Time?

items.abstract: ABSTRACT The Continuum Hypothesis featured top of Hilbert's list of 23 problems in 1900. Today, we still consider the question, with various programmes pulling in different directions. This conceptual diversity raises a puzzle: In what sense do we disagree when we talk about it? A standard assumption takes the content of our thought about classes and the Continuum Hypothesis to be uniform between agents . I argue that moderate views of content determination lead to a rejection of this assumption. However, I also argue that whilst the Continuum Hypothesis can have different content for different agents, it can also be determinate for them. In particular, I suggest that there is a fault line between those who think there are uncountable sets and recent countabilist views.
items.title: Metasemantics and the Continuum Hypothesis

items.abstract: ABSTRACT The dominant view in philosophy of trust is that trust and monitoring are opposed. I argue that not all forms of monitoring necessarily undermine trust, but that certain forms of it do because they signal distrust of those being monitored. Crucially, this type of signaling is not confined to interpersonal contexts. I defend the view that institutions can signal distrust and offer the concept of institutionalized distrust to describe a form of distrust that does not reside in individual attitudes, but is instead expressed through policies, practices, and procedures, including forms of monitoring that are intrusive or disproportionate. My primary example is the eligibility procedures of the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) in the United States. I show that food assistance recipients encounter distrust in their interactions with the institutions they rely on for support and whose distrust may, in turn, influence attitudes of distrust among the public.
items.title: Institutionalized Distrust and Monitoring in Means‐Tested Benefits Programs

items.abstract: ABSTRACT The crucial issue in housing policy is the appropriate degree of community discretion over housing development. I develop an improved account of the normative value of community discretion, building on the literature on gentrification. This shows that community discretion does have genuine value. But more community discretion tends to lead to higher housing prices, which are themselves a significant cause of gentrification and other harms. We need policies that appropriately reflect this tension. Land value taxation is one good approach; I suggest that a novel policy, the ‘affordability override’, is even better.
items.title: Local Housing Discretion and the Affordability Override
Can I Even Help Them? Thoughts, Feelings, and Cognitions of Bystanders to Gender-Based Violence and Harassment in the Workplace

items.abstract: Abstract The relationship between religiously grounded values and everyday leadership practice in organisations remains underexplored, particularly in small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). In Saudi Arabia, Islamic values such as justice, trust, consultation, and accountability are expected to underpin ethical leadership and organisational conduct. Yet interview accounts from employees and leaders suggest systematic value–behaviour gaps in how these values are interpreted and enacted in practice. Drawing on 30 semi-structured interviews with one leader and five employees in each of five Saudi SMEs, this exploratory qualitative study examines how Islamic values are mobilised in leadership practice and how different patterns of value enactment shape employees’ experiences. Using an inductively derived three-level framework – balanced, excessive and insufficient enactment – the study illustrates how the same values can support ethical leadership when applied in a balanced way, but become associated with harmful or destructive leadership practices when applied in excess or deficiency. The findings show how Islamic values may be selectively internalised or performatively invoked, creating misalignments between professed values and everyday leadership behaviours. Drawing on moral identity theory and virtue ethics as complementary theoretical perspectives, the study explains two dimensions of value enactment. Moral identity theory illuminates how Islamic values are internalised, selectively enacted, or invoked performatively, while virtue ethics explains how values can become dysfunctional when enacted excessively, insufficiently or without proportion and contextual judgement. Together, these perspectives clarify how value–behaviour gaps emerge and shape employees’ experiences in Saudi SMEs.
items.title: Islamic Values and Value–Behaviour Gaps in Saudi SMEs: A Qualitative Study of Leadership Practice

items.abstract: Abstract With generative AI, everyone can materialize whatever fantasy they can conjure​ up in their imagination, including transgressive ones. The ‘orthodox’ view on the moral status of fantasies, even of materialized ones, is that such content is outside the scope of morality, since fantasies are quarantined from the agent’s real-world beliefs and desires. In this paper, we challenge this view by arguing that even if we grant that that is the case, repeated engagement with fantasies can contribute to the cultivation of various affective dispositions, or tastes, that can themselves be morally criticizable. We then argue that generative AI allows users to enter a ‘co-creative feedback loop’, a near-instantaneous cycle of prompting, viewing, and refining one’s fantasy, which makes sustained engagement with the transgressive representations very easy. Our claim is that such repeated and focused engagement with transgressive content can contribute to the cultivation of a taste or sensibility for what is morally problematic in those fantasies. If such tastes are morally criticizable, then engaging in practices that cultivate them is also open to moral criticism, even when no one is directly harmed.
items.title: A taste for what should not be wanted: generative AI and transgressive fantasy
Measuring spatial extension
Pluralism, parity, and justification intransitivity
Superintelligent robots
What philosophy can learn from AI: methodological insights from deep learning and Chinese philosophy
Active ignorance as uncertainty reduction: an agnotological extension of predictive processing
Autonomous Vehicles, Moral Responsibility Gap, and the Ethics of Knowing Responsibly
Authorship as a Distinct Ethical Dimension in Speech BCIs

items.abstract: Abstract Machine learning (ML) systems are increasingly used in the credit, pricing, and collections decisions of financial institutions, including Islamic banks, yet Shariah oversight remains primarily contract-centred. This conceptual paper identifies three distinct pathways of algorithmic Shariah non-compliance. Algorithmic riba, used narrowly, concerns profit-rate models whose optimisation objective may reproduce the time-value logic prohibited by riba; conventional benchmarking of murabahah (cost-plus sale) margins is not itself impermissible. Algorithmic injustice concerns credit-scoring outcomes that may violate the ‘adl (justice) obligation, and algorithmic gharamah (penalty) concerns collections systems that may impose charges beyond ​ta’widh (compensation for documented loss). To support model-level review, we propose the Shariah Algorithmic Compliance Screen (SACS), a five-component protocol grounded in Maqasid al-Shariah and offered as a first-iteration design proposal. Model owners disclose use cases, training data, objective functions, and outputs; independent technical validators test the relevant model evidence; and Shariah Supervisory Boards (SSBs) determine compliance. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods are used descriptively, while established fairness diagnostics (subgroup calibration, error-rate comparison, and disparate-impact measurement) provide separate evidence on outcome equity. The three mechanisms are derived analytically from doctrine and the ML literature and are stated as conditional hypotheses. The study completes the construction stage of the design: SACS is conceptually grounded and operationally specified, and its components adapt existing artificial intelligence governance practice to jurisprudential review. SACS has not yet been evaluated. Practitioner evaluation, particularly in Small Island Developing States such as the Maldives, is the next stage and will assess intelligibility, implementation burden, and practical usefulness.
items.title: Algorithmic riba and algorithmic Shariah non-compliance: risk mechanisms and a proposed governance protocol for Islamic banks

items.abstract: Abstract The growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into everyday messaging systems is transforming the conditions under which interpersonal communication takes place. As AI-mediated communication (AI-MC) becomes increasingly seamless and context-sensitive, it blurs the boundary between human expression and algorithmic assistance. This development raises fundamental questions about potential challenges to authenticity in personal relationships and possible strategies to address them. In this regard, we make three main contributions. First, we offer a technically grounded analysis of emerging AI-MC architectures, distinguishing between external prompting, keyboard-level assistance, and fully integrated in-app co-authoring systems. Second, we develop a normative account of authenticity in AI-MC, understood as a second-person, relationship-sensitive notion, drawing on analytic theories of endorsement, relational normativity, and socially situated self-expression. On this basis, we argue that authenticity cannot be directly engineered by design, since it depends on reflective agency and context-dependent interpersonal obligations. Third, we advance a design-oriented proposal aimed at mitigating authenticity-related concerns without resorting to paternalistic restrictions: the introduction of optional and granular disclosure mechanisms (“AI ticks”) that allow users to signal the presence and degree of AI assistance in a context-sensitive manner. We argue that such forms of transparency function not as a substitute for authenticity, but as a pro-ethical condition that enables agents to negotiate authenticity-based obligations within their relationships. The analysis contributes to current debates on the ethics of AI-mediated communication and the conditions of responsible human–AI interaction.
items.title: Who am I really talking to? Authenticity, transparency, and the case for “AI ticks” in AI-mediated communication
Designing responsible AI competencies for software engineers: an exploratory pilot evaluation of a UbD-based professional development program on AI ethics awareness
Fabricated citations threaten the evidence base that clinical AI learns from: checks are needed at submission and at retrieval
Ethical consistency beyond single outputs: decision–criterion separability and trajectory-level evaluation in commercial language models
The delegation dilemma: human agency, inalienable obligations, and the legal-ethical permissibility of artificial intelligence in military operations

items.abstract: Abstract The accelerated deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) at an unprecedented pace leads to new opportunities and risks for organisations and their ecosystem. To support management and regulatory efforts with a deeper understanding of responsible conduct, this study addresses a salient research gap by developing a new theoretical model to describe the tenets of responsible deployment of AI. Applied through a grounded theory approach, existing adoption and integration practices are explored by drawing on literature studies and semi-structured interviews with 17 participants with professional experience with AI in an international context. Themes are synthesised through the Gioia technique. The theoretical model is underpinned by an objective-execution-outcome structure and described by the mnemonic STAGES. The contribution of the study is a new theoretical model to explain and encourage responsible deployment of AI, and explicate which elements organisations should consider when designing internal policies, and to further inform decision-making by management, and regulatory efforts.
items.title: STAGES: A model for responsible deployment of artificial intelligence
Accurate enough to trust, not authorised to act: Predictive Decision Authority and what institutions permit machine learning systems to do
Who decides? Decision-making risks and human control in AI-enabled military command
Can AI form moral character? Pseudo-character, akhlāq, and moral formation in AI-mediated education

items.abstract: Abstract This article formalises and develops an individual-centred framework to explain what I call the micro-foundations of EU law, and applies it to Johan Willem Beyen’s role in the creation of the Common Market. It argues that standard structural accounts in European integration overlook the micro-foundations: the ways in which the desires, beliefs and choices of specific actors shape integration outcomes. Drawing on methodological individualism, mechanism-based causal explanation and narrative legal history, the article reconstructs how Beyen’s liberal economic convictions, his experience in international finance and Bretton Woods institutions, and his reading of the 1930s crisis and post-war power shifts informed his preference for a general common market over sectoral integration. The narrative traces his 1952–55 initiatives, including the Beyen Plan, the Benelux Memorandum and the road to the Messina conference, highlighting environmental, cognitive and relational mechanisms that enabled a small-state minister to set the agenda for the Treaties of Rome. In dialogue with liberal intergovernmentalism and Weiler’s equilibrium theory, the article contends that individual-level explanations, the micro-foundations, provide the ‘prequel’ to both national preference-formation and integration-through-law, enriching structural causal accounts while telling a new story from the perspective of individuals.
items.title: Johan Willem Beyen and the creation of the internal market: Lessons from history and the social sciences for the micro-foundations of EU law

A Social History of Analytic Philosophy: How Politics Has Shaped an Apolitical Philosophy
                    by Christoph Schuringa, Verso, 2025, 336pp., £25 (hbk), ISBN 9781804292099

items.abstract: Abstract In early colonial Lagos, inheritance disputes laid bare the exclusionary and discriminatory character of British jurisprudence. British judges, ill-versed in Yorùbá customary law, mimicked Indigenous Yorùbá judicial structures without recognizing their communal or spiritual foundations. By privileging written testamentary documents and civil marriages over nuncupative wills and customary unions, the colonial legal regime engendered an unstable inheritance system that marginalized numerous Yorùbá litigants. In response, Yorùbá communities and intellectuals mobilized to foreground the sacred, ritualized basis of Indigenous inheritance practices, advocating for a legal framework that could legitimately reconcile colonial authority with the spiritual dimensions of Yorùbá personhood. This article examines tensions between Indigenous African and European laws during colonial rule. It is also an inquiry into the claims and counterclaims about who had the authority to speak on behalf of deceased Yorùbá subjects in colonial Lagos.
items.title: Voice of the Dead: Yorùbá Spiritual Justice, English Jurisprudence, and the Making of Inheritance Law in the British Colony of Lagos (1863–1938)

items.journal: International Journal of Law in Context
items.title: Legal Moves: Choreographies of Race, Law, and Empire - By Anna Jayne Kimmel , Stanford: Stanford University Press, 2026. 270 pp. ISBN: 9781503646087 $70.00 (hardback)

items.journal: Critical Review of International Social and Political Philosophy
items.title: Solidarity as a political value
A companion to Western legal traditions: from antiquity to the twentieth century
The Absence of Work: Foucault, Marxism, and History, and Politics

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Realism about tense comes in various forms. In “Tense and Reality” (2005) and “The Reality of Tense” (2006), Kit Fine offered a helpful taxonomy that contributed to shape the current debate on the topic. In our paper “Eternal Facts in an Ageing Universe” (2012), we improved upon this taxonomy, identifying a further type of view that Fine leaves out: Dynamic Absolutism. Both these taxonomies construe the different versions of tense realism in terms of first‐order quantification over facts or states of affairs. Our goal is to show that the logical space of these first‐order tense‐realist positions can be replicated using higher‐order quantification instead. Along the way, we rebut the claim that there is no coherent higher‐order version of Dynamic Absolutism—a claim that one would naturally attribute to Lukas Skiba in his “Higher‐Order Being and Time” (2025) given the way he formulates his critique, even though the view that he actually intends to put forward may plausibly be more moderate.
items.title: Higher‐Order Tense Realism

items.abstract: ABSTRACT History abounds with transformative moral heroes—agents devoting their lives to uprooting entrenched unjust structures. Though philosophy has said much about heroes generally, this distinctive class remains undertheorized. This matters because they are among our most celebrated moral exemplars, and much of our sense of moral progress rests on them. Yet they characteristically act against familiar constraints on responsible deliberation, pursuing apparently infeasible and inefficacious projects while foreclosing tractable alternatives that would secure demonstrable goods. We establish this tension and argue that the most promising attempts to dissolve it fail. At best, this shows that moral theory is structurally conservative, as its standards of responsible deliberation systematically favor mitigation over transformation. At worst, it reveals a deeper instability in moral theory, as it seems to depend for its progress on agents it cannot vindicate.
items.title: The Choiceworthlessness of Transformative Heroism

items.abstract: Abstract Ever since the American legal philosopher Wesley Hohfeld published his analyses of rights in the second decade of the twentieth century, numerous philosophers and legal theorists have grappled with his matrix of legal positions. Very seldom, however, have the commentators on Hohfeld recognized the importance of logical quantification for any endeavor to elaborate the categories of that matrix fully. This paper will mull over a few of the manifold ways in which quantification is operative in the legal relationships that Hohfeld delineated. After furnishing a short conspectus of the Hohfeldian analytical framework which distills those relationships, this paper will briefly discuss the two most prominent logical quantifiers and will then explore how one's awareness of the workings of those quantifiers can sharpen one's grasp of the Hohfeldian analysis.
