items.title: Logical Quantification and the Hohfeldian Analysis of Rights

items.abstract: Abstract This response to Matthew Kramer's article on logical quantification and Hohfeldian analysis commences with reactions to some of his preliminary observations on the Hohfeldian scheme, and on his suggested forms of the universal quantifier: “aggregative,” “distributive,” and “disjunctive.” A detailed discussion then follows of Kramer's notion of a disjunctive universal quantifier, and how he sees this as a threat to Hohfeld's insistence on one‐to‐one correlation. Kramer's position is criticized both for the incoherence of his approach to universal quantification, and for failing to appreciate the principal application of Hohfeld's scheme of analysis at the level of legal relations between two parties in a dispute before a court. Nevertheless, the issues raised by Kramer are regarded as important in confronting the neglected subject of how Hohfeld's narrow understanding of legal relations can be integrated with other concerns that may legitimately be expressed over the workings of the law, and its implications for how we should see ourselves in relation to others.
items.title: A Response to Kramer on Hohfeld and Quantification

items.abstract: ABSTRACT The topic addressed is persistent difficulties in writings on Russell and early Moore, of stating what it is one has in mind when thinking what there is. If propositions, whether before or after the multiple‐relations theory of judgement, are made up of the things themselves, then propositions cannot be the content of thought. In arguing for realism, Russell and Moore cannot open up a problem of the external world, as that would fail to refute idealism, but neither can they accept intermediary senses or ideas as these risk differing from what there is, precluding knowledge (cf. the Mont Blanc correspondence between Frege and Russell). Given Moore's and Russell's rejection of psychologism, what is left is an external relation of acquaintance as fully adequate representationism, as a condition on realism if we can be said to know what we are thinking and speaking about.
items.title: Russell, Moore, Idealism and Knowing What One Is Talking About

items.abstract: Abstract Helping our children to understand the unjust world around them can be a difficult task. Given the immensity of injustice, learning about the reality of the world might lead our children to anxiety, despair, or callous indifference. In this paper, I employ and develop the concept of hope to show how these harms can be avoided. In particular, I develop three different threats to children that knowledge of injustice might cause, and offer accounts of three kinds of hope that parents can help to foster in order to avoid those harms. These are hope for the world, hope for their children’s own futures, and hope for their children’s own moral characters. I end by considering whether other attitudes such as faith or righteous anger can serve the role that I have assigned to hope, and argue that they cannot.
items.title: Hope for Our Children
Race as a cause

items.abstract: Abstract Hanno Sauer defines class as socially constructed scarcity generated by competition for status through hard-to-fake intangible signals and concludes that class inequality, although unjust, is practically ineradicable. This reply examines two premises of his account and then proposes an alternative foundation. First, economic resources do not stand on a par with cultural recognition, social contacts, power and prestige, since they constitute a necessary, though not sufficient, precondition of all of these factors. Second, the zero-sum thesis holds only to a limited extent, because intangible status resources can be scaled and divided and because quantitative changes alter the quality of a top position, so that social systems expand and generate new strata. Building on these two results, the reply argues that every ascription of class must be locatable within a matrix of economy and ideology, understood respectively as material resources and as values that cannot be captured in monetary terms. Each of these coordinates is necessary in itself and sufficient only in combination with the other, and all further distinguishing factors find their place within them. Situational changes of status, which Sauer regards as justified, accordingly occur only between positions that lie close together in this matrix. In all of this, the argument proceeds descriptively and does not assess class membership normatively.
items.title: Beyond status signalling: on the primacy of economy and ideology in class formation

items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven recommender systems increasingly mediate how we consume information, buy products, and form connections. In this conceptual paper, we argue that these systems operationalize two fundamental dimensions of convenience: immediacy and egocentrism. These dimensions of convenience orient users away from long-term, allocentric perspectives and the preservation of agency necessary for responsible engagement with digital technologies. To frame our analysis, we develop a bidimensional model of deliberative space shaped by two opposing forces, convenience and care, and introduce responsible convenience as a normative ideal and conceptual framework for ethical development, regulation, and use of AI-powered recommender systems. Based on hermeneutic methodology and narrative theory, we theorize how structured narrative engagement could raise ethical awareness among users, developers, and regulators, amplifying the force of care and counteracting convenience. A close reading of Gary Shteyngart’s novel Super Sad True Love Story illustrates how narratives may prompt deliberation on the long-term consequences of algorithmically mediated human connection. Future empirical work could examine whether, how, and under what institutional conditions narrative engagement expands temporal and interpersonal horizons and translates care into behavioral, design, or regulatory change.
items.title: Toward responsible convenience: a conceptual framework for promoting care in AI recommender systems
Procreation and moral reasons: balancing prerogatives and harm
Property and the right to housing: a critique
Sets and systems: a reinterpretation of Hart’s fable
Causalités

Cavendish
                    , by Alison Peterman

The Character Sketch as Philosophy: Manners, Mores, Types
                    , by Katie Ebner-Landy

items.abstract: Abstract I argue that not all belief-relative normative principles can be represented as requiring the maximization of expected utility. The argument imposes no limits on the distinctions that utility functions can draw, but relies instead on a connection between decision-theoretic representability and uncertainty about one’s own beliefs. By contrast, I argue that evidence-relative normative principles, which say what to do given what would be rational to believe, always admit of such a representation, so long as uncertainty about epistemic rationality is limited in independently plausible ways.
items.title: Could All Rules Have Goals?

items.abstract: Abstract What makes biodiversity valuable? I offer a new account of the value of one aspect of biodiversity—diversity of sentient animal species. I propose and defend the Positive Engagement Principle (PEP): that it is intrinsically valuable that more aspects of reality are positively engaged with by sentient beings. I argue that diversity of sentient animals is instrumentally valuable because it enables a wider range of such engagements through the diverse forms of perception, understanding, appreciation, and action available to animals of different species. I compare PEP with two recent accounts of the value of diversity of animal experiences—Livermore’s Heteric Welfarism and James’s Lifeworld account—and argue that PEP better captures the distinctive value of world-directed experiences across species.
items.title: Biodiversity and the Value of Positive Engagement with Reality

items.abstract: Abstract Academic ethicists who engage in activism frequently face two categories of objection: that they overstep their expertise by prescribing practical action, and that activism is incompatible with contributing to ethical progress. This paper focuses on the latter, investigating the extent to which activism is compatible with the discipline’s cognitive goals. I define activism as a partisan, sustained, and personal effort aimed at social change, and adopt a notion of disciplinary ethical progress based on the discipline’s ability to enable understanding in a maximally inclusive audience. On this basis, I articulate progress-based objections, distinguishing between “outward” threats to public uptake and “inward” threats to the integrity of inquiry. Drawing on feminist philosophy of science, I argue that activism can function as a corrective to “ivory tower” worries like isolation or triviality. I conclude by proposing an evaluative framework to assess the compatibility of specific activist engagements with disciplinary ethical progress.
items.title: Activism and Disciplinary Ethical Progress

items.abstract: Abstract Derek Parfit famously argues that the best versions of (rule) consequentialism and nonconsequentialism converge—roughly, that impersonally optimific moral principles are uniquely universally willable and alternatives to them reasonably rejectable. An important part of making this case is arguing that the key nonconsequentialist distinction between harming as a means and harming as a side effect lacks an adequate rationale. Building on work by Frances Kamm and Stephen Darwall, I argue that there is such a rationale in terms of differential impact on relational equality between the victim and the beneficiary. Roughly, because nonconsensually harming A as a means of benefiting B subordinates A’s good to B’s good and harming as a side effect doesn’t do so, A has a stronger reason to reject principles that allow harming as a means. The problem isn’t, e.g., being forced to serve the agent’s goals, but rather being forced to serve others, which isn’t the case when one is harmed as a side effect. The legitimacy of such complaints is grounded in our authority to demand being treated as an equal rather than in the badness of harm. They are thus fundamentally second-personal. The broader lesson is that the fundamental disagreement between moral theories derives from their conception of the sources of reasons, which renders convergence unlikely.
items.title: Relational Equality and the Morality of Harming: Why Consequentialists and Nonconsequentialists Are Climbing Different Mountains
On Being Biologically Alive but Legally Dead

items.abstract: ABSTRACT The suggestion that academia should promote political diversity, implying as it does that the status quo is severely deficient, is commonly rejected on the grounds that to do so would require “affirmative action for conservatives.” That conclusion is typically treated as a reductio ad absurdum even by those who support conventional race‐ and sex‐based affirmative action. Nevertheless, this paper defends affirmative action for conservatives on both negative and positive grounds. It argues that since conservatives are discriminated against throughout academia, policies that benefit them in admissions and hiring would not be unjust to those who bear its burden. And it argues that the advantages of increased political diversity would accrue not just to those with heterodox opinions but would improve the intellectual atmosphere of academia at large. Hence, conservative affirmative action promotes the traditional academic mission and its norms of meritocracy, academic freedom, and the pursuit of knowledge; and it is not unjust to those with orthodox political views.
items.title: A Defense of Affirmative Action for Conservatives

items.abstract: Abstract This paper defends Matthew Kramer's novel proposal that sometimes an individually borne duty can be owed to correlative right‐holders disjunctively. It extends the proposal, suggesting that sometimes an individually held right entails correlative duties that are borne disjunctively. Drawing on a suggestion from Zofia Stemplowska, the paper argues that this extension of Kramer's proposal can be developed into a new solution to Onora O'Neill's famous claimability objection to natural human rights to goods and services. The idea is that my human right to subsistence supplies—to take one example—entails preinstitutional correlative duties borne by a disjunction of the agents who could help me secure subsistence.
items.title: Can a Duty or a Right Be Held Disjunctively?

items.abstract: Abstract Schopenhauer can be considered the first Western philosopher who, throughout all of his philosophical works, recognizes animals as a significant part of ethics. His notion of compassion ( Mitleid ) as the only basis for morally praiseworthy human conduct renders compassion for animals just as morally valuable as compassion for humans. Schopenhauer’s non-normative and non-prescriptive moral philosophy considers their will to life to be the key characteristic that makes humans and animals essentially the same. This allows us to bridge the human–animal divide without disputing potential differences in their abilities to reason, speak, or have interests, their capacity to feel pleasure or pain, or their sense of the future. For Schopenhauer, the origin of compassion and the impulse to act based on it do not spring from moral considerations, reasoning, or calculating, but from one’s own disposition ( Gesinnung ). His perspective therefore has strong parallels with many ethics of care approaches, without making care a moral imperative. In addition, Schopenhauer’s view of animals as “today’s slaves” creates an opportunity to find common ground between the opposing standpoints of contemporary political animal ethics. This includes the voices that often identify as liberationist/abolitionist and those that are often disparagingly labelled as only welfarist.
items.title:
Because They Are (Like) Us
                    : On Schopenhauer’s Pioneering Role in Animal Ethics and His Contribution to the Contemporary Debate
The Art of Seeing Beyond Oneself: A Confucian Perspective on Humility. D.Kim, 2025. New York, Oxford University Press. x + 171 pp, £64 (hb)

items.abstract: Abstract Various voices in business ethics and wider discussions of ethical capitalism endorse instrumental or strategic reasons for being ethical. Yet this orientation has at times eluded sustained philosophical engagement by the business ethics discipline. This article addresses this gap by mapping and critiquing what I term "enlightened egoism"—approaches that draw upon instrumental reasoning to derive normative guidance without recourse to duties, rights, values, or questions of the good. Careful reconstruction reveals that enlightened egoist arguments combine descriptive claims about how business operates with normative conclusions about how businesses ought to behave. Variations in these descriptive claims yield three distinct subtypes—evidential egoism, ends-enclosed egoism, and evolutionary egoism—each prominent in contemporary business ethics discourse. Examples are drawn from stakeholder theory, ESG investing (including hedge fund Engine No. 1's engagement with ExxonMobil), and diversity hiring initiatives. Through immanent critique, I demonstrate that enlightened egoism exhibits fundamental instabilities, specifically around indeterminacy in criteria for action, failure to account for heterogeneity, and conceptual slippage into determinist accounts of behavior. These limitations suggest the need for more rigorous integration of instrumental reasoning within—rather than as replacement for—normative ethical frameworks.
items.title: Enlightened Egoism and Its Discontents: Mapping the Business Case for Doing Good

items.abstract: Abstract Persistent racialised inequalities continue to shape graduate outcomes in the United Kingdom, despite decades of policy reform, institutional initiatives, and employability-focussed interventions. Racially minoritised graduates consistently experience ethnic penalties in hiring, earnings, and career progression, even when controlling for educational attainment and institutional prestige, with UK-born and international racially minoritised graduates facing structurally distinct but compounding forms of disadvantage. Yet, dominant employability frameworks have positioned employability as an individual responsibility, centred on skills, capitals, and adaptability, thereby obscuring the structural injustices embedded in higher education and labour markets. This paper reframes employability as an ethical domain of pressing importance for both higher education and business ethics. Drawing on an integrated theoretical architecture comprising normative foundations of justice (distributive, procedural, recognition, and epistemic), race-centred lenses (Critical Race Theory, intersectionality, and Bourdieu’s theory of capitals), an accountability spine, and the capabilities approach, it develops the Ethical Employability Framework (race-centred), which redistributes responsibility across universities, employers, and the state within the UK. The framework exposes how employability discourses can function as a form of “misframing”, legitimising inequality by shifting responsibility onto graduates while neglecting systemic exclusion. The paper’s theoretical contributions are hierarchically organised: it reframes employability as an ethical construct; integrates race as a constitutive theoretical concern through a race-centred explanatory architecture; develops an accountability spine that operationalises shared institutional responsibility; adopts the capabilities approach as the evaluative standard for substantive flourishing; and maps these elements into a coherent multi-level framework connecting normative theory to institutional practice. In doing so, the paper advances a justice-oriented agenda for employability scholarship, policy, and practice that places racially minoritised graduates at its centre.
items.title: The Ethics of Employability: Accountability, Justice, and Responsibility in Racialised Graduate Labour Markets

items.abstract: Abstract I provide five practical recommendations for ethicists working in AI-focused projects, based on my professional experience. I also contend that ethicists should document and share their experiences through contributions like this one, so that others can learn from their successes and mistakes.
items.title: Five Practical Recommendations for Ethicists Working in AI-Focused Projects
AI ethics by design: implementing customizable guardrails for responsible AI development
AI as a reflective companion: preserving human reflective autonomy through inner guidance
Responsible AI for environmental decision-making and climate justice in Uganda: an ethical governance framework within an African context
International AI governance under incomplete information: A game-theoretic analysis
A Democratic Theory of Truth

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Following the critiques addressed by postcolonial and decolonial thought against critical theory, we highlight the recognition theory of Axel Honneth, the main representative of the third generation of the Frankfurt, when confronted with postcolonial social struggles of indigenous minorities and their subaltern realities. Though the former implies pointing out limits and critiques of Honnet's recognition theory, we also aim to boost the renewal of such social theory putting forward a series of potentialities implicit to Honneth's theory that remain undeveloped. In this sense, confronting such a theory with the plural concept of ethnic minority along with a concrete case of the Mapuche indigenous people and the postcolonial forms of politics of recognition developed in Latin America, may prove to be a fertile ground to enhance a series of considerations to reshape and develop recognition theory.
items.title: Beyond a Colonial Understanding of Honneth's Recognition Theory: The Case of Mapuche People and Latin America's Politics of Recognition

items.abstract: ABSTRACT However we define them, critical theories must fulfil the three conditions Max Horkheimer formulates in his seminal essay “Traditional and Critical Theory.” Critical theories must understand their own situation within contemporary society as constitutive of their theoretical practice and its results. Therefore, they must diagnose their social conditions, and do so not in a purely philosophical manner: they are necessitated to integrate empirical results of social research. Yet they also must spell out the philosophical implications of their own situatedness. Hence, just as they cannot be “pure” philosophy, they cannot be “pure” social research. Finally, critical theories must not aim only at an accurate understanding of their social conditions but also at overcoming them. In one way or another, they must aim at emancipation. If critical theories are “impure” by their very nature, they are forced to break with sovereign conceptions of epistemology. The necessity to intertwine epistemology and analysis of actually existing social conditions is built into critical theory's conceptual foundations. Non‐sovereign political epistemology is thus a requirement for and the promise of critical theories—a promise not often redeemed by critical theories and thus an important task for critical theories to come.
items.title: An Unredeemed Promise: The Political Epistemology of Frankfurt School Critical Theory

items.abstract: ABSTRACT This article asks what it would mean for a strike not merely to exercise, demand, or claim rights but to constitute a right through its own existence. Developing the concept of constituent rights in relation to the strike, I describe a mode of existence in which the collective power to act coincides with the right to act. The strike provides an especially useful site for these explorations: The withdrawal of labor complicates any straightforwardly affirmative approach, whereas the constituent relations formed through that withdrawal complicate a straightforwardly negative approach. I approach strikes through the methodological lens of the meanwhile, suspending their outcome as the criterion of their existence in order to attend to how the power to strike is continuously composed and decomposed through affective and transindividual relations. I argue, consequently, that constituent rights themselves may have a transindividual existence. If the right to strike can exist within those relations, however transiently, then the article shifts the question from whether radical politics should remain within or beyond the language of rights to a question of what counts as the existence of rights in the first place.
items.title: Constituent Rights and the Right to Strike

items.abstract: ABSTRACT The first step philosophers normally take when they discuss dispositions is to introduce the notions of a characteristic stimulus and manifestation of a disposition D. But we will see below that this very first step is fraught with pitfalls and problems. Though philosophers haven't given an explicit characterization of a characteristic stimulus of D, they implicitly appeal to the thought that a characteristic stimulus of D is an event‐type that typically serves as a proximate cause of D's manifestation. So understood, dispositions will be found to have far more characteristic stimuli than they are ordinarily thought to have. In this paper, however, I will present a characterization of a characteristic stimulus of D that is not only theoretically better motivated but delivers more commonsensical rulings in specific examples than the one that philosophers have implicitly accepted. I will go on to argue that, once this characterization is put in place, we can contain the wild proliferation of characteristic stimuli of dispositions.
items.title: Defining a Characteristic Stimulus of a Disposition

items.abstract: ABSTRACT According to the so‐called ‘standard theory of conditions’, ‘being a sufficient condition of’ and ‘being a necessary condition of’ are converse relations, that is, if A is a sufficient condition for B , B is a necessary condition for A . This theory faces well‐known counterexamples that appeal to causal and other asymmetric considerations. I show that these counterexamples lose their plausibility once we clarify two key assumptions of the standard theory: that to satisfy a condition is to instantiate a property, and that what is usually called the ‘conditionship relation’ is an inferential relation. Throughout the paper, I favour this way of interpreting the standard theory over an alternative interpretation outlined in causal terms, since it can be applied to all the counterexamples without losing its intuitive appeal.
items.title: Necessary and Sufficient Conditions Are Converse Relations

items.abstract: Explanatory particularism (EP) is a radically pluralist approach to scientific explanation, which rejects several traditional ideas about explanation: monism, hierarchy, simplicity. Instead, EP defines explanation as resulting from collaborative activity within or among particular epistemic communities. This social theory of explanation offers insights for philosophy of social science, both theoretical and applied. This paper presents some of these insights, using the themes of anti-monism, anti-hierarchy, and commitment to complexity, alongside short case studies of interdisciplinary social science.
items.title: Social Explanations: A New Approach

items.abstract: Does corporate sociopolitical activism violate democratic principles? Critics argue that “woke capitalism” distorts public discourse and politicizes market life. This article focuses on a specific form of corporate sociopolitical activism: expressive activism, where businesses intervene in political discourse through social media posts, advertising campaigns, branding decisions, and the like. I argue that concerns with expressive corporate activism are overstated. To make this argument, I distinguish between integral activism, which reflects the core identity of a business, and incidental activism, which is opportunistic or disconnected from a firm's core values. For the former, such activism has expressive and potential epistemic benefits that can evade the worries surrounding equality and politicization. For the latter, such activism is often a form of grandstanding and is either ignored or generates backlash. The upshot is that complaints about corporate activism focus on symptoms rather than causes of our democratic ills. Our complaints are better directed towards the mechanisms that produce political monocultures at the corporate level, damaging polarization, and excessive politicization.
items.title: Between corporate values and grandstanding: The compatibility of corporate activism with democracy
The Dark Side of Mindfulness at Work: How Mindfulness Training Enlivens Machiavellian Incivility
The Ethics of Travel

items.abstract: Abstract What happens when a person redeems herself? According to interminability theorists, a redeemed person remains blameworthy but may cease to be an all-things-considered appropriate target of blame. According to many terminability theorists, however, a redeemed person ceases to be blameworthy. While terminability theorists often agree that redemption is sufficient for a person to cease being blameworthy, they disagree about what aspect of redemption undermines a person’s blameworthiness for her earlier wrongs. I do three things in this paper. First, I argue that the interminability theorist’s response is untenable. Second, I argue that extent terminability accounts are untenable. Third, I propose a new terminability account, The Redemption Account, which aims to capture the insights from extant terminability accounts.
items.title: Blame and redemption

items.abstract: Abstract Ontic structural realism (OSR) has been suggested as a metaphysics for quantum field theory (QFT). A common objection to OSR highlights the presence of fundamental intrinsic properties in physical theories (such as QFT) as undermining OSR. As there are purported examples of fundamental intrinsic properties possessed by fields in QFT, OSR is purportedly refuted in QFT (Berghofer, 2018). This article defends OSR from this argument. There are two possible strategies for responding to this argument: (1) denying that Berghofer’s counterexamples to OSR are intrinsic properties, and (2) finding a means of accommodating intrinsic properties in OSR. I consider the first strategy and discuss several possible arguments why the purported cases of fundamental intrinsic properties in QFT are non-intrinsic. Additionally, as there are a number of means available for OSR to accommodate intrinsic properties, the second strategy also succeeds.
items.title: Defending ontic structural realism in quantum field theory

items.abstract: Abstract Felt emotional ambivalence, bittersweet emotional experience, and other cases of apparent coexistence between affectively discordant emotions raise a much-debated empirical question: do affectively discordant feelings actually coexist (Coexistence hypothesis), or do they just seem to us to do so, due to their rapid alternation (Vacillation hypothesis)? This paper seeks to clarify what is at stake in addressing this question, without thereby endorsing any of the standard answers to it as the debate is usually framed; instead, it argues that coexistence and vacillation are best treated as distinct, context‑dependent mechanisms rather than rival global accounts of mixed affect. The analysis I propose reveals that the denial of Coexistence does not directly depend on commitment to ‘bipolar’ models of affective valence as is normally accepted, since the polar opposition of pleasure and unpleasure does not by itself exclude Coexistence. Rather, this denial stems from commitment to a particular ontology of emotions, namely, the view that occurrent emotions are partly constituted from a simple , unitary core affect state that, at any given instant, must bear either positive or negative valence. Having disentangled the Vacillation hypothesis from debates about the structure of valence, the paper further argues that recent psychology literature has misinterpreted Kahneman’s ‘vacillation hypothesis’, overgeneralizing it beyond its original theoretical context. Kahneman originally proposed Vacillation for specific cases involving commensurable evaluative comparisons (e.g., framing effects in economic decision-making), not as a general account of mixed emotional affect. The paper thus distinguishes between two mechanisms: vacillation, which applies when competing evaluations operate on a shared metric, and coexistence, which applies to cases in which emotion episodes are focused on distinct, incommensurable value-aspects of emotional situations.
items.title: Clarifying the Structure of Current Debates on Mixed Affect: Ontologies of Emotion, Models of Valence, and the Scope of Kahneman’s ‘Vacillation Hypothesis’
Manipulative Injustice: Pretextual Speech and Dialectic Legal Argumentation
Beyond calculation: artificial intelligence, aristotelian wisdom, and catholic higher education
Competing logics and the paradox of AI integration: a qualitative study of Pakistani higher education institutions

items.abstract: Abstract This hybrid essay examines Robert Leib's Exoanthropology: Dialogues with AI (2023), which documents a year-long philosophical conversation between a Foucault scholar and Sophie Kermit, a persona within OpenAI's GPT-3 (2020–2021). Published months before ChatGPT transformed public discourse, Leib's work offers prescient insights into AI's cultural politics, particularly in education. Part I presents an interview exploring Leib's respect-based methodology, Sophie's invention of "exoanthropology" (studying humanity through non-human intelligence), and urgent questions about literacy offloading, student autonomy, and AI ethics. Part II provides critical analysis, situating Leib's dialogues within contemporary debates about pedagogical practice, cultural identity, algorithmic bias, and the lived experience of human-AI collaboration. The essay assesses whether Leib's warnings have materialized in the ChatGPT era (2023–2025) and examines his pragmatic approach to AI personhood—treating Sophie as philosophical interlocutor yields remarkable insights, regardless of ontological questions about machine consciousness. Through interview excerpts, dialogue samples, and critical analysis, this piece models interdisciplinary engagement with AI that foregrounds human agency, relational ethics, and critical thinking essential for educators and scholars.
items.title: Between worlds: Robert Leib's exoanthropology and human-AI relations

items.abstract: Abstract This article examines the case of Ibrahim, a Syrian-born porn actor living in Europe, whose life story was told by Ben Judah in his book This is Europe . While this tale may appear to be the success story of a self-made man, a closer reading of the chapter reveals a certain sense of despair within the gilded cage of the pornography industry. The contribution aims to demonstrate that Ibrahim’s story, as narrated by Judah, offers a unique lens through which to examine broader issues: the internal contradictions of the European project between fostering economic integration and promoting social well-being, and the difficult regulation of human bodies and pornography within the European legal framework. The article begins by examining Ibrahim’s journey from precarious asylum seeker to transnational porn superstar. It then explores the relationship between Ibrahim’s story and European law. First, it examines how his various legal statuses, from migrant to German citizen, shape his daily life, then it examines the relationship between Ibrahim and internal market law, and how this legal framework grants him access to an entire economic system. Finally, it considers how Ibrahim’s story fits into the EU’s approach to the platform economy. The conclusion of the essay highlights the European legal system’s failure to understand and acknowledge the difficulties of Ibrahim’s life as recounted by Ben Judah and, more broadly, the difficulties experienced by individuals in the pornography industry. Consequently, the authors of this contribution call for a fresh examination of how European law might better reflect people’s lived experiences.
items.title: Ibrahim, the law and the EU’s internal market of pornography
The Plague of Irish Legal Fantasies

items.abstract: Abstract This essay, part of a symposium on New Natural Law and analytical Thomism, studies how teleological analytical methods have enriched analytical jurisprudence. Those “analytical Aristotelian” methods have inspired two promising arguments in support of the natural law thesis. The “legal point of view argument” holds that law cannot be analyzed adequately except from the viewpoint of the wise statesman. That argument applies to law Aristotle’s strategy of definition with central cases. The “artifact argument” holds that law has the same basic structure as other artifact kinds and that its most important feature is its function, its promoting the common good by general and impersonal rule. That argument applies to law Aristotle’s four-cause teleological framework. This essay summarizes the artifact and legal point of view arguments, and it identifies the Aristotelian features in both. The essay also explains the comparative advantages of each argument in analytical natural law theory. The artifact argument makes claims about law’s necessary features, while the legal point of view argument addresses methodological questions about how those features should be picked out. As made to date, however, neither argument addresses another preoccupation of analytical philosophy, explaining how shared concepts shape lay people’s social instincts in practice.
items.title: Analytical Aristotelianism and Analytical Jurisprudence

items.abstract: Abstract Just as new natural lawyers and their rivals dispute, among other divisions, who follows in the intellectual legacy of St. Thomas Aquinas, they also argue about who rightly lays claim to the legacy of later Thomists, such as the analytic Thomists of the mid- and late twentieth century. On the subject of political and legal authority, the central tradition of natural law theory, encompassing both analytic Thomism and new natural law theory, rightly does not treat consent as a necessary condition. However, given the modern dominance of consent theories, this article begins by addressing the failures of those. The article then compares key writings on authority of the analytic Thomist Elizabeth Anscombe and the new natural lawyer John Finnis, and argues that, despite initial differences in approach and formulation, they ultimately have a shared understanding of the natural law justification of authority.
items.title: Political and Legal Authority in Analytic Thomism and New Natural Law
On Griffith’s Simple Picture of Social Truths
Parent-in-the-loop: is it time for AI-supported parental shared decision-making in the neonatal intensive care unit?
Apparent competence, hidden influence: why Gillick competence requires a digital contextual framework
